the-agent-loop.explain:
## What it is

An **agent loop** is the control cycle that turns a language model into something that acts. The model looks at the goal and everything seen so far, decides the next step, the program executes that step, and the observation is appended. Then it repeats until the model returns a final answer with no tool request, or a guard stops it.

The loop is not the model. The loop is *your* runtime: it builds the message list, offers the tool list, executes calls, enforces caps, and decides what “done” means. The model is the policy inside that fence.

Write it as: `messages = [system, user_goal]`; call the model; if tool calls exist, run them and append results; else stop. That is the whole primitive. Frameworks add graphs, memory and interrupts on top of this cycle.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the first box interviewers want drawn. “How does an agent work?” is answered by naming decide → act → observe → repeat, then naming the forced exits. Teams that cannot draw the loop cannot debug it: they treat a 40-step runaway as a prompt problem instead of a missing cap.

On the job the loop is also the cost model. Each iteration is another model call plus tool latency. A support investigation that takes 12 steps is not “one chat”; it is 12 completions and whatever the tools billed. If you cannot explain that, you cannot forecast cost or pick a step budget.

The senior line is: the model chooses the branch at run time; ordinary code would have written the branch. That flexibility is why open-ended work is possible, and why the fence must live in code.

## How it works + one small example

Build the smallest loop that can search and then answer.

1. System text: goal, available tools, stop rule.
2. User: “Why did invoice 4419 fail validation last night?”
3. Model requests `get_logs(job_id=4419)`.
4. Runtime runs it, appends 2k tokens of logs (already truncated).
5. Model requests `get_schema("invoice")`.
6. Runtime returns the field list.
7. Model writes a final paragraph with no tool call. Stop.

Log each turn: step index, tool name, arguments hash, result tokens, cumulative cost. When the same `(tool, args)` appears twice, inject “you already did this; try a different query or finish” and continue toward the cap.

Natural exit: final text. Forced exits: max steps, max tokens, max wall time, user cancel. Always keep both.

## Failure modes

1. **No cap.** The model retries a useless search until money or context dies. A prompt that says “be concise” is not a stop condition.

2. **Unbounded history.** Every tool dump stays in the window. By step 15 the original goal is in the middle of 80k tokens and the model repeats itself.

3. **Silent tool failure.** A 500 is appended as empty text. The model invents an answer. Return a typed error the model can read, then let it choose another tool or stop.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

An agent loop is decide, act, observe, repeat. I own the runtime: I execute tools, I cap steps and cost, and I keep a trace. The model picks the next action; the fence that stops a runaway is code, not a polite system sentence.

## A concrete walk-through

A coding agent on a red CI job runs 9 steps: read the failure, open two files, edit, rerun tests, edit again, tests green, write a summary. Median cost $0.31. The same agent without a cap once ran 71 steps after a flaky test, $6.40, and produced nothing. You add max_steps=20, identical-call detection, and a partial-answer exit. The next flaky run stops at 12 with “tests still flaky after two reruns; here is the patch so far.”

## Interview follow-up

They ask whether the model should decide when to stop. Say: it proposes stop by emitting a final answer, but I always keep a hard cap. I do not outsource the budget to the policy.

## What I would measure

Steps per successful task, forced-stop rate, identical-call rate, tokens and dollars per success, and whether every run has a complete trace.
keyPoints: Loop: decide, act, observe, repeat until a final answer or a guard.
The model is the policy; the runtime executes and enforces limits.
Natural exit is a final message; forced exits are step, cost, time, cancel.
Each iteration is a billed model call plus tool latency.
Detect identical repeated calls and return typed tool errors.
A trace of every step is part of the product, not optional logging.

questions.q: What are the steps of one iteration of an agent loop and when does it end?
questions.a: Call the model with goal, history and tool definitions; if it requests tools, execute them and append the observations; call again. It ends when the model returns a final answer with no tool request, or when a guard such as max steps, token budget or timeout stops it.

questions.q: Your agent keeps calling the same search tool with the same query forever. What do you check and add?
questions.a: Check whether the tool result is unhelpful or truncated so the model cannot progress, and whether history shows the repetition. Add a max-step cap, detection of identical repeated calls, an error or hint message fed back, and a fallback that returns a partial answer. Log the trace.

questions.q: Why is an agent loop more expensive than a single call for the same user question?
questions.a: Each decide step is another completion. Tool results are fed back as more input tokens. Cost and latency scale with step count, so you forecast from median and p95 steps, not from one-call prices.

questions.q: A teammate wants the model to stop “when it is done” with no max steps. What do you reply?
questions.a: The model can propose a final answer, but a hopeful stop is not a budget. Keep a hard step, time and cost cap in the runtime and return a partial result when they fire.

questions.q: Where should you log the identity of each tool call in the loop?
questions.a: In a per-run trace: step index, tool name, argument hash, result size, error class, cumulative tokens. That is how you diagnose loops and cost spikes later.

call-vs-chain-vs-workflow-vs-agent.explain:
## What it is

These four sit on a spectrum of **who owns control flow**.

- **Single call:** one prompt, one response. Classification, extraction, a short rewrite.
- **Chain:** a fixed sequence of calls. Output of one is input to the next. The path is hard-coded.
- **Workflow:** a code-defined graph: branches, routers, parallel fan-out, loops with fixed conditions. Models fill the nodes; a developer wrote the edges.
- **Agent:** the model decides which step or tool comes next and when to stop.

Moving right buys flexibility. It costs predictability, latency, money and testability. A chain with a router is often most of what a team casually calls an agent. The interview distinction is not “does it use tools?” — both a workflow and an agent can. The distinction is whether the next edge was written by you or sampled by the model.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Picking too far right is the most common agent failure in production. A refund pipeline that is always verify → compute → write does not need a model to invent the order. Giving it an open loop adds variance, 10× cost tails, and a compliance story you cannot tell.

Interviewers use this spectrum as a filter. Junior answers name products. Senior answers say: I start at the leftmost option that solves the task and move right only when the step count or branching is genuinely unknown. Then they give a concrete counter-example: an agent on a three-step ETL job.

## How it works + one small example

Take “extract fields from an invoice PDF, validate, store.”

- Call: one shot that tries to do all three. Cheap, brittle, no validation.
- Chain: extract call → validate function → store. Known order.
- Workflow: same chain plus a retry branch on validation failure and a human node if the amount exceeds a threshold.
- Agent: the model may extract, then search email, then re-extract, then store, in any order.

You ship the workflow. You keep an agent only for “this PDF is a mess, figure out which source system it came from,” which is open-ended. Measure both on the same fifty invoices.

## Failure modes

1. **Agent as default.** Demo-driven teams wrap every feature in a loop. Cost and failure variance show up after launch.

2. **Confusing tools with agency.** A workflow that calls tools is still a workflow. Control flow ownership is the test.

3. **No rollback plan.** Once you ship an agent, replacing it with a workflow feels like a demotion. Keep the eval set so you can prove the simpler graph wins.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Call, chain, workflow, agent — ordered by who decides the next step. I start left and move right only when the path cannot be written down. Tools do not make it an agent; an unknown graph does.

## A concrete walk-through

A teammate proposes an agent for nightly invoice filing. You time a workflow: 3 calls, p95 8s, $0.04, 98% schema-valid. A prototype agent: median 6 calls, p95 28, $0.22, 91% valid because it sometimes skips validation. You keep the workflow and add a validation retry. The agent idea is parked for a different task: unknown vendor portals.

## Interview follow-up

They say “but the format might change.” Reply: then add a router or a new branch when you see the new format. Do not pay agent variance for a change you have not seen.

## What I would measure

Calls per task, p95 latency, cost per success, schema-valid rate, and how often the agent takes a path a workflow would not have taken.
keyPoints: Spectrum: call, chain, workflow, agent, defined by who owns control flow.
Tools can appear on a workflow; they do not make it an agent.
Each step right adds flexibility and costs predictability and money.
Start at the leftmost pattern that solves the job.
A chain plus a router is often enough.
Keep an eval so you can prove a simpler graph is better.

questions.q: Distinguish a workflow from an agent in one or two sentences.
questions.a: In a workflow the developer defines the graph of steps and branches in code and models fill the nodes; in an agent the model decides dynamically which action to take next and when to finish. The difference is where control flow lives, not whether tools are used.

questions.q: A feature extracts fields from an invoice, validates them, and files them. Which pattern and why?
questions.a: A chain or small workflow: the steps are known and fixed, so hard-coded order gives lower latency, cost and failure variance, plus easy testing. An agent would add uncertainty without benefit.

questions.q: A product manager calls any tool-using LLM an agent. How do you correct that?
questions.a: Ask who chooses the next step. If code does, it is a workflow or chain. If the model does, it is an agent. Tool use is orthogonal.

questions.q: You replaced a workflow with an agent and p95 cost rose 8×. What do you check first?
questions.a: Step-count distribution and whether the extra steps change the outcome. If the path is still the same three steps most of the time, revert to a workflow and keep an agent only for the unknown remainder.

questions.q: When is a single call the right choice?
questions.a: When one prompt can produce a constrained output (label, short extract, rewrite) and you do not need intermediate tools or branches. Measure accuracy before adding steps.

where-agents-are-useful.explain:
## What it is

Agents earn their cost when the task has an **unknown number of steps**, **branching that depends on intermediate results**, and **tools that gather information or act**. The problem is open-ended, but the result is checkable, and the value per task justifies several model calls.

Good fits: coding agents that read, edit and rerun tests; research that follows leads; support or ops triage that looks up an account then logs; browser tasks whose path depends on the page.

Poor fits: latency-critical paths, high-volume cheap classification, catastrophic actions without approval, and any procedure you can write down in advance. A rename of one field in one file is not an agent task.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you avoid building a theatre agent. Stakeholders see a demo that “just figures it out” and want that on every ticket. Your job is to name the properties that make the extra variance worth paying for: unknown path, tools, verifiable outcome, high enough value.

Interviewers will ask “where would you *not* use an agent?” A strong answer lists latency, fixed procedures, and irreversible actions, then asks how you would know it worked. If you cannot name a check (tests, a lookup, a human), you do not have an agent task; you have a hope.

## How it works + one small example

Score a candidate task on five axes: unknown step count, branching on observations, tools required, checkable result, value per task. Need most of them.

Example: “investigate this failing flaky test in a repo we have not seen.” Steps unknown, tools (read, grep, run), result checkable (test pass or a bounded report), value high. Agent.

Counter-example: “classify this email into five buckets.” One call, known label set, cheap. Not an agent.

If the score is mixed — known skeleton, unknown middle — use a workflow with one agentic node for the middle.

## Failure modes

1. **Uncheckable success.** “Research this market” with no rubric becomes a fluent essay. Define what “done” looks like first.

2. **Low-value high-volume.** An agent on every password-reset email will lose money even if it is cute.

3. **Catastrophic tools without a gate.** An agent that can refund or delete is not “useful”; it is a risk unless approval sits in the runtime.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use an agent when the path is unknown, tools exist, and I can check the result. I do not use one for fixed procedures, tiny edits, or latency-critical calls. Value per task has to pay for several completions.

## A concrete walk-through

Product wants an agent to rename `customer_id` to `account_id` in one handler. You decline: one search-and-replace plus a test is cheaper and safer. The same week they ask for “find every usage across 40 services and fix what breaks.” That scores well: unknown files, tests as the check, high value. You build the agent with a step cap and a dry-run diff.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how you know the agent worked. Say the check before the architecture: tests green, a ground-truth lookup, or a human review queue. No check, no agent.

## What I would measure

Task-success rate against the check, steps and cost per success, and the fraction of incoming work that actually needed an unknown path.
keyPoints: Good agent tasks: unknown steps, observation-dependent branching, tools, a check.
Value per task must justify multiple model calls.
Coding, research, triage and browser work are common fits.
Avoid latency-critical, high-volume cheap, or fixed-procedure work.
Define the success check before you build the loop.
A hybrid workflow-plus-agent-node covers mixed tasks.

questions.q: What properties of a task make an agent a good fit?
questions.a: Unknown or variable steps, branching that depends on intermediate observations, tools to read or act, a verifiable outcome, and enough value per task to pay for many model calls.

questions.q: A product manager wants an agent to rename a field in a form handler. Is that a good agent task? Justify.
questions.a: Usually not: it is a small, well-defined edit. Agents suit exploratory multi-step work such as finding all usages and running tests. Reason about cost, variance and verification.

questions.q: How would you know a research agent actually worked?
questions.a: Define a rubric or checklist before the run: required sources, claims that must be cited, a length or format constraint. Score against that, not against whether the prose sounded confident.

questions.q: Support wants an agent on every incoming chat. What do you ask first?
questions.a: What fraction of chats have an unknown path versus a known workflow, what the per-chat value is, and what the success check is. Most chats should stay on a workflow or a single call.

questions.q: Name one hybrid that is better than a pure agent for mixed work.
questions.a: A workflow skeleton that handles the known steps in code, with one agentic node only for the open-ended investigation, under a step cap.

when-a-workflow-is-better.explain:
## What it is

Prefer a **workflow** when you can write the steps down. That is the default in most production guidance. A workflow is a code-defined graph: prompt chaining, routing, parallel fan-out, an orchestrator-worker with a fixed plan, or an evaluator-optimizer with a capped retry count.

Choose it when the procedure is known and stable; when you need predictable latency and cost; when auditors want to see the path; when nodes must be unit-testable; when a model decision must be bounded (a router with a closed label set).

Workflows break on inputs the designer did not foresee. Agents degrade more gracefully and less predictably. A hybrid is common: a workflow skeleton with one agentic node where exploration is required.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the answer that saves a quarter. Teams reach for an agent because it demos well, then spend months fighting 20× cost variance. Saying “workflow first” in a design review is a seniority signal.

Interviewers will hand you a vaguely agent-shaped story (support, KYC, invoice). They want you to pull the known steps out and put them in code. If you immediately say “ReAct loop,” you have failed the product question even if the loop is technically correct.

## How it works + one small example

Write the happy path as a list. If you can, it is a workflow.

KYC: collect documents → extract fields → sanctions screen → risk score → decision. The order does not depend on a surprise observation. Implement nodes, add a retry on extract-fail, add a human node above a risk threshold. The model lives inside extract and maybe score, not in the edges.

Only if a step is “read whatever the customer uploaded and figure out which process this is” do you add an agentic router that *then* enters a known workflow.

## Failure modes

1. **Agent for SLA work.** A path that must finish in 3 seconds cannot be “up to 40 steps.”

2. **Un-testable nodes.** If you cannot unit-test extract and screen separately, you will not know which step failed.

3. **Hidden agent inside a “workflow” framework.** A graph with an unconstrained tool-calling node is still an agent. Name it honestly and cap it.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

If I can write the steps, I write a workflow. I want predictable cost, a path I can audit, and nodes I can test. I keep an agent only for the part I truly cannot draw in advance.

## A concrete walk-through

An “agent” that files insurance claims wanders through email search half the time. You extract the stable sequence (parse → validate → reserve number → store) into a graph. The agent remains only for “this attachment is not a claim form.” p95 latency drops from 47s to 9s and audit can replay the path.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about unexpected inputs. Say: workflows fail closed on unseen cases; that is a feature if you have a fallback queue. I would rather a known miss than a silent wander.

## What I would measure

Fraction of traffic that stays on the known graph, p95 latency and cost versus the agent prototype, and unit-test coverage of each node.
keyPoints: Default to a workflow when the steps are known and stable.
Workflows give predictable cost, latency, tests and audit trails.
Bound model decisions (closed routers) rather than open loops.
Hybrid: workflow skeleton plus one capped agentic node.
An unconstrained tool node inside a graph is still an agent.
Failing closed on unseen inputs is often better than wandering.

questions.q: Give three reasons to pick a workflow over an agent.
questions.a: Predictable latency and cost, easier testing and auditing because you know the path, and bounded failure at constrained decision points.

questions.q: You have an agent whose cost per task varies 20× and sometimes wanders. How might you restructure it?
questions.a: Hard-code the stable parts as a workflow; keep an agentic node only for the open-ended step, with a step cap. Add routing for known cases and evaluate before and after.

questions.q: A compliance officer asks which path a decision took. What architecture answers that?
questions.a: A workflow whose edges are in code and whose run is logged node by node. An open agent loop can only offer a post-hoc trace of sampled decisions.

questions.q: When does a workflow become the wrong tool?
questions.a: When the next step truly depends on observations you cannot enumerate, and a check exists for the end state. Then add an agentic node or a separate agent, still capped.

questions.q: Your graph framework lets any node call any tool. What did you just build?
questions.a: An agent with extra ceremony. Treat it as an agent: caps, traces, evals. Do not claim workflow predictability.

the-components-of-an-agent.explain:
## What it is

An agent is a few cooperating parts around a model:

- **Model (policy):** chooses the next action from context.
- **Instructions:** role, goals, rules, output format, when to propose stop.
- **Tools:** typed functions to read or act.
- **State / memory:** the running messages plus anything persisted.
- **Control loop (runtime):** executes calls, enforces limits, handles errors, trims context.
- **Stopping conditions:** natural (final answer) and forced (caps, cancel).
- **Guardrails and permissions:** who may call what, approvals, output checks.
- **Observability:** traces of every step.

Planner, verifier and sub-agents are patterns built from the same parts. When something misbehaves, localise the part: wrong tool is descriptions; forgotten fact is memory; endless loop is the runtime.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Drawing these boxes is the interview. A candidate who says “it’s just a prompt with tools” cannot assign a bug. A candidate who points at instructions versus runtime versus tool schema can.

On the job this list is also the staffing list. Prompt work is not the same as the runtime that persists state, and neither is the permission layer. Treat them as separate owners or they will all rot in one notebook.

## How it works + one small example

Debug by component.

Symptom: answers are right, tool choice is wrong half the time. Inspect tool names, descriptions, and how many tools are offered. Not the model size.

Symptom: it forgets a constraint from turn 1 after a long tool dump. Inspect state: was the constraint pinned or only in narrative history that got trimmed?

Symptom: it runs 40 steps. Inspect the runtime: missing max steps, no identical-call detector.

Write a one-page diagram with those boxes before you pick a framework. The framework must map onto them, not hide them.

## Failure modes

1. **One blob.** Prompt, tools, memory and caps live in a single function. You cannot test or replace a part.

2. **Guardrails only in the prompt.** “Do not delete” in instructions is not a permission. The runtime must not expose the delete tool, or must require a confirm.

3. **No trace.** Without step logs you cannot tell instructions from runtime failure.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I draw model, instructions, tools, state, loop, stops, permissions and traces. Bugs get assigned to a box. Frameworks are implementations of those boxes, not a substitute for naming them.

## A concrete walk-through

A refund agent pays twice. You walk the boxes: instructions said “only once”; the model requested pay twice; the runtime had no idempotency key and no approval node. You add a permission gate and an idempotency store. The prompt did not change. The incident was a missing component, not a “bad model.”

## Interview follow-up

They ask which component is the agent. Say: none of them alone. The agent is the composition. The policy without a loop is a call; the loop without permissions is a hazard.

## What I would measure

Tool-selection accuracy, constraint-retention after trim, forced-stop rate, approval-gate hit rate, and percent of runs with a complete component-level trace.
keyPoints: Core parts: model, instructions, tools, state, loop, stops.
Guardrails and traces are production components, not extras.
Debug by locating the failing box.
Planner and sub-agents are patterns on the same parts.
Permissions belong in the runtime, not only in the prompt.
Draw the boxes before you pick a framework.

questions.q: List the main components of an LLM agent and what each is responsible for.
questions.a: Model decides next action; instructions define role and rules; tools provide capabilities; memory/state holds history and persisted facts; the runtime loop executes calls and enforces limits; stops, guardrails and tracing keep it bounded and debuggable.

questions.q: The agent answers correctly but calls the wrong tool half the time. Which component do you inspect first?
questions.a: Tool definitions: names, descriptions and schemas, and whether too many overlap. Then instructions on when to use each. Measure tool-selection accuracy.

questions.q: Where should a “do not email the customer” rule be enforced?
questions.a: In permissions: do not expose the send tool, or require an approval interrupt. The instruction is documentation; the runtime is enforcement.

questions.q: A framework advertises “memory.” What do you still have to design?
questions.a: What is written, what is retrieved, what is forgotten, and what is pinned versus summarised. The product still owns those policies.

questions.q: Why list stopping conditions as their own component?
questions.a: Because “the model will stop” is not a design. You need explicit natural and forced exits with a partial-answer path.

state-tools-policy-and-the-loop.explain:
## What it is

Before you draw a fancy architecture, name four pieces: **state**, **tools**, **policy**, and **the loop**.

- **State** is what the system remembers this run (and maybe across runs): messages, scratchpad, pinned constraints, retrieved notes.
- **Tools** are the typed actions the policy is allowed to request.
- **Policy** is the model (plus instructions) that maps state to the next tool call or a final answer.
- **The loop** is the runtime that applies the policy, executes tools, writes new state, and stops.

Every agent diagram, including multi-agent and graph frameworks, is a rearrangement of these four. If you cannot point to them, you are drawing brands.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the whiteboard test. Interviewers watch whether you start with boxes that have owners or with product names. State/tools/policy/loop maps onto any stack: a hand-rolled Python while-loop, LangGraph, an Agents SDK, ADK.

On the job the four-piece list stops arguments. “The agent forgot” is a state problem. “It called refund instead of preview” is tools plus policy. “It never stopped” is the loop. You assign the ticket to the right layer.

## How it works + one small example

Sketch a one-run refund helper.

State: customer id, amount, already_previewed flag, message list.
Tools: `lookup_customer`, `preview_refund`, `execute_refund` (gated).
Policy: a mid-size model with instructions that require preview before execute.
Loop: while steps < 8: call policy; run tools; if execute requested without approval, interrupt; if final answer, break.

That sketch is enough to implement. Adding “Crew” or “Graph” later should not change the four names, only how they are stored and scheduled.

## Failure modes

1. **State in the prompt only.** A flag that lives in prose will be dropped by a summary. Put durable flags in structured state.

2. **Tools without a policy boundary.** Exposing execute_refund to the same policy that talks to the user is how accidental payouts happen.

3. **Loop as an afterthought.** A notebook that calls the model twice is not a loop with stops. You will ship it and then invent caps in a panic.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I name state, tools, policy and loop before I draw anything else. Frameworks implement those four. Bugs get filed against one of them, not against “the agent.”

## A concrete walk-through

You join a team whose diagram is twelve brand logos. You redraw: state in Redis, tools as ordinary functions, policy as the model call, loop as a worker with a cap. Two logos disappear because they duplicated the loop. The incident rate drops because people now know where to put a flag.

## Interview follow-up

They ask where memory lives. Say: memory is a kind of state with a write/retrieve/forget policy. I still start with the four pieces; memory is a refinement of state.

## What I would measure

Whether a new hire can map the running system onto the four boxes in ten minutes, and whether incident tickets name a box.
keyPoints: Four pieces: state, tools, policy, loop.
State is structured memory for this run (and maybe later).
Tools are the allowed actions; policy chooses among them.
The loop applies policy, executes, writes state, and stops.
Frameworks rearrange these four; they do not replace them.
File bugs against a piece, not against “the agent.”

questions.q: Name the four pieces you should list before drawing an agent architecture.
questions.a: State, tools, policy and the loop. State is what is remembered, tools are allowed actions, policy chooses the next action, the loop executes and stops.

questions.q: A payout ran twice. Which of the four pieces do you inspect first and why?
questions.a: State (was an already_paid flag missing?) and the loop (did a retry replay execute?). Then tools (was execute idempotent?). Policy last.

questions.q: Where does “the model” sit in the four-piece list?
questions.a: Inside policy, together with the instructions that constrain it. The model is not the loop and not the tool implementations.

questions.q: You are asked to add long-term memory. Which piece changes?
questions.a: State: you add a store and retrieve/forget rules. The loop must call retrieve at the right time. Tools might include an explicit remember/forget tool. Policy learns when to use them.

questions.q: Why is this list more useful than naming a framework first?
questions.a: Because any framework must implement the same four, and incidents map to them. Brands do not tell you where a flag or a cap lives.

interview.explain:
## What it is

The interview line is short: **use an agent when the next step is unknown; use a workflow when the graph is known.** That is the whole distinction that most hiring loops want, said in one breath.

Unknown means you cannot write the edges in advance: the next lookup depends on what the last tool returned, and the number of lookups is not fixed. Known means you can list the nodes and the branches (including “retry extract,” “send to human if amount > X”).

Do not hide behind product names. If they say “but LangGraph…”, answer: LangGraph can implement either. The question is whether *you* wrote the edges or the model is choosing them.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This question appears in almost every applied-LLM loop once the interviewer is done with RAG. They are testing taste, not memorised APIs. A candidate who always picks an agent sounds like a tutorial. A candidate who always picks a workflow sounds timid. A candidate who states the rule and then applies it to *their* prompt wins.

On the job the same sentence is how you push back on a demo-driven design without looking obstructionist. You are not anti-agent. You are matching structure to uncertainty.

## How it works + one small example

Practice on three prompts you will actually get.

1. “Classify tickets.” Graph known → workflow or a single call.
2. “Debug this failing job across unknown services.” Next step unknown → agent, capped.
3. “Refund a customer.” Graph known (verify → compute → pay) with a human gate → workflow, not an open agent.

Add the extra clause they like: I start left on the call/chain/workflow/agent spectrum and move right only when evidence says the path cannot be written. Then I name the check and the cap.

## Failure modes

1. **Name-dropping.** “We would use CrewAI” is not an answer. They asked when, not which logo.

2. **Unknown as a vibe.** “The world is messy” is not evidence the graph is unknown. Show a step you cannot enumerate.

3. **Forgetting the cap.** Even the agent branch of the answer must mention step/cost limits and a success check.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Agent when the next step is unknown; workflow when I can draw the graph. I start simple, I name a check, and I cap the loop. Frameworks implement that choice; they are not the choice.

## A concrete walk-through

In a mock interview you are given “onboard a vendor.” You split it: collect docs and write records is a workflow; “this PDF is in a language and layout we have never seen” is an agentic node. The interviewer asks why not one agent. You say the known steps have SLAs and an audit path; the unknown part is bounded. You get the follow-up offer to draw the graph.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for a time you picked wrong. Have one: you shipped an agent on invoice filing, cost tails were ugly, you rewrote the happy path as a workflow. That story is stronger than a perfect taxonomy.

## What I would measure

Whether you can classify five real product tickets in two minutes each, and whether your last design doc used this sentence in the first page.
keyPoints: Agent when the next step is unknown; workflow when the graph is known.
Unknown means you cannot enumerate the edges in advance.
Frameworks can implement either; they do not decide.
Start left on the spectrum; move right with evidence.
Always name the success check and the cap on the agent branch.
A short story of picking wrong and rewriting beats a taxonomy.

questions.q: What one-sentence rule do you use to choose an agent versus a workflow?
questions.a: Use an agent when the next step is unknown; use a workflow when you can write the graph. Mention a check and a cap for the agent case.

questions.q: The interviewer says “we use LangGraph so it is an agent.” How do you respond?
questions.a: LangGraph can run a fixed graph or an open tool loop. The question is whether the edges are written in code or chosen by the model at run time.

questions.q: Apply the rule to a refund that always verifies identity first.
questions.a: The graph is known: verify → compute → (approve) → pay. That is a workflow with a human node. An open agent would be the wrong control-flow owner.

questions.q: What extra clause should you add after the one-liner?
questions.a: I start at the simplest pattern that works and move right only when the path cannot be predetermined. I define the success check and a step/cost cap.

questions.q: You cannot yet tell if the path is known. What do you do in the interview?
questions.a: Say you would time-box a workflow for the happy path and keep a capped agent for residue, then measure which traffic actually needs the agent.

the-user-visible-contract.explain:
## What it is

Users did not buy a hidden chain of thought. The contract they can see is **progress**, **cancel**, and a **final artefact**. Progress means a user-safe title for the current step (“searching orders,” “drafting the reply”), not a dump of private reasoning. Cancel means the work actually stops and you report what already happened. The final artefact is the thing they asked for: a patch, a report, a filed ticket — plus sources or diffs when that is the product.

Private scratchpads, tool dumps and model reasoning stay in the trace for operators. Mixing those into the UI is not honesty; it is leakage and noise. If you cannot point to the progress event, the cancel path, and the stored artefact on a whiteboard, you do not yet have a user-visible contract.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Long-running agents fail socially before they fail technically. A four-minute silent spinner feels broken. A stream of raw “I am thinking…” can leak chain-of-thought or tool arguments that contain other customers’ data. A finish with no artefact (“done”) is not a product.

Interviewers who have shipped agents will ask what the user sees at minute two. If your answer is “the model’s thoughts,” you have not designed a contract. If your answer is steps, cancel, and the file they wanted, you have.

## How it works + one small example

Define three event types the UI understands:

- `step_started`: {id, title, started_at}
- `step_finished`: {id, title, summary, artefact_ref?}
- `run_terminal`: {status: done|cancelled|failed|budget, artefact, already_happened[]}

Map internal tool names to titles (`execute_sql` → “Querying billing”). Never stream raw arguments that might contain PII. On cancel, stop scheduling new tools, wait for in-flight work with a timeout, and fill `already_happened`.

The artefact is stored independently of the chat transcript so a refresh still finds it.

## Failure modes

1. **Spinner-only UX.** Users refresh and you lose the run because it was tied to a tab.

2. **Raw reasoning.** You expose a scratchpad that includes another tenant’s id from a tool dump.

3. **Cancel that does not cancel.** The worker keeps paying or emailing. Cancel is a runtime feature, not a button decoration.

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The user-visible contract is progress they can understand, a cancel that works, and a final artefact they can take away. I do not ship a hidden chain of thought as the product.

## A concrete walk-through

A research agent used to stream 2k tokens of planning. Legal asked you to stop. You replace the stream with four titles, a source list, and a downloadable memo. Cancel now writes “stopped after reading 6 sources; memo has the partial notes.” Support tickets about “is it stuck?” drop by half.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if hiding reasoning reduces trust. Say: trust comes from inspectable steps and sources, not from inner monologue. I show citations and the artefact.

## What I would measure

Time-to-first-step-event, cancel success rate, artefact retrieval after refresh, and tickets that say “is it stuck?” or “what did it do?”.
keyPoints: User contract: progress, cancel, final artefact.
Progress is user-safe titles, not private reasoning.
Cancel must stop work and report what already happened.
Store the artefact independently of the chat widget.
Map internal tool names before they hit the UI.
Traces stay for operators; the UI stays boring and clear.

questions.q: What three things should a user see from a long-running agent?
questions.a: Progress as safe step titles, a working cancel, and a final artefact (plus sources or diffs as appropriate). Not a hidden chain of thought.

questions.q: A PM wants to stream the model’s raw reasoning for “transparency.” What do you raise?
questions.a: Leakage of tool arguments and other users’ data, unstable UX, and that trust is better served by step titles, sources and the artefact.

questions.q: User hits cancel after a refund tool already succeeded. What must the UI say?
questions.a: That further steps stopped and that the refund already happened, with the id. Do not claim a full rollback you cannot do.

questions.q: Why store the artefact outside the chat transcript?
questions.a: So a refresh, a second device, or a later audit can retrieve the file or ticket without replaying the run.

questions.q: How do you turn `execute_sql` into progress the user can see?
questions.a: Map it to a safe title such as “Querying your orders,” never show the raw SQL or row dumps in the default UI.

the-react-pattern.explain:
## What it is

**ReAct** (Reason + Act) interleaves a short reasoning step with an action and an observation: Thought, Action, Observation, repeat. The model writes what it intends to do, calls a tool, reads the result, and reasons again.

**Example (illustrative):** goal "Which team won in the year the Eiffel Tower opened?" Thought: need the year. Action: search("Eiffel Tower opening year"). Observation: 1889. Thought: now look up the champion. Action: search(...). Observation: ... Final answer.

**Why it works:** reasoning grounded in fresh observations beats reasoning from memory alone (fewer hallucinated facts), and acting guided by explicit reasoning beats blind tool use. Reasoning also makes traces readable.

**Modern note:** with native tool calling and reasoning models, the pattern is often implicit: the model emits optional thinking text plus structured tool calls. The loop shape is the same.

**How it goes wrong:** the thought rationalises a wrong plan, errors in an early observation propagate, the model loops on the same action, and long traces eat context. Interviewers like: "What is the difference between ReAct and chain-of-thought?" CoT reasons without acting; ReAct reasons and acts on the world.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

ReAct is the pattern interviewers name when they ask how an agent thinks. The useful claim is not the acronym. It is that reasoning without a tool is just chain-of-thought, and a tool without a reason is a blind call. Interleaving them grounds the next thought in an observation.

On the job this is also the trace format operators can read. A list of tool names is not enough; a thought that says why this search, then the observation, then the next thought, is how you debug a wrong turn at step 4.

## How it works + one small example

Keep the loop even when the provider hides “Thought” inside a reasoning channel.

Example: “Which team won the year the Eiffel Tower opened?”
1. Thought: I need the year. Action: search(“Eiffel Tower opened”). Observation: 1889.
2. Thought: look up the champion that year. Action: search(“1889 league champion”). Observation: … 
3. Final answer with both facts cited.

Modern APIs emit structured tool calls plus optional thinking text. Your runtime still does Action → Observation. If thoughts are hidden, log the tool name, arguments and a one-line “why” you ask the model to put in a comment field so the trace stays readable.

## Failure modes

1. **Thought that ignores the last observation. The model rationalises a plan it already liked. Make errors loud and instruct it to address the observation first.**

2. **Action with no thought and no argument check. You cannot tell why it searched that string.**

3. **A long thought that eats the window. Cap thought tokens; the observation matters more.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

ReAct is thought, action, observation, repeat. CoT reasons without acting. I keep the loop even when thinking is implicit, and I log a why so a wrong step is visible.

## A concrete walk-through

A docs bot used to call search three times with the same query. You require a one-line thought before each call and reject identical (tool, args). Repeat rate falls from 31% to 4% and answers start citing the observation instead of memory.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if reasoning models make ReAct obsolete. Say: the channel may change; the loop does not. You still execute, observe and stop.

## What I would measure

Paired thought-action rate, identical-call rate, and success when the needed fact is not in the model’s memory.
keyPoints: ReAct interleaves thought, action and observation.
Observations ground the next thought; CoT never leaves the model.
Native tool calling keeps the same loop with implicit thoughts.
Log a why with each call so traces are readable.
Cap thought tokens; do not let reasoning crowd out observations.
Identical (tool, args) is a loop, not thoroughness.
ReAct alternates Thought, Action, Observation
Observations ground the reasoning in real data

questions.q: What does ReAct add over plain chain-of-thought?
questions.a: It interleaves reasoning with actions (tool calls) and feeds observations back, so the reasoning is grounded in external information instead of only the model's memory. This reduces hallucinated facts and allows multi-step information gathering.

questions.q: An agent's traces show confident thoughts that ignore a tool error. How do you improve it?
questions.a: Make observations unmissable (clear error text, structured status), instruct the model to address errors before proceeding, add a rule to re-plan after a failed action, and cap repeated failures. Evaluate on traces with injected tool errors.

questions.q: Why keep a thought field when the API already returns tool calls?
questions.a: Operators need a why. A tool name alone does not explain a wrong search. A one-line thought or comment field makes step 4 debuggable.

questions.q: When would you skip an explicit thought step?
questions.a: Tiny single-tool tasks where the call is obvious and latency matters. You still log the action and observation.

writing-the-loop-by-hand-first.explain:
## What it is

Before adopting a framework, **write the agent loop yourself** in 30-60 lines. It teaches what the framework hides and makes debugging far easier.

Minimal skeleton:
- keep a `messages` list
- `for step in range(MAX_STEPS)`: call the model with tools
- append the assistant message; if no tool calls, return the text
- for each tool call: validate args, run the function in try/except, append a tool-result message tied to the call id
- after the loop, return a safe fallback

You will quickly meet the real issues: matching tool-result ids to calls, serialising errors, truncating big results, logging each step, and timeouts.

**Why it matters:** frameworks (LangGraph, agent SDKs) add state persistence, streaming, retries and tracing, which you want eventually, but if you cannot read a raw trace you cannot judge whether the abstraction is helping.

**Interview angle:** many panels ask you to code this on a whiteboard. Know the stop conditions and where errors are caught.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Frameworks hide the awkward parts: call ids, error serialisation, truncation, timeouts. If you have never written the 40-line loop, you cannot tell whether LangGraph is helping or only renaming your bugs.

Interview panels still ask you to sketch this on a whiteboard. The people who pass name MAX_STEPS, try/except around tools, and one result per call id.

## How it works + one small example

Write it before you import a graph library.

```
messages = [system, user]
for step in range(MAX_STEPS):
    reply = model(messages, tools)
    messages.append(reply)
    if not reply.tool_calls:
        return reply.text
    for call in reply.tool_calls:
        try:
            out = run(call)
        except Exception as e:
            out = typed_error(e)
        messages.append(tool_result(call.id, truncate(out)))
return partial_fallback(messages)
```

You will hit: two calls in one turn, a 30k result, a timeout, a missing id. Those are the production issues. Log step, tool, arg hash, result tokens.

## Failure modes

1. **Handling only the first tool call. The second id never gets a result and the next request is invalid.**

2. **Letting exceptions escape the loop. One bad tool kills the run instead of becoming an observation.**

3. **No fallback when the cap hits. The user sees a 500 instead of a partial answer.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I write the loop by hand first: messages, cap, execute, one result per call id, truncate, fallback. Then I adopt a framework for persistence and interrupts, not for the primitive.

## A concrete walk-through

A new hire starts in LangGraph and cannot explain a missing tool result. You pair-write the 50-line loop. They find the bug: they appended one result for two calls. After that, the graph version is readable because they know the primitive.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if this is wasted time. Say: an afternoon now, or a week later when you cannot read a vendor trace.

## What I would measure

Whether every engineer on the team can write the loop from memory, and whether traces always contain one result per call id.
keyPoints: A working loop is about 40–60 lines.
Match every tool call id with exactly one result.
Catch tool errors and return them as observations.
Truncate results; cap steps; return a partial fallback.
Hand-writing it teaches what frameworks hide.
Whiteboard the stop conditions and error path.
A working loop is about 30-60 lines
Tool results must be matched to call ids

questions.q: Outline the code of a minimal tool-calling agent loop.
questions.a: Maintain a messages list; loop up to MAX_STEPS calling the model with tool definitions; append the reply; if it has no tool calls, return its text; otherwise execute each call safely with try/except, append tool-result messages keyed by call id; finally return a fallback when the cap is hit.

questions.q: Your hand-written loop crashes on a model reply with two tool calls. What is a likely bug?
questions.a: The code handles only the first tool call or fails to append a result for every call id, so the next request is invalid. Iterate over all calls, append one result per id, and run independent ones concurrently if safe.

questions.q: Your hand-written loop crashes on a reply with two tool calls. What is a likely bug?
questions.a: It handled only the first call or failed to append a result for every id. Iterate all calls and append one result each.

questions.q: Where do timeouts belong in the hand-written loop?
questions.a: Around each tool, and around the whole loop. A hung HTTP call should become a typed error observation, not a stuck worker.

questions.q: What do you implement before adding streaming or persistence?
questions.a: Correct call-id pairing, truncation, caps and a fallback. Streaming a wrong loop just streams a wrong loop.

step-by-step-vs-plan-first.explain:
## What it is

Two ways to organise an agent's thinking:

- **Step-by-step (reactive):** decide only the next action from current observations (classic ReAct). Cheap to start, adapts instantly, but can wander and lacks global structure.
- **Plan-first (plan-then-execute):** one call produces a full plan (a list of steps); an executor works through it, often with cheaper calls per step; optionally a re-plan on failure.

**Trade-offs:**
- Plan-first gives better coherence on long tasks, parallelisable steps, a human-reviewable plan, and less repeated reasoning. It is brittle when early steps reveal facts that invalidate the plan.
- Reactive handles surprises and unknown environments, but each step re-reads the entire history, costing tokens, and it may lose the thread.

**Practical default:** hybrid. Draft a short plan, execute reactively, and re-plan when an observation contradicts it. Use plan-first when steps are mostly predictable and you want approval before acting.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Choosing reactive versus plan-first is a control-flow decision, not a model-quality decision. Reactive (classic ReAct) picks only the next action. Plan-first writes a list, then executes. Interviewers want the trade-off: coherence and reviewability versus brittleness when step 1 surprises you.

On the job, plan-first is how you put a human in front of side effects. Reactive is how you survive an unknown filesystem.

## How it works + one small example

Default to a short hybrid.

1. Draft a 3–7 step plan as structured state.
2. Execute the next pending step reactively.
3. Compare observation to the step’s expected output.
4. If it contradicts, mark the plan stale and re-plan; do not blindly continue.

Use plan-first when steps are mostly known and you want approval. Use pure reactive when the environment is hostile to prediction (a live site, an unfamiliar repo). Never freeze a 20-step plan with no revision trigger.

## Failure modes

1. **A beautiful plan executed after the world changed. Step 1 returned “no such table” and steps 2–8 still ran.**

2. **Pure reactive wander on a task that had a known skeleton. Cost tails grow and you cannot show a reviewer a plan.**

3. **Re-planning every step. You paid for a plan and then threw it away.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Reactive picks the next action; plan-first writes the list. I draft a short plan, execute, and re-plan when the observation kills an assumption. I show the plan when I need approval.

## A concrete walk-through

A migration agent planned eight ALTERs. Step 1 discovered the column already existed. Without revision it kept going and failed loudly. You add a contradiction trigger and a three-step re-plan. The next run skips the exists case and finishes in four steps.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which is “more agentic.” Say: neither. Agency is unknown edges. This is how you structure thinking inside the loop.

## What I would measure

Re-plan rate, success after contradiction, and human-approval time when a plan is shown first.
keyPoints: Reactive: next action only; plan-first: list then execute.
Plans give structure and a review point; reactive adapts.
Hybrid with a contradiction trigger is the usual default.
Keep the plan as explicit state with step statuses.
Do not freeze a long plan with no revision.
Approval belongs in front of a plan, not after a surprise side effect.
Reactive: next action only; plan-first: full plan then execute
Plans give structure and reviewability; reactive gives adaptivity

questions.q: Compare plan-then-execute with step-by-step ReAct.
questions.a: Plan-then-execute drafts all steps upfront, which gives structure, reviewability and parallelism, but is brittle if early results invalidate the plan. ReAct chooses each action from fresh observations, which adapts well but can drift and costs more tokens over long runs.

questions.q: A task needs human approval before any side effect, and steps are mostly known. Which style?
questions.a: Plan-first: generate the plan, show it for approval, then execute with limited deviation and a re-plan trigger. This puts the review point before consequential actions and reduces mid-run surprises.

questions.q: The plan said “read file A then B” but A does not exist. What should happen?
questions.a: Treat it as a contradiction, mark the plan stale, and re-plan instead of executing B as if A had been read.

questions.q: When is pure reactive the better default?
questions.a: When you cannot enumerate useful steps — unfamiliar repo, live UI — and a pre-written list would be fiction.

decomposing-and-revising-plans.explain:
## What it is

**Decomposition** means breaking a goal into subtasks small enough that each one is a clear, checkable action. **Revision** means updating that plan when reality disagrees.

**Good decomposition:**
- Each subtask has an input, an expected output and a success check.
- Subtasks are ordered by dependency; independent ones are marked parallel.
- Granularity matches the tools: "search for X" is fine, "do the research" is too vague.

**Revising:**
- After each step compare the observation with the expectation.
- Triggers for re-plan: tool failure, empty or contradicting result, new information that changes scope, budget about to be exceeded.
- Keep the plan as explicit state (a list with statuses: pending, done, failed) in the context so the model sees progress.

**How it goes wrong:** over-granular plans waste calls; plans never revised after a wrong assumption; the model marks steps done without verifying. Mitigate with explicit success criteria and a verification step before marking complete.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A goal is not a step. “Research the vendor” will produce a wander. Decomposition is making each step small enough to have an input, an expected output and a check. Revision is updating the list when the check fails.

Interviewers listen for “success check” and “visible plan state.” If your plan is only prose in the prompt, it will be marked done without evidence.

## How it works + one small example

Store the plan as data: `[{id, action, expect, status}]` with statuses pending / done / failed / skipped.

Granularity matches tools: `search("SOC2 report 2025")` is a step; `do diligence` is not. Independent steps get a `parallel` flag.

Revise when: tool error, empty result, contradiction, scope change, budget nearly gone. Do not revise because the model feels like a new idea. After revision, keep completed evidence; do not redo finished checked steps.

## Failure modes

1. **Steps with no expect field. The model marks them done because it wrote a paragraph.**

2. **Over-decomposition: forty micro-steps that waste calls.**

3. **Revision that forgets done work and repeats paid tools.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I break a goal into checkable steps at tool granularity, keep the plan as state, and revise when the observation disagrees. Done means the check passed, not that the model said so.

## A concrete walk-through

“Prepare a vendor brief” becomes: fetch filings, extract risk factors, compare to last year, write two pages. Step 2 returns an empty extract. You fail that step, re-plan to try the HTML source, and keep step 1’s filings. The brief cites real excerpts.

## Interview follow-up

They ask who writes the first plan. Say: the model can draft it, but the schema and the revise triggers are mine.

## What I would measure

Fraction of steps with a check, false-done rate, and wasted-repeat rate after revision.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Fraction of steps with a check, false-done rate, and wasted-repeat rate after revision. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Each step needs input, expected output and a success check. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Each step needs input, expected output and a success check.
Granularity should match a tool call, not a wish.
Keep the plan as structured state with statuses.
Re-plan on failure, contradiction, scope or budget.
Do not redo steps whose checks already passed.
Done is verified, not declared.
Each subtask needs input, output and a success check
Re-plan on failure, contradiction, or scope change

questions.q: What makes a plan step well-formed, and when should an agent revise the plan?
questions.a: A well-formed step has a clear input, expected output, success check and sits at tool granularity. Revise on tool failure, empty or contradictory results, new information that changes scope, or budget pressure.

questions.q: The agent marks all plan steps done but the output is wrong. What process fix do you add?
questions.a: Require verification per step against its success criterion before marking done, add a final check against the original goal, and surface failed or unverified steps. Possibly use a separate verifier call.

questions.q: Why store the plan outside the chat prose?
questions.a: Prose gets summarised away and statuses get faked. A structured list survives trimming and can be shown to a reviewer.

questions.q: How do you avoid redoing finished work after a re-plan?
questions.a: Carry forward steps with passed checks and their artefacts. The new plan starts from remaining gaps.

reflection-self-correction.explain:
## What it is

**Reflection** is a step where the agent critiques its own output or trajectory and then fixes it. Patterns: generate, critique, revise (self-refine); reflect on a failed attempt and retry with the lesson in context (Reflexion-style); or a separate **critic** call.

**What works:** reflection helps most when the critique can use **external signals**: failing unit tests, a schema validator, a compiler error, retrieved evidence. The model then corrects a concrete defect.

**What does not:** pure self-critique with no new information often fails to find real errors, may talk itself out of a right answer, and costs extra calls. Models are better at fixing a flagged problem than at discovering it unaided.

**Design rules:**
- Prefer verifiable feedback over opinion.
- Cap rounds (1-3).
- Keep the critique and the revision distinct in the prompt.
- Measure: does the loop improve the pass rate on an eval set enough to justify its latency and cost?

**Interview probe:** "When would you not use reflection?" Latency-sensitive paths or tasks with no way to verify.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Reflection is a second pass that critiques a draft or a trajectory and then edits. It is fashionable and often useless. It works when the critique sees a new signal: test failures, a schema error, a compiler log, a retrieved passage. It fails when you ask the model to “think harder” at the same text.

Interviews: “when would you not reflect?” Latency paths, or no verifier.

## How it works + one small example

Separate generate, critique and revise. Cap at 1–3 rounds.

Code agent: generate → run tests → feed failures → targeted patch → rerun. That is reflection with a spine.

Support draft: generate → checklist (must mention refund window, must not promise a date) → revise. The checklist is the rubric.

Skip reflection on a classifier that already has a programmatic check. Do not add a critic model just to look serious.

## Failure modes

1. **Self-critique with no new bits. The model congratulates itself or talks itself out of a correct answer.**

2. **Unbounded rounds. Cost doubles and the third revise introduces a new bug.**

3. **Critique mixed into the same prompt as the draft so the model cannot disagree with itself.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Reflection needs a rubric or a test, not “think harder.” I cap rounds and keep critique separate from the draft. If I cannot name the signal, I do not add the call.

## A concrete walk-through

A SQL agent’s self-review never caught a missing WHERE. You pipe EXPLAIN and a row-count guard into the critique. Catch rate on the golden set goes from 12% to 61%. You drop the ungrounded “please double-check” pass.

## Interview follow-up

They mention Reflexion papers. Say: the lesson is storing a textual lesson from failure. The lesson still needs a real failure signal.

## What I would measure

Pass-rate delta with versus without reflection, extra latency, and how often round 2 changes a correct answer into a wrong one.
keyPoints: Reflection works when the critique sees external evidence.
Pure self-critique is weak and can degrade good answers.
Cap rounds at one to three and measure the gain.
Keep critique and revision as distinct steps.
Skip it on latency-sensitive or already-checked tasks.
A rubric or a test is the spine.
Reflection works best with external verification signals
Pure self-critique can miss errors or degrade correct answers

questions.q: When is reflection effective and when is it not?
questions.a: It is effective when the critique is grounded in external feedback such as test failures, validators or retrieved evidence. It is weak when the model only re-reads its own answer without new information, and it adds latency and cost either way.

questions.q: Design a reflection loop for a code-generation agent.
questions.a: Generate code, run unit tests and the linter, feed failures back as the critique, ask for a targeted fix, rerun. Cap at about three rounds, keep prior failing output in context to avoid repeating it, and return the best attempt with a failure report if tests still fail.

questions.q: Your critic pass doubles cost and accuracy is flat. What next?
questions.a: Slice the eval. Keep reflection only on the failing slice. Drop it elsewhere.

questions.q: Why separate the critic prompt from the generator prompt?
questions.a: So the critic can disagree. A single prompt tends to defend the draft it just wrote.

stopping-conditions-loop-protection.explain:
## What it is

An agent without stop rules is an unbounded bill. Use layered guards.

**Natural stop:** the model returns an answer with no tool call.

**Hard limits (code, not prompt):**
- **max steps** (iterations)
- **token or cost budget**
- **wall-clock timeout** and per-tool timeouts
- **max tool errors** in a row

**Loop detection:** hash recent (tool, args) pairs; if the same call repeats N times or results stop changing, inject a nudge ("this approach is not working, try another") and then terminate.

**Graceful exit:** on a forced stop return the best partial result, state what was not finished, and log the reason. Avoid raising an opaque error.

**Other protections:** progress checks (is the plan advancing?), human-in-the-loop escalation after repeated failures, and idempotent tools so retries are safe.

**Gotcha:** relying on the prompt ("stop after 5 tries") is not a guarantee; enforce limits in the runtime.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A loop without a fence is an unbounded bill and a stuck UI. Prompts that say “stop after five tries” are wishes. Production stop rules live in the runtime: max steps, max tokens or dollars, wall time, per-tool time, consecutive errors, identical-call detection.

This is a reliability question as much as an agent question. Interviewers want graceful exit, not just a break.

## How it works + one small example

Layer the guards.

Natural: model returns text with no tool call.
Hard: steps, cost, wall clock, N identical (tool, args), N errors in a row.
Progress: plan status must change every k steps or you nudge, then stop.

On forced stop: return the best partial artefact, list what is unfinished, log the reason. Do not 500. Idempotent tools make the last retry safe.

## Failure modes

1. **Prompt-only caps. The model miscounts and you pay for 80 steps.**

2. **Hard kill with no partial. The user loses ten minutes of work.**

3. **No identical-call detector. The same search runs until the cost cap, which is later than you wanted.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Stops are code: steps, cost, time, identical calls, cancel. The model may propose done; I always keep a fence and a partial-answer exit.

## A concrete walk-through

A research agent burned $18 overnight on a repeated empty search. You add identical-call N=2, max_steps=15, and a partial memo. The next stuck run ends at $0.40 with “three sources, search stalled.”

## Interview follow-up

They ask about user cancel. Say: it is a stop condition equal to the others, and it must report already_happened.

## What I would measure

Forced-stop rate, identical-call rate, median and p95 cost, and whether forced stops include a partial artefact.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Forced-stop rate, identical-call rate, median and p95 cost, and whether forced stops include a partial artefact. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Natural stop plus hard step, cost and time limits. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

Detect repeated identical calls and stalled plans.
Enforce limits in the runtime, not only in the prompt.
Forced stop returns a partial result and a reason.
User cancel is a first-class stop.
Idempotent tools make retries and stops safer.
Combine natural stop with hard step, cost and time limits
