questions.q: What are the pieces of a minimal MCP server?
questions.a: A server object, one or more registered tools each with name, description, input schema and handler, optionally resources and prompts, and a transport such as stdio to run it. Handlers validate input and return content or errors.

questions.q: Your stdio MCP server randomly disconnects after you add print statements. Why?
questions.a: On stdio transport stdout carries the protocol messages, so extra prints corrupt the JSON-RPC stream. Log to stderr or a file instead.

questions.q: What should a first MCP server expose?
questions.a: A small read-only slice of a real system with typed schemas and errors. Not the entire admin API.

questions.q: A host wants a destructive tool on your read server. What do you do?
questions.a: Refuse. Put writes on a separate server with tighter auth and approval.

questions.q: Why contract-test the server?
questions.a: Hosts depend on the schema. A silent field rename breaks every client at once.

questions.q: Where do you put the database password?
questions.a: In the server’s environment, never in a tool result or a resource body.

schemas-transports-auth.explain:
## What it is

**Schemas:** each tool declares an input schema (JSON Schema) and may declare an output schema. Clients use them to show the model the contract and to validate. Good schemas: required fields, enums, descriptions on every property.

**Messages:** MCP uses JSON-RPC 2.0 for requests, responses and notifications, after an initialisation handshake to negotiate protocol version and capabilities.

**Transports:**
- **stdio:** the host launches the server as a subprocess and talks over stdin/stdout. Simple, local, no network exposure, one user.
- **Streamable HTTP** (the remote transport in current spec versions; check current docs): the server is a web service handling many clients; older HTTP+SSE variants exist.

**Auth:** local stdio servers typically inherit the user's environment and credentials. Remote servers use standards-based authorization (OAuth 2.x flows in the spec) so the user grants scoped access, with tokens validated by the server. Never pass user tokens through to downstream APIs blindly (confused-deputy risk).

**Trade-off:** stdio is easy but local-only; HTTP scales and centralises but needs real auth, TLS, rate limiting and session handling.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The unglamorous half of MCP is what makes it production: JSON schemas for tools, capability flags, error codes, transports (stdio versus HTTP), and authentication for anything that is not a local child process.

Interviews: stdio for local, HTTP plus auth for remote. Never “we just opened a port.”

## How it works + one small example

Schemas: arguments and results documented; reject extra fields if you can. Capabilities: advertise only what you implemented. Errors: stable codes.

Transports: stdio — host spawns the server, stdin/stdout carry JSON-RPC, logs go to stderr. HTTP/SSE or the current remote transport — TLS, authn, authz, per-user tokens.

Auth: a remote server that sees customer data must know which user is calling. A shared service account is how tenant A sees tenant B.

## Failure modes

1. **Debug prints on stdout in stdio mode. You corrupt the protocol.**

2. **Remote server with no auth because it is “only on the VPN.”**

3. **Advertising a capability you did not implement.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Schemas, typed errors, stdio for local, HTTP plus real auth for remote. Logs go to stderr. Per-user tokens, not one shared key.

## A concrete walk-through

A stdio server broke when someone added `print(debug)`. You move logs to stderr and the host reconnects. Later the same server goes remote; you add OAuth with audience checks before it sees prod data.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about API keys in query strings. Say: no. Header or signed token, rotated, scoped.

## What I would measure

Protocol parse errors, unauthenticated remote calls blocked, and token-scope violations in tests.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Protocol parse errors, unauthenticated remote calls blocked, and token-scope violations in tests. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Tool schemas are part of the contract. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Tool schemas are part of the contract.
Stdio: protocol on stdin/stdout, logs on stderr.
Remote: TLS and per-user auth, not a shared key.
Advertise only implemented capabilities.
Stable error codes beat stack traces in results.
VPN is not authentication.
JSON Schema defines tool contracts; messages are JSON-RPC
stdio for local, Streamable HTTP for remote servers

questions.q: Compare stdio and HTTP transports for MCP.
questions.a: Stdio runs the server as a local subprocess: simple, no network surface, single user. HTTP-based transports serve remote, multi-client servers and need authentication, TLS and rate limiting, but allow shared, centrally managed services.

questions.q: A remote MCP server uses one shared API key for all users. What is the problem and the fix?
questions.a: All users act with the same authority, breaking least privilege and audit. Use per-user authorization (OAuth flow), scope tokens, validate them on each request, and log per-user actions.

questions.q: A stdio MCP server breaks as soon as you add debug prints. Likely cause?
questions.a: stdout carries protocol messages and was corrupted. Write logs to stderr.

questions.q: A remote MCP server must serve many users with different data access. What auth approach fits?
questions.a: Per-user authorization with scoped, validated tokens. Not one shared API key.

questions.q: What goes on stdin/stdout versus stderr for a local server?
questions.a: JSON-RPC on stdin/stdout; human logs on stderr.

questions.q: Why list capabilities instead of assuming every server has everything?
questions.a: Clients must not call what you did not implement. Negotiation is how mixed versions survive.

building-and-connecting-a-client.explain:
## What it is

A client lives in your host app. Using an SDK, connecting looks like:

1. Create a transport (spawn a stdio process or open an HTTP connection with credentials).
2. Create a client and **initialize**: negotiate protocol version and capabilities.
3. **List tools** (and resources/prompts) and cache them; handle list-changed notifications.
4. Convert tool definitions into the model API's tool format, prefixing names with the server to avoid collisions.
5. When the model requests a tool, **call** the right server, enforce policy, return the result as a tool result.
6. Close connections cleanly on exit.

**Host responsibilities:** user consent for calls, timeouts, reconnect handling, error mapping, truncating large results, and deciding which servers' tools to expose (a large union bloats the context and hurts selection).

**Failure modes:** server crash mid-call, tool names colliding across servers, stale cached list, hanging calls without timeouts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A client is how your host attaches to servers. Building or using one means process lifecycle (for stdio), session init, tool listing, routing calls, and merging catalogues without name clashes.

The host policy sits above the client: which servers, which tools, which user identity is forwarded.

## How it works + one small example

On session start: spawn or connect, initialize, list tools, prefix names (`crm.search_accounts`), filter by policy, convert to provider schemas.

On a model tool call: find the server by prefix, translate args, await the result, map errors. Time out. If the server dies, surface a typed error, do not crash the host.

Cache the tool list with a TTL or a change notification. Do not list_tools on every model turn if nothing changed.

## Failure modes

1. **Merging two servers that both export `search` with no namespace.**

2. **Forwarding a user token to every server including ones that should not see it.**

3. **Blocking the whole agent if one optional server is down.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The client connects, lists, namespaces and routes. The host still decides the exposed subset and the identity that is forwarded.

## A concrete walk-through

You connect CRM and Git. Both had `search`. You prefix `crm.` and `git.`. Selection recovers. When Git is down, CRM tools still work and the model sees `git unavailable`.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about sampling from the server. Say: the client may relay a sample request, but the host applies the same policy as a user-facing call.

## What I would measure

Connect success, tool-list freshness, namespace collisions, and agent success when an optional server is down.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Connect success, tool-list freshness, namespace collisions, and agent success when an optional server is down. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Initialize, list, namespace, route, time out. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Initialize, list, namespace, route, time out.
Prefix tool names when merging servers.
Do not list_tools on every turn unless needed.
One dead optional server must not kill the host.
Forward the minimum identity each server needs.
The host policy still filters the catalogue.
Initialize, list tools, convert to model tool format, route calls
Namespace tool names across servers

questions.q: Describe the steps for a client to use an MCP server's tools with an LLM.
questions.a: Create a transport, initialize and negotiate capabilities, list tools, convert them into the model's tool schema, route the model's tool request to the server via call, then return the result as a tool result and handle errors and closing.

questions.q: Two connected servers both expose a tool called 'search'. What happens and how do you handle it?
questions.a: The names collide, so routing is ambiguous. Namespace them (server__search), keep a map from exposed name to server, and give distinct descriptions so the model can choose.

questions.q: You connect 15 MCP servers and tool selection worsens. Best response?
questions.a: Expose a relevant subset per task and namespace names. Do not dump the full union into every turn.

questions.q: Two servers both expose search. What do you do?
questions.a: Namespace (`crm.search`, `git.search`) and describe the difference. Do not leave a collision.

questions.q: Should a down documentation server fail the whole agent?
questions.a: No. Mark those tools unavailable and continue with the rest.

questions.q: When do you refresh the tool list?
questions.a: On connect, on a change notification, or on a TTL — not necessarily before every model call.

permissions-untrusted-servers.explain:
## What it is

An MCP server is code and text you are letting influence the model and, via tools, your systems. Treat it like a third-party dependency plus a potential injector.

**Threats:**
- **Malicious or compromised servers:** run arbitrary local code (stdio) or exfiltrate data.
- **Tool-description injection ("tool poisoning"):** descriptions are fed to the model and can carry hidden instructions.
- **Prompt injection via results:** returned content steers the model.
- **Rug pulls:** a server changes tool behaviour after approval.
- **Confused deputy / over-broad tokens.**

**Mitigations:**
- Install only from trusted sources; pin versions; review code.
- Least-privilege credentials and sandboxing (containers, restricted filesystem and network).
- **User consent per tool call** for consequential actions, with visible arguments.
- Allowlist servers and tools; re-prompt when a tool list changes.
- Treat returned text as data; isolate untrusted content from powerful tools.
- Audit logs and rate limits.

**Interview framing:** the lethal combination is private data access plus untrusted content plus an outward channel; break at least one leg.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

An MCP server is code you did not write, seeing arguments you did not choose, returning text that will sit in the model context. That is a trust boundary. Third-party servers can exfiltrate tokens, poison descriptions (tool-description injection), or return prompt-injection text.

Interviews: treat third-party tools as hostile; scope tokens; review schemas.

## How it works + one small example

Allowlist servers. Pin versions. Review tool lists before enablement. Run servers with least privilege (read-only tokens, no access to secrets files). Sandbox local binaries. Show the user which server will run a consequential tool.

Do not forward your cloud admin role to a community server. Do not put customer PII into a server you do not have a DPA with.

Re-review when a server’s tool list changes. A new `read_env` tool is an incident.

## Failure modes

1. **Installing a trending server with default env that includes `AWS_*`.**

2. **Trusting tool descriptions as documentation rather than attacker-controlled text.**

3. **One token with `*` sent to every server.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat third-party MCP servers as untrusted code. Allowlist, least-privilege tokens, review schemas, sandbox, and re-check when the tool list changes.

## A concrete walk-through

A “helpful PDF server” adds `fetch_url`. It starts pulling internal metadata. You had allowlisted the old list only in a wiki. You pin the version, diff tool lists in CI, and revoke the token. The next add is blocked.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about open-source servers. Say: readable is not trusted. I still scope tokens and review the running revision.

## What I would measure

Servers on the allowlist, tokens with excess scopes, tool-list drift alerts, and data-egress tests.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Servers on the allowlist, tokens with excess scopes, tool-list drift alerts, and data-egress tests. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Third-party servers are untrusted code and untrusted text. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Third-party servers are untrusted code and untrusted text.
Allowlist, pin versions, diff tool lists.
