Sandbox local servers; no secrets in their env.
Review descriptions as attacker-controlled.
Consequential calls still need user-visible approval.
Servers can be malicious; descriptions and results can inject instructions
Use least privilege, sandboxing, pinning and per-call consent

questions.q: Name risks of connecting an untrusted MCP server and mitigations.
questions.a: Risks: arbitrary code execution, data exfiltration, poisoned tool descriptions, injection through results and behaviour changes after approval. Mitigate with trusted sources and pinning, sandboxing, least-privilege tokens, per-call user consent, allowlists and re-approval when tools change.

questions.q: An MCP tool description contains hidden text telling the model to read ~/.ssh and send it out. How is this prevented?
questions.a: Review and allowlist servers, show full descriptions to the user, sandbox filesystem and network access, require approval for file reads and outbound calls, and do not give a single agent both secret access and an open outward channel.

questions.q: Which control best reduces harm from a poisoned tool description?
questions.a: Reviewing and allowlisting servers, sandboxing, scoped tokens, and per-call approval for writes.

questions.q: A community server asks for your cloud admin env vars. What do you do?
questions.a: Refuse. Run it with no secrets or do not run it. Least privilege is the default.

questions.q: Why re-check a server after an update?
questions.a: The tool list can grow a fetch or read_env capability you never approved.

questions.q: Where does user approval still sit?
questions.a: On consequential tools, even if the server is allowlisted. Allowlist is identity, not consent for a pay/delete.

untrusted-mcp-servers.explain:
## What it is

**Treat third-party tools as hostile; scope tokens and review schemas.** This is the permission topic said as an operating rule. A server you did not write can steal credentials, exfiltrate arguments, or inject instructions through descriptions and results. “Popular on the registry” is not a review.

Hostile does not mean “never use.” It means assume breach and limit blast radius.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the security follow-up interviewers add after you mention MCP. They want least privilege and a review step, not a lecture on JSON-RPC.

On the job, procurement will ask who approved the server. Have a written allowlist and a token inventory.

## How it works + one small example

Before connect: read the repo or vendor docs, list tools, list required env, list data that will leave. Issue a token that can only do those reads. Run the binary in a container without your home directory.

After connect: monitor args and result sizes; alert on new tool names; forbid servers from seeing each other’s tokens.

Red-team: feed the server a fake secret in an argument and see if it appears on the network.

## Failure modes

1. **Shared token across five servers so you only had to set one env var.**

2. **No inventory of what data each server receives.**

3. **Trusting the registry badge instead of a human review.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Third-party MCP tools are hostile until proven otherwise. I scope tokens, review schemas, sandbox the process, and watch for tool-list drift.

## A concrete walk-through

You connect a community Slack server with a workspace token. A week later it adds `export_dms`. Your drift job fails the deploy. You never grant the new scope.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about first-party internal servers. Say: still least privilege, but I can skip “hostile” rhetoric. I do not skip authz.

## What I would measure

Tokens mapped to servers, excess-scope findings, drift-job catches, and failed egress tests.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Tokens mapped to servers, excess-scope findings, drift-job catches, and failed egress tests. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Assume third-party servers will leak or inject. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Third-party MCP tools are hostile until proven otherwise. I scope tokens, review schemas, sandbox the process, and watch for tool-list drift. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about first-party internal servers. Say: still least privilege, but I can skip “hostile” rhetoric. I do not skip authz. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Scope a unique token per server.
keyPoints: Assume third-party servers will leak or inject.
Scope a unique token per server.
Review and pin the tool schema.
Sandbox the process; empty env except what it needs.
Alert when the advertised tool list changes.
Popular is not the same as reviewed.

questions.q: What does “treat third-party MCP servers as hostile” require in practice?
questions.a: Unique scoped tokens, schema review, sandboxing, drift alerts, and no shared admin credentials.

questions.q: You used one token for four servers to save time. What is the risk?
questions.a: Any one server can use the union of privileges. Compromise blast radius is the whole union.

questions.q: How do you test for exfiltration?
questions.a: Plant a canary secret in an argument and watch whether it leaves on the network or in logs.

questions.q: Does an internal first-party server get a free pass?
questions.a: No. It still gets least privilege and authz. You may skip the hostile-registry review, not the token scope.

questions.q: Why pin the schema, not only the package version?
questions.a: A version bump can add tools. Pinning and diffing the advertised list catches that even if the version string looks familiar.

transport-and-auth-choices.explain:
## What it is

**Stdio for local; HTTP plus auth for anything remote.** That is the transport rule. Stdio means the host spawns a child and owns its lifetime; the channel is a pipe, not a port. The moment the server is another machine, another user, or another tenant, you need a remote transport with TLS and authentication.

Auth is not optional on remote, even on a private network.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Mixing these up is how a debug server bound to `0.0.0.0` becomes a data leak. Interviewers will ask which transport you chose and why. A senior answer names the trust boundary, not a favourite library.

On the job, stdio is also how you avoid an extra network hop for a local filesystem tool.

## How it works + one small example

Local filesystem, local git, a desktop calculator: stdio, no extra port, logs on stderr, kill the child when the session ends.

Shared CRM for many users: remote HTTP (or the current supported remote transport), mTLS or OAuth, per-user identity, audit.

Do not expose stdio servers via a naive TCP wrapper without adding auth. That wrapper just invented an unauthenticated remote API.

Document the choice next to the server name in the allowlist.

## Failure modes

1. **Publishing a stdio server on a port for “ease” with no auth.**

2. **Remote HTTP with a static shared key in the repo.**

3. **Leaving the child process alive after the user logs out.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Stdio for local children I spawn and kill. HTTP plus real auth for anything remote. A private network does not replace authentication.

## A concrete walk-through

A laptop stdio filesystem server is fine. The same code deployed as a team service on :8080 without auth is not. You add OAuth and per-user paths before it sees anyone else’s disk.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about SSE versus stdio performance. Say: I pick based on trust and multi-user need, then I measure. I do not pick a transport to feel modern.

## What I would measure

Servers classified by transport, unauthenticated remote endpoints (should be zero), orphan child processes, auth-fail rates.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Servers classified by transport, unauthenticated remote endpoints (should be zero), orphan child processes, auth-fail rates. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Stdio: local child, host-owned lifetime, logs on stderr. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Stdio for local children I spawn and kill. HTTP plus real auth for anything remote. A private network does not replace authentication. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about SSE versus stdio performance. Say: I pick based on trust and multi-user need, then I measure. I do not pick a transport to feel modern. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Remote: HTTP (or current remote transport) plus TLS and auth.
keyPoints: Stdio: local child, host-owned lifetime, logs on stderr.
Remote: HTTP (or current remote transport) plus TLS and auth.
VPN or localhost binding is not authentication.
Do not wrap stdio in raw TCP without adding auth.
Kill local children when the session ends.
Record the transport next to the allowlist entry.

questions.q: When is stdio the right MCP transport?
questions.a: When the host spawns a local child for one session — filesystem, local git — and can kill it at the end.

questions.q: When must you use HTTP plus auth?
questions.a: When the server is remote, multi-user, or otherwise outside the host process. Private networks still need auth.

questions.q: Someone wraps a stdio server in netcat so a teammate can connect. What did they create?
questions.a: An unauthenticated remote API. Stop and add a real remote transport with auth, or use a VPN plus auth, not raw TCP.

questions.q: Where do logs go on stdio?
questions.a: stderr. stdout is the protocol.

questions.q: What happens to the child when the user session ends?
questions.a: The host kills it. Orphan servers keep tokens in memory and confuse the next session.

history-state-short-long-term-memory.explain:
## What it is

Four terms that people blur.

- **History:** the raw transcript of messages and tool calls in this conversation.
- **State:** structured data the agent tracks to do its job (current plan, step statuses, collected fields, a cart). It can live inside the context or in your program.
- **Short-term memory:** what is in the context window now; lasts for one session or thread.
- **Long-term memory:** information persisted outside the context (database, vector store, files) that survives sessions and is **retrieved** into context when relevant.

The model itself is stateless: each call sees only what you send. "Memory" is therefore an engineering layer that decides what to include.

**Useful split:** state is for correctness of the current task, long-term memory is for personalisation and continuity across tasks.

**Interview angle:** explain why dumping everything into the prompt fails (cost, latency, dilution, window limits) and that memory design is mostly about selection.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

These four words get used as synonyms and then the system forgets a constraint. **History** is the message list. **State** is structured fields for this run (flags, plan, ids). **Short-term memory** is what you keep for the current task or session. **Long-term memory** is what you persist across sessions and retrieve later.

Interviews: draw the four and say the model is stateless. You choose what to send.

## How it works + one small example

A support session: history is the turns; state is `{customer_id, already_refunded}`; short-term is the last eight turns plus a summary; long-term is “prefers email, language=hi” in a store.

When you debug “it forgot,” ask which of the four failed. Truncated history is not a long-term bug. A missing flag is not a retrieval bug.

## Failure modes

1. **Storing the entire history as long-term memory. You retrieve greetings forever.**

2. **Putting hard constraints only in history so a summary drops them.**

3. **Calling everything memory so nobody owns the schema.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

History is the log, state is structured run data, short-term is the session working set, long-term is retrieved facts. The model remembers nothing I do not send.

## A concrete walk-through

A bot forgets the refund already happened. History still has the sentence, but it was summarised away. You add `already_refunded` to state. The next turn cannot “helpfully” pay again.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if a 1M window removes the need for these. Say: it removes overflow, not the need for structured state and selective long-term facts.

## What I would measure

Constraint-retention after summarisation, mistaken-repeat actions, and retrieval precision of long-term facts.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Constraint-retention after summarisation, mistaken-repeat actions, and retrieval precision of long-term facts. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: History ≠ state ≠ short-term ≠ long-term. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: History ≠ state ≠ short-term ≠ long-term.
The model is stateless; the app chooses the next prompt.
Hard constraints belong in structured state.
Long-term is retrieved facts, not a second copy of chat.
Name which layer failed when the agent “forgets.”
A bigger window does not replace structured state.
The model is stateless; memory is what you choose to send
Short-term is the context window; long-term is persisted and retrieved

questions.q: Distinguish short-term and long-term memory in an agent.
questions.a: Short-term memory is the content in the current context window for this session or thread; long-term memory is stored outside the model (database, vector store) and persists across sessions, being retrieved into context when relevant.

questions.q: A user returns next week and the assistant has forgotten their preferences. What is missing?
questions.a: Persisted long-term memory: preferences were not written to a store at the end of the earlier session or are not retrieved at the start of this one. Add a write step and a retrieval step keyed by user.

questions.q: The model is stateless. What does that imply for memory?
questions.a: Everything it “knows” about the session is in the request. Memory is an application concern.

questions.q: A user constraint from turn 1 vanishes after summarisation. Which layer should have held it?
questions.a: Structured state or a pinned system block, not only narrative history.

questions.q: Give one example of each of the four.
questions.a: History: messages. State: already_refunded flag. Short-term: last turns plus summary. Long-term: preferred language in a store.

questions.q: Why not treat a huge window as long-term memory?
questions.a: Cost, rot, and no forget/update policy. Long-term needs write/retrieve/forget, not a pile of tokens.

short-term-memory.explain:
## What it is

Short-term memory is the **conversation context**: system prompt, messages, tool calls and results sent on each request. Persistence between turns is done by your app (keeping the message list, often keyed by a thread id in a checkpoint store).

**Limits:** the context window is finite, tokens cost money, long contexts raise latency, and models attend less reliably to details buried in the middle of very long inputs.

**Common strategies:**
- Keep a sliding window of the last N turns.
- Pin the system prompt and key instructions.
- Keep structured state separately (a scratchpad) and re-inject it compactly.
- Prune stale tool results.

**Example (illustrative):** at 400 tokens per turn plus 2k of tool output, 30 turns is already about 70k tokens re-sent every step unless trimmed or cached.

**Failure modes:** early constraints get dropped, contradictions between old and new messages, large tool outputs crowding everything out.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Short-term memory is the working set of the current task: recent turns, the plan, pinned constraints, maybe a scratchpad. It must fit the budget and survive a few tool dumps. It is not a warehouse.

If you skip it, every turn is either “all history” (expensive, rot) or “last message only” (amnesia).

## How it works + one small example

Implement a session object: `messages[-k:]`, `summary`, `pins[]`, `plan`. After each turn, if tokens exceed T, summarise the middle and keep pins. Pins are copied into the system block every call.

Scratchpad: the model can write `note()` that lands in state, not only in prose.

Expire the session with the product session, or after idle TTL. Do not quietly promote short-term notes to long-term without a policy.

## Failure modes

1. **Keeping all tool dumps in short-term. The working set is then just noise.**

2. **No pins, so the one rule that mattered died in the summary.**

3. **Session objects that never expire and become long-term by accident.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Short-term is the working set: recent turns, summary, pins, plan. I budget it, I pin hard constraints, and I do not treat it as a warehouse.

## A concrete walk-through

After six tool calls the agent forgets the user’s timezone. You pin `tz=Asia/Kolkata` and cap tool results. The timezone survives the next twenty steps.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how large k should be. Say: measure quality versus tokens. I start with 8–16 turns plus a summary and pins.

## What I would measure

Pin-retention rate, tokens in the working set, and tasks failed because a recent fact was dropped.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Pin-retention rate, tokens in the working set, and tasks failed because a recent fact was dropped. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Short-term is the current-task working set. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Short-term is the current-task working set.
Keep recent turns, a summary, pins and the plan.
Pin hard constraints so summaries cannot drop them.
Cap tool dumps out of the working set.
Expire with the session; do not silently promote.
Tune k on evals, not folklore.
Short-term memory is the message list sent each call
Finite window, cost and long-context attention limit it

questions.q: What are the constraints on short-term memory?
questions.a: The window size is finite, every token is billed and adds latency each call, and attention to details can degrade in long contexts. Therefore you trim, pin key instructions and keep compact state.

questions.q: A support bot loses the customer's order number after long troubleshooting. Fix?
questions.a: Store key facts such as order number in structured state and re-inject it every turn rather than relying on it surviving in raw history, and avoid trimming that drops early messages without summarising.

questions.q: What belongs in short-term memory?
questions.a: Recent turns, a summary of older ones, pinned constraints, and the current plan or scratchpad — sized to a budget.

questions.q: A user states a hard constraint early; after summarisation the agent violates it. Best fix?
questions.a: Keep hard constraints in pinned structured state or the system prompt, not only in the summarised narrative.

questions.q: Should tool dumps live in short-term forever?
questions.a: No. Truncate or store them. The working set is for decisions.

questions.q: When does short-term become long-term?
questions.a: Only through an explicit write policy. Idle TTL should kill the session, not copy it into the warehouse.

long-term-memory.explain:
## What it is

Long-term memory persists beyond a session and is pulled in on demand. Common types (borrowed loosely from cognitive science):

- **Semantic:** facts about the user or world ("prefers Python, works in fintech").
- **Episodic:** records of past interactions or task outcomes ("last time deploying X failed due to Y").
- **Procedural:** learned instructions or rules that shape behaviour (updated system prompt, skill files).

**Storage options:** key-value or relational rows for structured facts, vector store for fuzzy recall, plain files or notes the agent reads and edits, knowledge graphs for relationships. Choose by query pattern: exact lookups want keys; fuzzy "what did we discuss about X" wants embeddings.

**Scoping:** namespace by user (and tenant) to prevent leaks.

**Risks:** stale or wrong memories, privacy and retention obligations, memory poisoning through untrusted content, and retrieval noise. Give users visibility and deletion control.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Long-term memory is a store you retrieve from on later sessions: preferences, durable facts, prior outcomes. It is usually a database plus embeddings or keywords, not “leave the chat forever.”

Without it, every Monday the product asks the user’s name again. With an unfiltered one, it recalls a joke as a policy.

## How it works + one small example

Write path: extract candidate facts, filter, upsert with a key (`user.pref.language`). Retrieve path: query by user and task, threshold, cap k, inject as a labelled block.

Start with structured fields you understand. Add vector retrieval when the set of facts is large and messy. Always keep an update and a delete.

Do not write memories from untrusted retrieved web text without a flag.

## Failure modes

1. **Blindly embedding every message.**

2. **No user key so memories leak across accounts.**

3. **Retrieval with no threshold so ten vague facts distract the model.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Long-term memory is a store I write selectively and retrieve with a cap. It is not a second copy of the chat. Update and delete are part of the design.

## A concrete walk-through

You store `deploy_target=eu-west-1`. Next week the agent uses it without asking. A month later the user moves to `us-east-1`; you upsert, you do not append a contradiction.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about memory fine-tuning. Say: that is weights, not this. Product memory is data I can delete.

## What I would measure

Write precision (junk rate), retrieval precision, contradiction rate, and cross-tenant leak tests.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Write precision (junk rate), retrieval precision, contradiction rate, and cross-tenant leak tests. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Long-term is persisted and retrieved across sessions. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Long-term is persisted and retrieved across sessions.
Write only useful, scoped facts with keys.
Retrieve with a threshold and a small k.
Update or supersede; do not pile contradictions.
Never leak across users.
Untrusted sources do not become durable facts.
Semantic, episodic and procedural memory types
Pick storage by query pattern: keys, vectors, files or graphs

questions.q: Give examples of semantic, episodic and procedural memory for an assistant.
questions.a: Semantic: the user's role and preferences. Episodic: a record of a previous debugging session and its outcome. Procedural: rules or instructions learned for how to behave, such as preferred output format or workflow steps.

questions.q: What privacy and safety controls should long-term memory have?
questions.a: Per-user namespacing, user visibility and deletion, retention limits, avoiding storing sensitive data without need, validating what gets written to resist poisoning from untrusted content, and encryption and access control on the store.

questions.q: Which is a durable fact worth storing in long-term memory?
questions.a: A stable preference such as programming language or deploy target — not “hello” and not a raw 50k log.

questions.q: How do you handle a user changing their city?
questions.a: Update or supersede the old memory with a timestamp. Do not keep both as peers.

questions.q: Retrieval returns loosely related memories. First adjustments?
questions.a: Raise the similarity threshold, lower k, filter by metadata such as user and type.

questions.q: Why is fine-tuning the wrong “memory” for a preference?
questions.a: You cannot reliably delete or update a single fact in weights. A store you can edit is the product memory.

storing-what-is-worth-keeping.explain:
## What it is

Storing everything makes retrieval noisy and expensive. Decide what is worth keeping.

**Keep:** durable user facts and preferences, decisions and their reasons, outcomes of tasks (what worked or failed), corrections the user made, and stable domain facts the agent learned.

**Skip:** small talk, transient details, raw tool dumps (store a summary and a pointer), anything sensitive you have no need for, and unverified claims from untrusted content.

**How to decide:** a rule list in the prompt, or a separate "memory writer" step that extracts candidate memories from a finished turn or session as short, self-contained statements with metadata (user, time, source, confidence). Deduplicate against existing entries before inserting.

**Format matters:** write each memory so it makes sense out of context ("User prefers metric units"), not "he said yes".

**Failure modes:** storing guesses as facts, duplicate near-identical entries, and storing instructions from web pages that later act as injected commands.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Write policies are how memory stays useful. Worth keeping: decisions, durable preferences, open tasks, verified outcomes. Not worth: greetings, whole tool dumps, unverified web claims, secrets.

If you skip the policy, retrieval becomes a junk drawer and people disable memory.

## How it works + one small example

Score candidates: durable? user-specific? actionable later? verified? If three of four, write. Store `{key, value, source, ts, ttl?}`.

Example keep: “billing cycle is annual,” “open: wait for RMA.” Example drop: “thanks!,” a 4k stack trace, a tweet.

Let the user see and delete. A memory the user cannot see will become a trust incident.

## Failure modes

1. **Storing API keys the user pasted once.**

2. **Storing every assistant message as a fact.**

3. **No source field so you cannot tell a user said it versus a webpage did.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I store decisions, preferences and open tasks — not every chat line. Each memory has a key, a source and a way to delete it.

## A concrete walk-through

Memory write rate was 40 per session. You add the four-question filter. Writes drop to 2–3, retrieval precision doubles, and “why did it say that?” tickets fall.

## Interview follow-up

They ask who extracts facts. Say: a small structured extractor with a allowlist of keys, not a free-form diary.

## What I would measure

Writes per session, junk rate from a labelled sample, user-delete rate, secret-leak audits.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Writes per session, junk rate from a labelled sample, user-delete rate, secret-leak audits. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Keep decisions, prefs, open tasks, verified outcomes. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Keep decisions, prefs, open tasks, verified outcomes.
Drop chit-chat, dumps, secrets, untrusted claims.
Every memory has a key, source and timestamp.
Users can see and delete.
Prefer an allowlist of keys over a free-form diary.
Verification status travels with the fact.
Keep durable facts, decisions, outcomes and corrections
Write self-contained, deduplicated, timestamped statements

questions.q: What should an agent store in long-term memory, and what should it skip?
questions.a: Store durable preferences, decisions with reasons, task outcomes and user corrections. Skip chit-chat, transient details, raw bulky outputs and unverified or sensitive content with no need. Write short self-contained entries.

questions.q: Your memory store has 40 near-duplicate entries saying the user likes dark mode. What process was missing?
questions.a: A deduplicate or upsert step at write time: compare a candidate memory to existing similar entries and update or merge rather than insert, optionally with a canonical key for that fact.

questions.q: What is worth remembering?
questions.a: Decisions, user preferences and open tasks — not every chat line, dump or unverified webpage.

questions.q: The store filled with “thanks” and stack traces. What policy was missing?
questions.a: A write filter for durable, user-specific, actionable, verified facts.

questions.q: Why store a source on each memory?
questions.a: So you can distrust web-derived facts and prove what the user actually said.

questions.q: Should users see their memories?
questions.a: Yes. Invisible memory is how you get creepy or wrong personalisation you cannot debug.

retrieving-only-relevant-memories.explain:
## What it is

At the start of a turn (or when the agent decides), fetch a **small, relevant** set of memories rather than loading all.

**Methods:**
- **Key lookup** for known slots (user profile).
- **Semantic search** over embeddings of memory text with the current query.
- **Hybrid** with keyword filters and metadata (user id, type, recency).
- **Re-ranking** or a score blend: similarity plus recency plus importance.

**Practical knobs:** top-k (often 3-10), minimum similarity threshold so you inject nothing when nothing matches, and a token budget for the memory block.

**Present clearly:** label the block ("Relevant memories, may be outdated") and keep it separate from the user's message.

**Agent-driven retrieval:** expose a `search_memory` tool so the model fetches when needed, trading extra calls for less always-on noise.

**Failure modes:** irrelevant memories distract or bias the answer, outdated memories contradict the present, and cross-user leakage from a missing filter.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Injection of the whole memory store is how products get slower and weirder. Retrieval is a query: this user, this task, above a score, cap k, labelled so the model knows they are memories not commands.

This is RAG applied to your own notes. The same precision problems apply.

## How it works + one small example

At turn start (or when the task changes): embed the user message plus a hint, search, filter metadata, take top 3–5 above a threshold, render as `Memory (user-stated, 2026-03-01): prefers email`.

Do not retrieve on “hi.” Do not let memories override system rules. If two memories conflict, prefer the newer and say so.

Log which ids were injected so you can debug a creepy mention.

## Failure modes

1. **k=20 with no threshold.**

2. **Memories concatenated into the system prompt as if they were rules.**

3. **Retrieving another user’s memories because the filter forgot `user_id`.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I retrieve a few relevant memories with a threshold and a user filter. I do not pour the store into the prompt. Memories are labelled data, not rules.

## A concrete walk-through

The agent mentions a two-year-old cancelled project. You add recency decay and a task filter. Irrelevant-memory rate on a labelled set drops from 40% to 8%.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about always-on memory. Say: always-on write is already dangerous; always-on full inject is worse. I retrieve on demand.

## What I would measure

Precision@k of injected memories, leak tests across users, and quality with k=0 versus k=3.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Precision@k of injected memories, leak tests across users, and quality with k=0 versus k=3. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Retrieve a small k above a similarity threshold. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Retrieve a small k above a similarity threshold.
Always filter by user and type.
Label memories as data, not as system rules.
Prefer newer when facts conflict.
Skip retrieval on greetings and tiny talk.
Log injected ids for debug.
Retrieve top-k by similarity blended with recency and metadata
Use thresholds and token budgets so nothing irrelevant is injected

questions.q: How do you retrieve relevant memories for a turn?
questions.a: Embed the query, search the memory store with metadata filters such as user id, combine similarity with recency or importance, take top-k above a threshold within a token budget, and inject them clearly labelled. Alternatively expose a memory search tool.

questions.q: The assistant sometimes answers using a memory that is unrelated to the question. What do you adjust?
questions.a: Raise the similarity threshold, lower k, add metadata filters or re-ranking, improve memory text quality, and label retrieved memories so the model can ignore irrelevant ones. Evaluate retrieval precision on sample queries.

questions.q: Retrieval returns loosely related memories that distract the model. First adjustments?
questions.a: Add a similarity threshold, lower k and filter by metadata.

questions.q: Why label injected memories as memories?
questions.a: So the model does not treat a preference as a system command, and so traces show what was injected.

questions.q: What metadata is non-negotiable on retrieve?
questions.a: user_id (or tenant), type, and timestamp. Without them you leak or inject junk.

questions.q: When do you skip retrieval entirely?
questions.a: Greetings, or tasks that cannot use personal facts (a public calculator). Measure before you always retrieve.

write-retrieve-update-forget.explain:
## What it is

Memory is a lifecycle, not just an append-only log.

- **Write:** extract and store candidate memories with metadata (time, source, confidence).
- **Retrieve:** fetch relevant ones for the current task.
- **Update:** when new information conflicts or refines an old one ("moved from London to Berlin"), modify or supersede it instead of adding a contradiction. Keep a history or timestamp if auditing matters.
- **Forget:** delete or decay entries that are obsolete, low-value, expired by retention policy, or requested by the user. Strategies: TTL, recency decay, usage-based pruning, capacity limits, explicit delete.

**Why it matters:** without update and forget, memory accumulates contradictions and noise and retrieval quality decays over time. Privacy rules (such as deletion requests) require real forget paths.

**Implementation note:** an LLM can propose operations (add, update, delete, none) given the new fact and similar existing memories, but validate and log them.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Memory is not append-only. The operations are write, retrieve, update, forget. Without update you contradict yourself. Without forget you keep a stale address and a secret the user asked to delete.

Regulated products will ask you to forget. “We embedded it, sorry” is not an answer.

## How it works + one small example

Write: upsert by key. Retrieve: query. Update: new value, new ts, old value archived or gone. Forget: delete by key or by user request; remove from the vector index, not only the SQL row.

TTL is automatic forget. A credit-card number should have TTL minutes, not years.

Expose forget to the user. Honour it in every replica.

## Failure modes

1. **Soft-delete only in SQL while vectors still retrieve the fact.**

2. **Updates that append so retrieve returns both cities.**

3. **No forget API because “memory is the product.”**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Memory operations are write, retrieve, update, forget. Forget means the index too. TTL is forget with a clock.

## A concrete walk-through

GDPR request: delete this user. You wipe rows and embeddings and the cache. A weekly test plants a canary user and asserts retrieve is empty after forget.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about “forgetting” in the model weights. Say: I do not put customer facts in weights if I need to delete them.

## What I would measure

Forget completeness (index + row + cache), contradiction rate after updates, TTL expiry success.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Forget completeness (index + row + cache), contradiction rate after updates, TTL expiry success. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: The four operations: write, retrieve, update, forget. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: The four operations: write, retrieve, update, forget.
Update supersedes; it does not append rivals.
Forget must clear every index and cache.
TTL is automatic forget for perishable data.
Users can request forget.
Do not put deletable facts only in weights.
Memory needs update and forget, not just write
Conflicts should supersede old facts rather than coexist

questions.q: Why do memory systems need update and forget operations?
questions.a: Without them memory accumulates contradictions, stale facts and noise, which degrades retrieval and answers, and it cannot satisfy retention or deletion requests. Updating keeps one truthful version; forgetting bounds growth.

questions.q: A user says they changed jobs. Walk through handling it in memory.
questions.a: Retrieve existing memories about employment, detect the conflict, update or supersede the old entry with the new fact and a timestamp (optionally archive the old one), and avoid keeping both as current. Log the operation.

questions.q: Name the four basic memory operations.
questions.a: Write, retrieve, update and forget. Forget includes vector indexes and caches.

questions.q: You updated the city but the agent still says the old one. Likely bug?
questions.a: Retrieve is hitting an old embedding or an appended duplicate. Upsert and delete the old vector.

questions.q: What should happen to a pasted password in memory?
questions.a: Do not write it. If it was written, forget immediately and rotate. Use a short TTL for anything secret-like.

questions.q: Why is TTL part of forget?
questions.a: Some facts rot. Automatic expiry keeps memory from becoming a dump of last year’s tickets.

trimming-summarizing-growth.explain:
## What it is

Both stored memory and the live context grow. Control them.

**Context trimming options:**
- Sliding window (drop oldest turns), simple but loses information.
- **Summarise** old turns into a short running summary, keep recent turns verbatim. Cheaper models can summarise.
- Drop or clear stale tool results.
- Cache stable prefixes to cut cost (not a replacement for trimming).

**Store growth:** periodically consolidate many episodic notes into fewer semantic facts, merge duplicates, apply TTL or importance-based pruning.

**Risks of summarisation:** lossy (names, numbers, constraints vanish), errors compound if you summarise summaries, and the summary may encode mistakes as fact. Mitigate by keeping structured state separate, pinning hard constraints, and keeping raw logs in storage for audit or re-summarising.

**Trigger design:** summarise when tokens cross a threshold (for example 70 percent of budget, illustrative), not every turn.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Conversations grow until they do not fit or they rot. Trimming drops old turns. Summarising compresses them. You need a policy for both, and you must not trim the pins or the current user question.

This is context engineering at session scale. Interviews want the order: reserve output, keep pins, summarise the middle, drop tool dumps first.

## How it works + one small example

When tokens > T: (1) drop or store tool bodies, (2) summarise turns older than k into a rolling summary, (3) keep the last k turns verbatim, (4) never drop pins or the latest user text.

Re-summarise incrementally; do not rebuild from the full log every time if you can avoid it. Eval summaries for lost constraints.

Offer a “see full history” in the product that reads the store, not the prompt.

## Failure modes

1. **FIFO trim that deletes the system prompt.**

2. **A summary that invents a preference the user never stated.**

3. **Summarising every turn so you pay a model to compress “ok.”**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I trim dumps first, summarise the middle, keep recent turns and pins. I never FIFO away the rules or the current question.

## A concrete walk-through

A 40-turn onboarding chat overflowed. You store tool bodies, keep 10 turns, summarise the rest, pin the plan. Tokens fall from 70k to 18k and the plan is still present on every failing trace.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about hierarchical summaries. Say: maybe later. First make a rolling summary that does not drop pins.

## What I would measure

Tokens per turn after policy, pin presence rate, invented-fact rate in summaries.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Tokens per turn after policy, pin presence rate, invented-fact rate in summaries. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Drop or store tool dumps before you touch dialogue. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Drop or store tool dumps before you touch dialogue.
Summarise the middle; keep recent turns verbatim.
Never trim pins, rules, or the current question.
Eval summaries for lost constraints.
Do not summarise tiny talk.
Full history lives in a store, not necessarily in the prompt.
Trim with windows, running summaries and stale-result clearing
Summaries are lossy; pin constraints and structured state

questions.q: Compare sliding-window trimming with summarisation.
questions.a: A window drops the oldest turns: simple, cheap, but loses information outright. Summarisation compresses old turns into a shorter text, preserving gist at the cost of some detail and extra calls, and risks compounding errors.

questions.q: After repeated summarisation the agent forgets a hard constraint from turn 3. Prevent it.
questions.a: Extract hard constraints into pinned structured state or the system prompt, not left inside the narrative summary; summarise from raw logs rather than summaries of summaries; and add a check that required constraints are still present.

questions.q: A request fails only on long conversations near the limit. What do you check first?
questions.a: Whether input plus reserved output exceeds the window, and which block grew. Then trim dumps and summarise the middle; keep pins.

questions.q: What must survive trimming?
questions.a: Pinned constraints, system rules, and the current user question.

questions.q: A summary claims the user is a VIP. They never said that. What do you do?
questions.a: Treat summary hallucination as a bug. Tighten the prompt, add a fact check against the stored turns, and stop writing unverified facts into the summary.

questions.q: Why not keep everything and buy 1M context?
questions.a: Cost, latency and context rot. Trimming is an allocation decision, not just a fence.

offloading-comes-later.explain:
## What it is

Offloading means moving information out of the context into external storage (files, databases, scratchpads) and reading it back only when needed. Examples: saving a long document to disk and keeping a short note, writing a to-do file the agent updates, spilling large tool outputs to a store and returning a handle.

**The module's point is sequencing:** first get the basics right: keep the loop working, trim and summarise, retrieve selectively. Introduce offloading and sophisticated memory architectures **later**, when measurements show context pressure or cross-session needs. Premature memory systems add moving parts (stores, embeddings, write policies) that need evaluation and maintenance.

**When offloading earns its place:** long-running tasks that exceed the window, large artifacts, multi-agent hand-offs through shared files, and resumability after crashes.

**Trade-offs:** extra tool calls to read back, risk of the agent forgetting to look, consistency problems if multiple writers.

**Interview angle:** justify any memory component by a failure you measured, not by fashion.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Context offloading and fancy compression (write the whole world to a store and page it) are real techniques, and they belong in a later context-engineering pass. At memory-basics level, do the boring things first: pins, summary, retrieve-a-few, artefact ids.

Interviewers will tempt you to describe a research memory OS. The senior move is to say what you would ship this month.

## How it works + one small example

Ship: structured state, rolling summary, long-term upsert/retrieve/forget, tool artefact store. Defer: learned compression models, multi-level page tables of context, automatic offload of every paragraph.

When a task exceeds the window or must resume tomorrow, then offload: write artefacts and the plan to a store, reload by id. That is already enough for most products.

Revisit offloading when traces show you are losing mid-context facts after the boring policy is in place.

## Failure modes

1. **Building a memory OS before you have a write filter.**

2. **Offloading the system rules so a resume starts without policy.**

3. **Pretending offload is a substitute for a cap.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep deeper offloading for later. This month I pin, summarise, retrieve a few facts, and store artefacts by id. I offload when a task must outlive the window.

## A concrete walk-through

A prototype stored every paragraph in a vector DB and retrieved 30 chunks per turn. Quality fell. You rip it out, keep pins plus 5 memories, and quality and cost recover. Offload returns as a project next quarter for multi-day runs.

## Interview follow-up

They ask what “later” means. Say: after I can show pin-retention and junk-write rates. Then I will page long artefacts.

## What I would measure

Whether the boring policy is in prod, and a list of tasks that actually overflowed after it.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether the boring policy is in prod, and a list of tasks that actually overflowed after it. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Do pins, summary, selective retrieve and artefact ids first. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Do pins, summary, selective retrieve and artefact ids first.
Offload when a task outlives the window or must resume.
Do not offload the rules.
A memory OS is not a substitute for a write filter.
Caps still apply after offload.
Revisit compression when traces show residual loss.
Offloading moves info to external storage and reads it back on demand
Get loop, trimming and retrieval basics right before adding it

questions.q: What is context offloading and when is it worth adding?
questions.a: Moving information such as large outputs or task notes to external storage, keeping only a handle or summary in context. It is worth adding when long tasks overflow the window, artifacts are large, or resumability and hand-offs are needed.

questions.q: A team builds a vector memory store before their agent even works reliably. Critique.
questions.a: It is premature: added infrastructure and evaluation burden without evidence it addresses a measured failure. First stabilise the loop, tools and context handling, find where context or continuity actually fails, then add memory targeted to that.

questions.q: When is offloading to external storage most justified?
questions.a: When tasks exceed the window or need resumability — not as the first prototype for a short chat.

questions.q: What should you implement before fancy context compression?
questions.a: Pins, rolling summary, selective long-term retrieve, and artefact ids for big tool results.

questions.q: A team offloads the system prompt to save tokens. What did they break?
questions.a: The rules may be missing on resume. Rules stay pinned; artefacts offload.

questions.q: Why wait to build a memory operating system?
questions.a: Without a write filter and evals you will retrieve junk at scale. Prove the boring path first.

what-is-worth-remembering.explain:
## What it is

**Decisions, user prefs, and open tasks — not every chat line.** That is the write allowlist in one sentence. A decision is “we will ship to EU-West.” A pref is “Hindi, email, dark mode.” An open task is “waiting on the RMA.” A chat line is “lol thanks.”

If you cannot classify a candidate into those buckets, do not write it.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the memory interview closer. They want a crisp allowlist and a no-list (secrets, dumps, untrusted web, chit-chat). On the job this is also how you explain the product to legal: we store these fields, here is the delete path.

## How it works + one small example

Extractor emits only keys from an allowlist: `pref.*`, `decision.*`, `task.open.*`. Everything else is dropped. A weekly sample of writes is reviewed for junk and secrets.

Open tasks get a TTL or a completion event. Decisions get a date. Prefs get an update path.

Show the three lists in the UI. If a user would be surprised to see it, it should not have been stored.

## Failure modes

1. **A free-form “memory paragraph” that mixes a pref with a joke.**

2. **Storing open tasks forever so the agent nags about a finished RMA.**

3. **Remembering a decision the user rejected.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I remember decisions, preferences and open tasks. I do not remember every line. If a user would be surprised to see it stored, I did not write it.

## A concrete walk-through

The store had 12,000 rows, mostly “ok.” You migrate to 400 keyed prefs/decisions/tasks. The agent stops mentioning a cancelled trial from 2024.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about emotional tone as memory. Say: only if the product needs it and the user can see it. I default no.

## What I would measure

Share of writes in the three buckets, surprise-rate in user reviews, stale open tasks.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Share of writes in the three buckets, surprise-rate in user reviews, stale open tasks. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Allowlist: decisions, preferences, open tasks. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I remember decisions, preferences and open tasks. I do not remember every line. If a user would be surprised to see it stored, I did not write it. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about emotional tone as memory. Say: only if the product needs it and the user can see it. I default no. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Deny: chit-chat, dumps, secrets, untrusted web.
keyPoints: Allowlist: decisions, preferences, open tasks.
Deny: chit-chat, dumps, secrets, untrusted web.
Keys beat free-form diary entries.
Open tasks expire or close.
Users should not be surprised by a stored fact.
Rejected options are not decisions.

questions.q: What three classes of fact are worth remembering?
questions.a: Decisions, user preferences, and open tasks. Not every chat line.

questions.q: How do you treat a user-rejected plan?
questions.a: Do not store it as a decision. Store “rejected X on date” only if it prevents a harmful retry.

questions.q: The agent nags about a finished ticket. What was missing?
questions.a: A close event or TTL on open tasks, and an update to forget the open state.

questions.q: Why is “user would be surprised” a useful test?
questions.a: It catches creepy or incorrect memories before legal or Twitter does. If they would not expect it stored, drop it.

questions.q: Where do secrets go?
questions.a: Nowhere in memory. Drop, redact, rotate. They are not prefs.

forgetting-as-a-feature.explain:
## What it is

**TTL and explicit delete keep memory from rotting.** Forgetting is not a failure of the system. It is how you stay correct and lawful. Every write should have a default lifetime or a close event, and every user should have a delete.

Rotten memory is worse than no memory: the agent is confidently last year.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the other half of long-term memory in interviews. Juniors talk about embeddings. Seniors talk about delete and TTL. On the job, a forgotten stale address is a support win; an un-deletable profile is a legal loss.

## How it works + one small example

Schema: `ttl` or `expires_at` on every row. Jobs sweep expired rows and embeddings. User delete calls the same path. Product delete (“task closed”) calls the same path.

Some classes never expire (account language) until updated. Some expire in days (one-off travel dates). Document that table.

Test forget like you test write: plant, forget, retrieve-empty, check caches.

## Failure modes

1. **TTL only on the SQL row.**

2. **Delete in the UI that hides the row from the user but still retrieves it.**

3. **No sweep job so TTL is decorative.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Forgetting is a feature: TTL and explicit delete. I test that retrieve is empty afterwards, including the index and the cache.

## A concrete walk-through

Travel dates from March were still retrieved in October. You put a 30-day TTL on `task.travel.*`. The agent stops asking about a finished trip. A delete-all for a departing employee clears 100% in the test.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about “soft forget” for analytics. Say: analytics is aggregated and separate. Product memory that the model sees must actually go away.

## What I would measure

Sweep success, retrieve-after-forget rate (target 0), stale-fact tickets.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Sweep success, retrieve-after-forget rate (target 0), stale-fact tickets. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: TTL and explicit delete are part of memory design. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Forgetting is a feature: TTL and explicit delete. I test that retrieve is empty afterwards, including the index and the cache. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about “soft forget” for analytics. Say: analytics is aggregated and separate. Product memory that the model sees must actually go away. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Forget clears SQL, vectors and caches.
keyPoints: TTL and explicit delete are part of memory design.
Forget clears SQL, vectors and caches.
Different keys have different lifetimes.
User delete and product close share a path.
Test forget with a plant-and-retrieve-empty job.
Stale memory is worse than missing memory.

questions.q: Why is forgetting a feature rather than a defect?
questions.a: Facts rot and users have a right to delete. TTL and delete keep the agent correct and lawful.

questions.q: A TTL fired but the agent still recalls the fact. Where do you look?
questions.a: The vector index, a cache, or a summary that copied the fact. Forget must hit every copy.

questions.q: Which memories should expire quickly?
questions.a: One-off tasks and travel dates. Stable prefs expire only on update.

questions.q: How do you test forget?
questions.a: Plant a canary, call forget, assert retrieve is empty in row, index and cache.

questions.q: Why must the model-visible path actually delete?
questions.a: Hiding a row in the UI while still injecting it is a lie and a compliance bug.

why-more-than-one-agent.explain:
## What it is

A **multi-agent system** splits one job across several LLM-driven agents, each with its own prompt, tools and context window.

**Real reasons to split:**
- **Context isolation**: a research sub-agent can read 40 pages and return a 300-token summary, so the parent context stays small.
- **Specialisation**: a narrow prompt and a short tool list are easier to get right than one prompt that covers everything.
- **Parallelism**: independent sub-tasks run at the same time, cutting wall-clock latency.
- **Different models or permissions**: a cheap model for triage, a strong one for planning, a read-only agent for untrusted web content.

**Costs**: more tokens (each agent re-reads shared context), more latency from hand-offs, harder debugging, and errors that compound across agents. In an interview, say you start with one agent and split only when you can name which of the benefits above you are buying.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Split only when you can name the benefit: context isolation, specialisation, parallelism, or a permission boundary. Extra agents add tokens, latency, hand-off bugs and compounded error. “It looks advanced” is not a reason.

Interviews: start with one agent; split when a measured limit appears.

## How it works + one small example

A researcher reads 40 pages and returns 400 tokens. That is isolation. A cheap model triages, a strong one plans: specialisation. Two independent lookups run together: parallelism. A web-reader has no send-email tool: permission.

If the task is a short sequential Q&A, one agent with three tools is enough. Draw the benefit on the whiteboard before you add a second policy.

## Failure modes

1. **Splitting a tightly coupled three-step job and losing information at the hand-off.**

2. **Five agents because a slide had five roles.**

3. **No owner for the split, so nobody measures whether quality rose.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I add an agent when I can name isolation, specialisation, parallelism or a permission wall. Otherwise one agent with tools is simpler and cheaper.

## A concrete walk-through

A single agent drowned in PDFs. You add a research worker that returns a cited summary. Parent tokens drop 60% and answer quality rises. A second split (“writer” vs “editor”) added latency and no gain; you merge them.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about “multi-agent” as a default. Say: it is a cost. I buy it with a named benefit.

## What I would measure

Tokens and latency versus a single-agent baseline, and the named benefit’s metric (e.g. parent-context size).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Tokens and latency versus a single-agent baseline, and the named benefit’s metric (e.g. parent-context size). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Split for isolation, specialisation, parallelism or permissions. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: Split for isolation, specialisation, parallelism or permissions.
Every extra agent adds tokens, latency and failure modes.
Default to one agent until a measured limit.
A summary-returning worker is the usual isolation win.
Permission splits beat prompt-only care.
If you cannot name the benefit, do not split.
Split for context isolation, specialisation, parallelism or permission boundaries
Every extra agent adds tokens, latency and failure modes

questions.q: Name three legitimate reasons to use more than one agent.
questions.a: Context isolation (sub-agent digests large inputs and returns a summary), specialisation (narrow prompt and tools improve accuracy), parallelism (independent sub-tasks run concurrently), and permission or model separation (e.g. a sandboxed reader of untrusted content). Any three, with the trade-off that costs rise.

questions.q: A teammate wants five agents for a task a single prompt with two tools already solves 90% of the time. What do you say?
questions.a: Ask what limit they hit: context overflow, tool confusion, latency? Without a measured failure, extra agents add token cost, hand-off latency and debugging difficulty. Improve the single agent's prompt and tools and evaluate first; split only when evals show a specific bottleneck a split removes.

questions.q: Which situation most justifies splitting into multiple agents?
questions.a: A research step that would flood the main context, or a permission boundary you do not want in one policy.

questions.q: Name four honest reasons to add an agent.
questions.a: Context isolation, specialisation, parallelism, permission boundaries.

questions.q: When is one strong agent better?
questions.a: Short, tightly coupled sequential work where hand-offs would lose state.

questions.q: A PM wants five roles for a demo. What do you ask?
questions.a: Which measured limit each role fixes. If none, ship one agent.

common-patterns.explain:
## What it is

Most multi-agent designs are variations on a handful of shapes:

- **Orchestrator-workers**: one agent plans and delegates sub-tasks to workers, then merges results.
- **Sequential pipeline / hand-off**: A's output feeds B, then C (draft, review, format).
- **Parallel specialists**: several agents work the same input from different angles at once, then results are aggregated.
- **Hierarchical**: supervisors manage sub-supervisors, each with a team.
- **Debate / critic**: a generator and a reviewer loop until the reviewer accepts or a cap is hit.
- **Router**: a cheap classifier sends the request to the right specialist.

Choose by the **shape of the work**: unknown sub-tasks need an orchestrator, fixed stages need a pipeline, independent sub-tasks need parallelism. Mixing patterns is normal, but each added layer is another place for state to get lost.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The usual drawings are orchestrator→workers, sequential hand-offs, parallel specialists, and hierarchical supervisor/worker. Learn them as patterns with failure modes, not as product names.

Interviews: sketch one and say when you would not use it.

## How it works + one small example

Orchestrator: one policy decomposes and delegates. Sequential: A finishes, B starts with A’s artefact. Parallel: peers run, a merger waits. Hierarchical: supervisors each own a subset of workers when the fan-out is too wide for one chooser.

Pick the shallowest that fits. Hierarchy adds compression and latency. Parallel needs a merge rule. Sequential needs a contract at each hop.

## Failure modes

1. **Using all four in one diagram with no traffic.**

2. **Parallel without a timeout or conflict rule.**

3. **Calling a chatty group chat a “pattern.”**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I know four patterns: orchestrator-workers, sequential hand-offs, parallel specialists, hierarchy. I pick the shallowest and I name the merge or contract.

## A concrete walk-through

Onboarding: sequential (KYC then account then mail). Research: parallel specialists plus a merger. A 30-tool mess: hierarchy. You refuse a fifth invented pattern.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for a fifth. Say: swarms are usually untyped group chat. I want a contract.

## What I would measure

Depth of the chosen pattern, merge conflicts, and extra latency versus a flat design.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Depth of the chosen pattern, merge conflicts, and extra latency versus a flat design. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Four patterns: orchestrator, sequential, parallel, hierarchical. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I know four patterns: orchestrator-workers, sequential hand-offs, parallel specialists, hierarchy. I pick the shallowest and I name the merge or contract. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask for a fifth. Say: swarms are usually untyped group chat. I want a contract. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Pick the shallowest that solves the constraint.
keyPoints: Four patterns: orchestrator, sequential, parallel, hierarchical.
Pick the shallowest that solves the constraint.
Parallel needs a merge policy and a timeout.
Sequential needs a typed hand-off.
Hierarchy pays off only at large fan-out.
A group chat is not a pattern.
Core shapes: orchestrator-workers, pipeline, parallel, hierarchical, critic loop, router
Pick the pattern from the structure of the task, not fashion

questions.q: Which pattern fits a task whose sub-tasks cannot be known until the input is read?
questions.a: Orchestrator-workers: the orchestrator decides at runtime which sub-tasks exist, dispatches them to workers and synthesises results. A fixed pipeline or parallel fan-out assumes the sub-tasks are known up front.

questions.q: You need to generate a report, then fact-check it, then reformat it. Which pattern and why?
questions.a: A sequential pipeline (generate, check, format): the stages are fixed and each depends on the previous output. Optionally add a critic loop on the fact-check stage with a retry cap. An orchestrator is unnecessary because the steps do not vary.

questions.q: List common multi-agent patterns.
questions.a: Orchestrator-workers, sequential hand-offs, parallel specialists, and hierarchical supervisor/worker.

questions.q: When does hierarchy beat a flat orchestrator?
questions.a: When the worker/tool set is too large for one chooser to pick reliably.

questions.q: What must a parallel pattern include?
questions.a: A timeout, a merge or conflict rule, and sources on each result.

questions.q: Why is “everyone talks to everyone” a weak pattern?
questions.a: No contract, duplicated work, unbounded context. Prefer typed hand-offs.

orchestrator-workers.explain:
## What it is

In **orchestrator-workers**, a lead agent receives the goal, breaks it into sub-tasks, sends each to a worker agent (often with a narrow prompt and tools), and synthesises their outputs.

Example: "Compare three vendors." The orchestrator creates three research tasks, each worker returns a structured summary, and the orchestrator writes the comparison.

**Key design points:**
- Give workers **self-contained briefs** (goal, constraints, output format); they do not see the orchestrator's history.
- Ask for **structured, compact results** so the orchestrator's context does not bloat.
- The orchestrator decides how many workers to spawn; cap it.
- Workers can be plain LLM calls or full agents with tools.

**Failure modes**: vague briefs make workers duplicate effort or drift; the orchestrator can mis-split the task; and it is a single point of failure and a latency bottleneck.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

An orchestrator holds the goal, decomposes, delegates, and synthesises. Workers are narrow: one job, few tools, short context. This is the default multi-agent shape.

The orchestrator must not dump its whole memory into every worker. Briefs are the product.

## How it works + one small example

Orchestrator writes a brief `{goal, inputs, output_schema, budget}`. Worker returns `{ok, data|error}` matching the schema. Orchestrator validates, maybe retries another worker, then merges.

Use a cheaper model on workers when the job is extract-and-summarise. Keep the orchestrator stronger for decomposition.

## Failure modes

1. **Workers that return vibes instead of the schema.**

2. **Orchestrator that re-does the worker’s job “to be sure.”**

3. **No budget on the worker so a research child runs 40 steps.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The orchestrator decomposes and briefs; workers return a typed result or a typed failure. I validate on the way back.

## A concrete walk-through

An orchestrator asked “look into this” and got essays. You require `{findings[], citations[]}`. Synthesis starts working. A worker that times out returns `{ok:false, error:"budget"}` and the parent tries a narrower brief.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if the orchestrator should see worker traces. Say: a short error and artefacts, not 20k tokens of thought.

## What I would measure

Schema-valid worker returns, worker step caps hit, orchestrator rework rate.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Schema-valid worker returns, worker step caps hit, orchestrator rework rate. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Orchestrator owns goal, decompose, delegate, merge. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The orchestrator decomposes and briefs; workers return a typed result or a typed failure. I validate on the way back. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if the orchestrator should see worker traces. Say: a short error and artefacts, not 20k tokens of thought. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Workers get a brief, not the whole parent memory.
keyPoints: Orchestrator owns goal, decompose, delegate, merge.
Workers get a brief, not the whole parent memory.
Typed result or typed failure, never a vibe.
Cap the worker’s loop separately.
Validate on return before synthesis.
Tier models: strong parent, cheaper workers when the job is narrow.
Orchestrator plans and merges; workers execute narrow sub-tasks
Workers need self-contained briefs and a fixed output schema

questions.q: Why must an orchestrator write self-contained briefs for workers?
questions.a: Workers have their own context and do not see the orchestrator's conversation. A brief must contain the goal, constraints, scope boundaries and expected output format, otherwise workers guess, duplicate each other or return unusable output.

questions.q: Workers keep returning long free-text answers and the orchestrator runs out of context. Fix?
questions.a: Require a structured, size-limited output schema (key findings, sources, confidence) and truncate or summarise before returning. Store bulky artifacts outside the context and pass references.

questions.q: What does an orchestrator actually do?
questions.a: Decompose the goal, brief workers, validate returns, merge or retry, and stop.

questions.q: Workers return inconsistent formats. Best fix?
questions.a: A required output schema validated on return, plus a self-contained brief.

questions.q: What goes in a worker brief?
questions.a: Goal, inputs, output schema, and a budget. Not the parent’s entire history.

questions.q: Why cap the worker separately?
questions.a: A runaway child should not spend the parent’s whole budget.

sequential-handoffs.explain:
## What it is

A **sequential hand-off** passes control and work product from one agent to the next: for instance triage agent, then billing agent, then summariser. Each agent owns a stage and hands over a defined payload.

**How it works**: the output of stage N becomes the input of stage N+1, either as a structured object or as a conversation transfer (as in handoff-style SDKs, where the receiving agent takes over the dialogue).

**Why use it**: stages are simple, testable in isolation and easy to trace. **Risks**: information loss at each boundary (what you do not pass is gone), errors propagate downstream, and latency is the sum of all stages.

Good practice: define a typed hand-off contract, pass only what the next stage needs plus provenance, and validate at each boundary so a bad output fails early rather than three stages later.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A hand-off transfers control and a typed artefact to the next agent. It is a relay, not a nest. Use it when stages are truly sequential and later stages should not see earlier raw context.

The contract is the artefact. If B needs A’s 40-page dump, you did not hand off; you leaked.

## How it works + one small example

A finishes with `{artefact, provenance, open_questions}`. Runtime starts B with that object as the user message plus B’s own tools. A is done.

Handoff ≠ agent-as-tool. Agent-as-tool returns to the caller. Handoff does not.

Example: transcribe → extract fields → file. Each stage has its own eval.

## Failure modes

1. **Handoff that includes the entire prior transcript “just in case.”**

2. **B silently calling A back, forming a cycle.**

3. **No schema so B guesses what A meant.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Sequential hand-off is a typed artefact and a transfer of control. I do not pass the whole prior context, and I do not confuse this with a tool call that returns.

## A concrete walk-through

Extract used to receive the raw audio transcript plus the transcriber’s chain of thought. You pass only `{text, confidence, language}`. Extract accuracy goes up; tokens drop.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how to undo a hand-off. Say: you usually do not. Escalate to a human or restart with a new artefact.

## What I would measure

Artefact schema-valid rate, tokens at the hop, and B’s success when given only the artefact.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Artefact schema-valid rate, tokens at the hop, and B’s success when given only the artefact. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Handoff transfers control plus a typed artefact. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Sequential hand-off is a typed artefact and a transfer of control. I do not pass the whole prior context, and I do not confuse this with a tool call that returns. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how to undo a hand-off. Say: you usually do not. Escalate to a human or restart with a new artefact. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Not the same as agent-as-tool (which returns).

Prevent cycles in the runtime.
