Validate at every boundary to fail early

questions.q: What is the main risk at each hand-off boundary?
questions.a: Information loss and error propagation: anything not included in the payload is unavailable downstream, and an upstream mistake silently flows to later stages. Mitigate with typed contracts, validation and carrying key context or provenance forward.

questions.q: A support flow hands off from triage to a specialist, who asks the customer for details already given. Diagnose.
questions.a: The hand-off dropped conversation context or extracted facts. Pass the structured case summary (customer id, issue, steps tried) or the transcript with the transfer, and test that the specialist's prompt uses it.

questions.q: What is the key difference between a handoff and agent-as-tool?
questions.a: Handoff transfers control; agent-as-tool returns a result to the caller.

questions.q: What must a hand-off artefact contain?
questions.a: The data the next stage needs, provenance, and open questions — not the prior raw dump.

questions.q: B keeps asking A questions after a hand-off. What is wrong?
questions.a: You built a cycle. Runtime should treat A as finished or use agent-as-tool instead.

questions.q: When is sequential the wrong pattern?
questions.a: When stages are independent and could run in parallel, or when one agent with tools would keep the state cheaper.

parallel-specialists.explain:
## What it is

**Parallel specialists** run several agents concurrently on the same input or on independent slices, then combine results.

Examples: a code review where security, performance and style agents each read the diff; or research across five sources at once.

**Mechanics**: fan out (async calls or graph branches), set a per-branch timeout, collect results, then aggregate by merging, voting or having a synthesiser agent reconcile.

**Benefits**: lower wall-clock time and diverse perspectives. **Costs**: token spend multiplies, results can conflict or overlap, and a slow branch holds up the join unless you use timeouts and partial results.

Use only when branches are truly independent; if one needs another's output, you have a pipeline, not parallelism. Always decide up front what happens when one branch fails.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Parallel specialists cut wall-clock time when work is independent: sanctions, PEP, media checks. They also create merge problems: conflict, stragglers, cost multiplied by N.

Interviews: timeout plus a conflict policy, not “average the text.”

## How it works + one small example

Fan out N briefs. Each specialist has its own tools and a cap. A merger waits until all return or a timeout. Policy: require k of N, or fail if a required specialist fails.

Conflicts: surface both answers with sources; do not silently pick the first. If the task is boolean (sanction hit), OR may be the rule. If it is a summary, a judge with citations.

## Failure modes

1. **Wait-forever for a slow specialist.**

2. **Picking the first to finish as truth.**

3. **Specialists that secretly share a write tool and race.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Parallel specialists need independence, a timeout, and a merge rule. I surface conflicts with sources instead of averaging prose.

## A concrete walk-through

Three KYC checks: two return in 1.2s, media takes 8s. You time out media at 3s and mark it `unknown`. Onboarding continues with a flag instead of stalling.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about averaging embeddings of answers. Say: that hides disagreement. I show the conflict.

## What I would measure

p95 wall time versus sequential, timeout rate, conflict rate, silent-pick incidents (target 0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: p95 wall time versus sequential, timeout rate, conflict rate, silent-pick incidents (target 0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Parallel only if work is independent. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Parallel specialists need independence, a timeout, and a merge rule. I surface conflicts with sources instead of averaging prose. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about averaging embeddings of answers. Say: that hides disagreement. I show the conflict. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Timeout stragglers; define k-of-N.
keyPoints: Parallel only if work is independent.
Timeout stragglers; define k-of-N.
Merge with a rule, not “first done.”
Surface conflicts with sources.
Do not give parallel writers the same record.
Cost is roughly N times a single specialist.
Fan out independent work, then join and aggregate
Per-branch timeouts and partial-result policy are required

questions.q: When is parallel fan-out inappropriate?
questions.a: When branches depend on each other's outputs (that is a pipeline), when token cost matters more than latency, or when the work is too small to justify the overhead. Parallelism needs independent sub-tasks.

questions.q: Four of five parallel agents finished; one hangs. What should the design do?
questions.a: Apply a per-branch timeout, then proceed with partial results while noting the missing branch, or retry it once. Decide this policy in advance; waiting indefinitely blocks the whole request, and silently dropping it hides incomplete output.

questions.q: Two parallel specialists contradict and one is slow. Sound policy?
questions.a: Apply a timeout, surface the conflict with sources, resolve by rule or disclosure.

questions.q: When is parallel the wrong default?
questions.a: When specialists need each other’s outputs or share a write.

questions.q: Why not pick the first result?
questions.a: Speed is not truth. A fast empty search can beat a slow correct one.

questions.q: What does k-of-N mean here?
questions.a: You can finish when k specialists return, as long as required ones are in the k or explicitly optional.

hierarchical-supervisor-worker.explain:
## What it is

A **hierarchical** design has a top supervisor delegating to sub-supervisors, which manage their own workers (e.g. a "research lead" with web and database workers, and a "writing lead" with drafting and editing workers).

**Why**: it keeps each supervisor's prompt and tool list small, and mirrors how large tasks are organised. Each level only sees summaries from the level below.

**Costs**: every level adds latency, tokens and a place where detail is compressed away. Errors can be hidden by an overly confident summary at a middle layer. Routing mistakes at the top send work to the wrong team.

**Rule of thumb**: go hierarchical only when a flat orchestrator has too many workers or tools to choose from reliably. Two levels is usually enough; deeper trees are rarely worth the debugging pain.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A flat orchestrator that chooses among 40 workers will mis-pick. Hierarchy narrows each decision: a top supervisor picks a team lead, the lead picks a worker. You pay extra hops and compressed briefs.

Use it at scale, not at three workers.

## How it works + one small example

Top: route to domain (billing, identity, docs). Domain lead: pick a worker and brief it. Worker: do the job. Returns climb the same way, validated at each level.

Keep depth at two unless you have evidence. Each level should have a tiny catalogue (5–8 choices), not 40.

## Failure modes

1. **Three layers for a four-tool product.**

2. **Leads that rewrite worker output until the user’s question is gone.**

3. **No path for a worker to escalate past a bad lead.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Hierarchy narrows choices when one orchestrator cannot pick among many workers. I keep it shallow and I validate at each hop.

## A concrete walk-through

A 25-tool support bot misroutes. You add billing vs identity leads. Routing accuracy rises 12 points; p95 grows 1.4s. You accept the trade because misroutes were costly.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about deeper trees. Say: each layer multiplies failure. I want two until a metric says three.

## What I would measure

Routing accuracy by layer, extra latency per layer, and escalations past a lead.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Routing accuracy by layer, extra latency per layer, and escalations past a lead. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Hierarchy is for large choice sets. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Hierarchy narrows choices when one orchestrator cannot pick among many workers. I keep it shallow and I validate at each hop. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about deeper trees. Say: each layer multiplies failure. I want two until a metric says three. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Keep depth shallow (usually two).
keyPoints: Hierarchy is for large choice sets.
Keep depth shallow (usually two).
Each node sees a small catalogue.
Validate returns at every hop.
Allow escalate-past-lead.
Do not use hierarchy as decoration.
Supervisors delegate to sub-supervisors to keep each scope small
Each level compresses information and adds latency

questions.q: What problem does a hierarchy solve that a flat orchestrator does not?
questions.a: When a single orchestrator must choose among too many workers or tools, selection accuracy and prompt size degrade. Grouping workers under sub-supervisors narrows each decision.

questions.q: A final report omits a key finding that a worker discovered. How could the hierarchy cause this?
questions.a: A middle supervisor's summary dropped it as it compressed results upward. Mitigate with structured outputs that preserve findings, pass-through of cited evidence, and traces to inspect each level's input and output.

questions.q: When does a hierarchical supervisor beat a flat orchestrator?
questions.a: When the number of workers or tools is too large for one chooser to pick reliably.

questions.q: What is the cost of an extra layer?
questions.a: Latency, compression of the brief, and another place to drop the user’s goal.

questions.q: A lead keeps “improving” a correct worker answer. Fix?
questions.a: Validate against the schema and stop rewrite-by-default. Escalate if the lead disagrees.

questions.q: How many choices should a supervisor see?
questions.a: A handful. If it sees 40, you have not hierarchised, you have nested a mess.

building-an-orchestrator.explain:
## What it is

Building an orchestrator is mostly engineering around one LLM call that plans.

**Steps:**
1. **Plan**: ask the model for a structured plan (a list of sub-tasks with ids, inputs and dependencies) validated against a schema.
2. **Dispatch**: run ready tasks, in parallel when dependencies allow, via a worker function or agent.
3. **Collect**: store each result keyed by task id.
4. **Decide**: after results arrive, either synthesise a final answer or re-plan (bounded number of rounds).
5. **Guard**: max sub-tasks, max rounds, token and time budgets.

```
plan = llm(goal, schema=Plan)
results = {}
for batch in ready_batches(plan):
    results |= await run_all(batch)
answer = llm(goal, results)
```
Keep the plan as data, not prose, so you can log, test and resume it. Interview point: the orchestrator should be dumb about execution and smart about decomposition.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Building the orchestrator is product work: a decomposer, a router, a brief writer, a validator, a merger, and a stop. If you only write “you are the manager” in a prompt, you built a vibe.

Interviews: list those jobs and where they live (code vs model).

## How it works + one small example

Decompose and route can be a model with a closed label set, or a classifier. Briefs are templates filled from state. Validation is code. Merge can be code (concat sections) or a model with citations.

Write the orchestrator so a worker can be replaced by a function. If every worker is “just another LLM,” you still need the same envelope.

## Failure modes

1. **Orchestrator prompt that also executes tools “to help.” It stops being an orchestrator.**

2. **No max workers or max depth.**

3. **Merger that ignores worker errors and writes a confident essay.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build an orchestrator as decompose, brief, validate, merge, stop — with code on the envelope and a model only where a label or a synthesis is needed.

## A concrete walk-through

Your first orchestrator called tools itself and raced the workers. You strip its tools to `delegate` and `finish`. Duplicated work disappears from traces.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if the orchestrator should be a bigger model. Say: only if decompose quality needs it. The envelope stays in code.

## What I would measure

Duplicate-work rate, invalid merges, depth, and success versus a single-agent baseline.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Duplicate-work rate, invalid merges, depth, and success versus a single-agent baseline. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Orchestrator jobs: decompose, route, brief, validate, merge, stop. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

Keep the envelope in code.
A closed label set beats an open “invent a worker.”
Cap depth and worker count.
Do not let the orchestrator do the workers’ tools.
Replaceable workers prove the envelope works.
Structured plan with dependencies, validated by schema
Dispatch ready tasks in parallel; collect by task id

questions.q: Why represent the orchestrator's plan as validated structured data?
questions.a: It can be checked before execution, logged, resumed after a crash, tested and used to schedule dependencies, whereas prose plans cannot be reliably parsed or enforced.

questions.q: Your orchestrator sometimes re-plans forever. How do you stop it?
questions.a: Add a max re-plan round count and a token/time budget, require each re-plan to cite what new information justifies it, and fall back to synthesising a best-effort answer or escalating when the cap is hit.

questions.q: List the jobs of an orchestrator you would actually implement.
questions.a: Decompose, route, write a brief, validate the return, merge or retry, and stop.

questions.q: The orchestrator duplicates worker tool calls. What do you change?
questions.a: Remove those tools from the orchestrator; leave delegate and finish.

questions.q: Which orchestrator jobs belong in code?
questions.a: Validation, caps, routing to a closed set, and stop. Synthesis may be a model.

questions.q: Why make workers replaceable by functions?
questions.a: If the envelope only works with LLMs, you do not have an orchestrator — you have a group chat.

passing-state-aggregating-output.explain:
## What it is

Agents in a system need to share information without drowning each other in tokens.

**Passing state**
- **Explicit payloads**: typed objects passed along edges (preferred).
- **Shared state store**: a dict or database keyed by task id that agents read and write.
- **By reference**: store large artifacts (documents, tables) outside the prompt and pass an id.

**Aggregating**
- **Concatenate** structured results into a synthesiser prompt.
- **Reduce** programmatically (merge lists, dedupe, sum) when results are data.
- **Vote** for classification-like answers.
- **Reconcile** conflicts: ask a synthesiser to flag disagreements instead of silently choosing.

Pitfalls: concurrent writes to shared state need reducers or locks, unbounded history inflates every call, and aggregation that hides provenance makes errors untraceable. Keep source ids with every claim.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

State across agents is a leak surface and a gift. Pass the minimum that the next agent needs. Aggregate with a schema, a conflict rule and provenance. “Stick the transcripts together” is how you blow the window and hide disagreement.

## How it works + one small example

Define a run state the orchestrator owns: `{goal, artefacts{}, decisions[]}`. Workers get a slice. They return a patch, not a new universe.

Aggregation: validate each patch, apply reducers (append findings, max risk, union citations). On conflict, record both and apply the rule. Render the user answer from the aggregated state, not from the last worker’s essay.

## Failure modes

1. **Passing full transcripts between three agents.**

2. **Last-writer-wins on `risk_score`.**

3. **Aggregation that drops citations.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I pass slices of state, not transcripts. I aggregate with reducers and provenance. The user answer is rendered from the merged state.

## A concrete walk-through

Two workers both set `risk`. Last write was “low” after “high.” You change the reducer to `max` and keep both notes. A high-risk customer stops getting a green letter.

## Interview follow-up

They mention LangGraph reducers. Say: same idea even if you do not use the library. Concurrent writes need a merge function.

## What I would measure

Tokens passed per hop, conflict rate, citation-retention, last-writer incidents.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Tokens passed per hop, conflict rate, citation-retention, last-writer incidents. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Pass the minimum slice, not the transcript. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I pass slices of state, not transcripts. I aggregate with reducers and provenance. The user answer is rendered from the merged state. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They mention LangGraph reducers. Say: same idea even if you do not use the library. Concurrent writes need a merge function. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Workers return patches to a shared schema.

Prefer typed payloads; pass large artifacts by reference

questions.q: Why pass large documents by reference between agents?
questions.a: It keeps prompts small and cheap, avoids repeated tokens, and lets only the agent that needs the content load it. Passing full text through every hop wastes context and cost.

questions.q: Two parallel workers return conflicting numbers. How should aggregation behave?
questions.a: Do not silently pick one. Surface the conflict with each worker's source, then either resolve with a rule (most recent, most authoritative), a verifying tool call, or flag uncertainty to the user.

questions.q: How should workers share state?
questions.a: Through a typed run state and patches, not by forwarding full transcripts.

questions.q: Two workers write results and only one survives. Likely cause?
questions.a: A replace merge. Define an append or domain reducer.

questions.q: What must aggregation preserve?
questions.a: Provenance and conflicts. Do not drop the losing finding silently.

questions.q: Why render from aggregated state rather than the last essay?
questions.a: The last essay may ignore a high-risk patch. The state is the source of truth.

worker-failure-escalation.explain:
## What it is

Workers fail: tool errors, timeouts, malformed output, refusals, or plausible but wrong answers. A robust system decides the response ahead of time.

**Ladder of responses:**
1. **Validate** the output (schema, sanity checks).
2. **Retry** with the error fed back, a small bounded number of times, with backoff for transient faults.
3. **Fallback**: a different model, simpler method or cached result.
4. **Degrade**: continue with partial results and say what is missing.
5. **Escalate** to a human or fail loudly with context.

Distinguish **transient** (retry) from **permanent** (do not retry) errors. Make retried actions idempotent. Track failures per worker so the orchestrator can stop routing to a broken one. Never let one worker's failure produce a confident final answer that hides the gap.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Workers fail. The orchestrator retries, reassigns, or escalates. Infinite reassignment is a loop. Silent ignore is a wrong answer. Escalation is a first-class outcome: human or a fallback workflow.

## How it works + one small example

On typed worker failure: (1) retry once if transient, (2) reassign to an alternative worker if one exists, (3) escalate with the brief and the error, (4) never mark the parent success.

Budgets: max retries per worker, max reassigns per goal. Escalation payload is something a human can act on.

## Failure modes

1. **Retrying a schema error five times.**

2. **Reassigning forever between two equally bad workers.**

3. **Parent success when a required worker failed.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I retry transients, reassign once if there is an alternative, then escalate with the brief and the error. A required worker failure fails the parent.

## A concrete walk-through

A web worker 403s. You do not retry. You reassign to an internal corpus worker. If that misses, you escalate “no source for claim X.” The parent no longer invents a citation.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about automatic model upgrade on failure. Say: only if evals show it helps that slice; it is a reassign, and it still has a cap.

## What I would measure

Recovery rate, escalate rate, false-parent-success (target 0), reassign loops.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Recovery rate, escalate rate, false-parent-success (target 0), reassign loops. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Classify worker failures like tool failures. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I retry transients, reassign once if there is an alternative, then escalate with the brief and the error. A required worker failure fails the parent. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about automatic model upgrade on failure. Say: only if evals show it helps that slice; it is a reassign, and it still has a cap. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Retry transients; do not retry bad briefs forever.

what-goes-wrong-with-many-agents.explain:
## What it is

More agents multiply failure modes:

- **Compounding errors**: if each of five steps is 90% reliable, the chain is about 59% (illustrative arithmetic).
- **Context loss** at hand-offs and **telephone-game** distortion of facts.
- **Duplicated or conflicting work** when briefs overlap.
- **Infinite loops**: agents bouncing a task between each other or critics never satisfied.
- **Cost and latency blow-ups** from repeated shared context.
- **Debugging difficulty**: failure appears far from its cause.
- **Prompt injection spreading**: one agent reading untrusted content can instruct others.
- **Unclear ownership**: no agent is accountable for the final answer.

Mitigations: tracing with a run id across agents, typed contracts, step and budget caps, loop detection, least-privilege tools per agent, and evals on the end-to-end task, not just each agent.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The failure mode list is predictable: duplicated work, coordination overhead, context growth, conflicting results, latency and cost. Interviewers want this list and one mitigation each. If you only praise multi-agent, you have not run one.

## How it works + one small example

Duplication: workers overlap tools — namespace and split permissions. Overhead: every hop is a call — measure hops per success. Context: transcripts pile up — pass slices. Conflict: merge rules. Latency: parallelise only independents, timeout. Cost: N models × steps — justify each agent.

A weekly review of traces that involved >2 agents should ask: would one agent have sufficed?

## Failure modes

1. **Adding agents to fix a prompt problem.**

2. **No hop budget.**

3. **Ignoring conflicts because the UI only shows one answer.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Many agents fail by duplication, overhead, context bloat, conflict, latency and cost. I can name a mitigation for each, and I keep asking whether one agent would do.

## A concrete walk-through

Five agents, 0.9 reliable each, end-to-end ~0.59. You drop two ceremonial roles, add validation, and measured success rises even though “the system looks simpler.”

## Interview follow-up

They quote 0.9^5. Agree it is illustrative, then show your hop-fail rate.

## What I would measure

Agents per successful task, hops, duplicate-tool rate, conflict rate, $ per success versus one-agent.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Agents per successful task, hops, duplicate-tool rate, conflict rate, $ per success versus one-agent. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Expect duplication, overhead, bloat, conflict, latency, cost. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Many agents fail by duplication, overhead, context bloat, conflict, latency and cost. I can name a mitigation for each, and I keep asking whether one agent would do. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They quote 0.9^5. Agree it is illustrative, then show your hop-fail rate. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Mitigate each; do not just add roles.

a2a-vs-mcp.explain:
## What it is

**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** standardises how an agent connects to **tools and data** (servers expose tools, resources and prompts). **A2A (Agent2Agent protocol)** standardises how **agents talk to other agents** across vendors or services, including discovering capabilities (agent cards) and managing tasks.

Mental model: MCP is agent to tool ("USB port"); A2A is agent to agent ("colleague who has their own tools and judgement").

**Choose**
- Need a function or data source: MCP (or plain function calling).
- Need to delegate a goal to an autonomous remote agent that runs its own loop, possibly long-running and opaque: A2A.

They are complementary: an A2A-reachable agent may use MCP tools internally. Details and adoption evolve, so check current specs. Interview point: do not use agent-to-agent protocols when a deterministic tool call is enough.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

MCP connects agents to tools and resources. A2A (agent-to-agent) is an interoperability idea for independently built agents that delegate goals to each other. Mixing the words is a common interview fail.

You do not need A2A to call your own worker function. You need it when another vendor’s agent must take a goal and return later.

## How it works + one small example

MCP: your host calls `search_tickets` on a server. A2A: your agent sends a goal to a counterpart that has its own loop, tools and vendor, and you wait for an artefact or a failure.

Treat a remote agent as more dangerous than a tool: longer time, unclear side effects, weaker schemas. Use a contract (typed result, deadline, cancel) and never share your user token wholesale.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling a local worker “A2A” because two prompts exist.**

2. **Using A2A for a calculator.**

3. **Forwarding admin credentials to a foreign agent.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

MCP is tools and resources. A2A is independently built agents delegating goals. I use A2A only across trust boundaries, with a contract and a deadline.

## A concrete walk-through

A partner’s research agent takes a goal and a deadline, returns `{memo, sources}` over an agreed protocol. Your CRM tools stay MCP. You do not wrap the partner as a fake local function that hides the long wait.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which to implement first. Say: MCP or local tools. A2A when a real foreign agent exists.

## What I would measure

Foreign-agent timeouts, contract-valid returns, credential-scope reviews.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Foreign-agent timeouts, contract-valid returns, credential-scope reviews. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: MCP: connect to tools/resources. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.
keyPoints: MCP: connect to tools/resources.
A2A: connect independently built agents.
Local workers are not A2A.
Foreign agents need a deadline, cancel and typed result.
Do not share wholesale user tokens.
Pick MCP first unless a real foreign agent exists.
MCP connects agents to tools/data; A2A connects agents to agents
They are complementary, not competing

questions.q: Explain the difference between MCP and A2A in one answer.
questions.a: MCP standardises agent-to-tool/data access (tools, resources, prompts). A2A standardises agent-to-agent communication for delegating tasks to independent agents with their own reasoning. An A2A agent can itself use MCP tools.

questions.q: A partner company runs its own booking agent. How should your agent reach it?
questions.a: Via an agent-to-agent interface such as A2A (discover its card, send a task, handle status and results), since it is an autonomous agent with its own logic, not a simple tool. If they only expose a deterministic API, wrap it as a tool.

questions.q: Which is the right use of A2A rather than MCP?
questions.a: Delegating a long-running goal to another vendor’s autonomous agent — not reading a file or querying a database.

questions.q: Is two internal workers A2A?
questions.a: Usually no. That is your orchestrator calling functions. A2A is interoperability across independently built agents.

questions.q: What extra risks does A2A add versus a tool?
questions.a: Unknown duration, unknown side effects, weaker control of the inner loop. You need a contract and a deadline.

questions.q: What must you not forward to a foreign agent?
questions.a: Your admin or full user token. Issue a scoped, short-lived capability.

when-one-strong-agent-is-better.explain:
## What it is

A single capable agent with good tools often beats a team.

**Prefer one agent when:**
- The task is sequential and context-heavy (each step needs the full history).
- Sub-tasks are tightly coupled, so splitting loses information.
- Latency and cost matter and the work does not parallelise.
- You cannot yet evaluate end-to-end; fewer parts are easier to debug.
- A strong model with a clear prompt and 5-10 well-described tools already hits the target.

**Move to multiple agents when** context overflows, tools exceed what one prompt handles reliably, you need parallel breadth, or you need isolation for security.

Advice: build the single-agent baseline, measure it, and justify every added agent with an eval improvement. Better models keep shrinking the set of problems that need multi-agent designs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

One strong agent with a few tools beats a crew when the work is tightly coupled, the state must stay consistent, or you cannot afford hop latency. Specialisation is real; coordination bugs are more common than people admit.

The interview line: extra agents add coordination bugs faster than they add quality — until you measure otherwise.

## How it works + one small example

Run a bake-off: one agent vs the crew on the same eval. If the crew wins on a named slice (huge context, hard permission split), keep the split only there.

Coupled editing of one file, one customer record, or one SQL migration: one agent. Parallel research across corpora: maybe more.

## Failure modes

1. **Crew-first as a fashion.**

2. **Refusing to merge after the bake-off said so.**

3. **One agent with 40 overlapping tools — that is not “strong,” that is a mess.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I default to one strong agent with a tight tool list. I split when a bake-off shows isolation or permissions winning. Extra agents add bugs faster than quality until proven otherwise.

## A concrete walk-through

A four-role writer crew took 70s and still contradicted itself. One agent with a outline-then-draft prompt took 22s and scored higher. You keep the crew only for the multilingual review slice.

## Interview follow-up

They say “but Netflix of agents.” Ask for the metric. If there is none, you have a slogan.

## What I would measure

Quality, latency, $ , and incident rate for one vs many on the same set.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Quality, latency, $ , and incident rate for one vs many on the same set. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Default: one agent, few tools. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I default to one strong agent with a tight tool list. I split when a bake-off shows isolation or permissions winning. Extra agents add bugs faster than quality until proven otherwise. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They say “but Netflix of agents.” Ask for the metric. If there is none, you have a slogan. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Bake-off any crew on a real eval.

questions.a: Tightly coupled sequential steps needing shared context, and tasks that do not parallelise where latency and cost matter. Also when evals show the baseline already meets the target.

questions.q: How would you justify a multi-agent redesign to a sceptical lead?
questions.a: Show the single-agent baseline's measured failure (context overflow, tool-selection errors, latency) and an eval where the multi-agent version improves it enough to cover added cost and complexity, plus tracing to keep it debuggable.

handoff-contracts.explain:
## What it is

**Workers return a typed result or a typed failure, never a vibe.** That is the hand-off contract. `ok` plus a schema, or `error` plus a class and a hint. Prose that “kind of found it” cannot be merged, tested, or retried sanely.

This is the multi-agent version of typed tool errors.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Most crew demos die in aggregation because the parent has to read novels. In interviews, “typed result or typed failure” is the sentence that shows you have merged outputs for real.

On the job the contract is also your eval: you can unit-test a worker without the parent.

## How it works + one small example

Specify `WorkerResult = {ok: true, data: T} | {ok: false, error: class, hint, retryable}`. Validate in the runtime. Invalid JSON is a typed failure, not a chance for the parent to guess.

Version the schema. A worker that adds a field must not break old parents. Keep a golden set of worker outputs.

## Failure modes

1. **Accepting markdown with a heading as success.**

2. **Parent parsing natural language for a number.**

3. **Failure that looks like success (“I couldn’t find it, but here’s a guess”).**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Hand-off contracts are typed result or typed failure. I validate in the runtime. Vibes are invalid, not “close enough.”

## A concrete walk-through

A research worker returned a bloggy memo. The parent invented citations. You require `{claims[{text, source_id}]}` or `{ok:false, error:"no_sources"}`. Invented citations on that path go to zero.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about streaming vibes for UX. Say: stream progress titles; the contract is still the final object.

## What I would measure

Schema-valid rate, parent-guess rate (target 0), worker unit-test coverage.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Schema-valid rate, parent-guess rate (target 0), worker unit-test coverage. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Typed result or typed failure, never a vibe. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Hand-off contracts are typed result or typed failure. I validate in the runtime. Vibes are invalid, not “close enough.” If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about streaming vibes for UX. Say: stream progress titles; the contract is still the final object. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Validate in the runtime before the parent sees it.

## What would change my mind

Most crew demos die in aggregation because the parent has to read novels. In interviews, “typed result or typed failure” is the sentence that shows you have merged outputs for real. On the job the contract is also your eval: you can unit-test a worker without the parent. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Invalid JSON is a failure class. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

questions.a: A typed result that matches a schema, or a typed failure with a class and hint — not a free-form vibe.

what-langgraph-is-for.explain:
## What it is

**LangGraph** is a library for building agents and workflows as an explicit **graph** of steps with shared state. It targets what a plain "call the model in a while loop" struggles with: controllable branching, retries, persistence, pauses for humans and long-running work.

You describe nodes (functions), edges (what runs next) and a state schema; LangGraph runs the graph, and can **checkpoint** state after each step.

**Use it when** the flow has branches, loops, multiple agents, needs durable resume, or human approval. **Skip it when** a single tool-calling loop or a straight prompt chain does the job: the framework adds concepts to learn and debug.

Interview angle: be able to say what the graph gives you (explicit control flow, persistence, interrupts, observability) and what it costs (abstraction, versioned APIs, check current docs).

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

LangGraph is a low-level runtime for long-running, stateful agents: you model the work as a graph over shared state, with checkpoints, loops and interrupts. It is not “a smarter model” and it is overkill for a one-shot tool loop.

Interviews: name control flow, persistence, human-in-the-loop, observability.

## How it works + one small example

You declare state, nodes (functions), edges (including conditional). The library runs a step, checkpoints, and can pause. Use it when you need resume after deploy, approval mid-graph, or branching you want in code.

Skip it when a 60-line loop is enough. Learn the primitive loop first so you can read a LangGraph trace.

## Failure modes

1. **Adopting it to look modern on a linear chain.**

2. **Treating it as a replacement for evals.**

3. **Ignoring that APIs change — read current docs.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

LangGraph is an orchestration runtime for stateful, interruptible graphs. I use it when I need explicit control, checkpoints or human nodes — not for a simple loop.

## A concrete walk-through

A refund flow needed verify → approve → pay across deploys. A while-loop died on restart. You move it to a graph with a checkpointer and an interrupt. Resumes work.

## Interview follow-up

They ask “LangGraph vs Agents SDK.” Say: graph when I need durable control; SDK when I want a light loop and handoffs.

## What I would measure

Resume success after kill, interrupt correctness, time-to-debug a bad node.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Resume success after kill, interrupt correctness, time-to-debug a bad node. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Graph + shared state + checkpoints. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: LangGraph is an orchestration runtime for stateful, interruptible graphs. I use it when I need explicit control, checkpoints or human nodes — not for a simple loop. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask “LangGraph vs Agents SDK.” Say: graph when I need durable control; SDK when I want a light loop and handoffs. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Wins: control flow, persistence, interrupts, inspectability.

questions.a: Explicit branching and cycles, durable checkpointed state for resume, human-in-the-loop interrupts, multi-agent composition and step-level inspection. A bare loop leaves these to ad hoc code.

questions.q: When would you not choose LangGraph?
questions.a: For simple tasks: one prompt or one tool-calling loop with few tools. The graph abstraction adds learning and debugging overhead without benefit if no branching, persistence or approval is required.

questions.q: What problems does LangGraph address that a bare loop does not?
questions.a: Explicit branching, durable checkpoints, interrupts, multi-node composition and step inspection.

questions.q: Is LangGraph a better model?
questions.a: No. It is orchestration. Model quality is unchanged.

questions.q: What should you be able to do after a crash?
questions.a: Resume from the last checkpoint instead of restarting the whole run.

state-nodes-edges.explain:
## What it is

A LangGraph program has three parts:

- **State**: a typed schema (often a `TypedDict` or Pydantic model) holding everything the run knows: messages, plan, results, counters.
- **Nodes**: functions that take the state and return a **partial update** (e.g. `{"results": [...]}`).
- **Edges**: define the next node. Normal edges are fixed; conditional edges choose at runtime.

**Reducers** define how updates merge into a key: replace by default, or append (as for message lists) so parallel nodes do not overwrite each other.

```
class S(TypedDict):
    question: str
    docs: Annotated[list, add]
graph.add_node("search", search_fn)
graph.add_edge(START, "search")
```
Then compile and invoke. Think of it as a state machine whose transitions can be LLM-decided. Pitfall: forgetting a reducer on a key written by parallel branches. Exact API names change, so check current docs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The mental model is three words. **State** is the typed blob the run carries. **Nodes** are functions that take state and return a patch. **Edges** say who runs next, including conditionals.

If you cannot draw those, you will fight the framework.

## How it works + one small example

Define state with reducers on keys that multiple nodes touch (`append` for messages). A node should do one job: call a model, call a tool, decide, or transform. Edges are static or conditional functions of state.

Example: `retrieve` → `generate` → conditional to `tool` or `end`. Keep state small enough to checkpoint.

## Failure modes

1. **A mega-node that does retrieve, generate and pay.**

2. **Default replace reducer on a list two nodes append.**

3. **Putting huge blobs in state every step.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

State is the typed blob, nodes return patches, edges choose the next node. I set reducers on concurrent keys and I keep state checkpoint-sized.

## A concrete walk-through

Two parallel search nodes both wrote `results` and one vanished. You add an append reducer. Both findings survive.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about messages as state. Say: messages are one key, with an add-message reducer, not the whole story. Pins live in other keys.

## What I would measure

Lost concurrent updates, checkpoint size, node fan-in/out complexity.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Lost concurrent updates, checkpoint size, node fan-in/out complexity. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: State is typed and reduced. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: State is the typed blob, nodes return patches, edges choose the next node. I set reducers on concurrent keys and I keep state checkpoint-sized. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about messages as state. Say: messages are one key, with an add-message reducer, not the whole story. Pins live in other keys. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Nodes are single-purpose functions.
keyPoints: State is typed and reduced.
Nodes are single-purpose functions.
Edges, including conditionals, own control flow.
Set reducers on keys many nodes write.
Keep state small enough to persist.
Do not hide a whole agent inside one node without a reason.
State schema + node functions returning partial updates + edges
Reducers decide how concurrent updates merge

questions.q: What does a reducer do in a graph state?
questions.a: It defines how a node's update is merged into an existing key, for example appending to a list instead of overwriting. It is essential when several nodes or parallel branches write the same key.

questions.q: Two parallel nodes both write `results`, and one's output disappears. Why?
questions.a: The key uses the default replace behaviour, so the later write overwrote the earlier one. Annotate it with an append/merge reducer or give each branch its own key.

questions.q: Two parallel nodes append findings but only one set survives. Fix?
questions.a: Define an append/merge reducer for that key. Default is replace.

questions.q: What does a node return?
questions.a: A patch to state, not necessarily the whole object.

questions.q: What decides the next node?
questions.a: An edge — static or a function of state.

questions.q: Why not put a 20k PDF in state every step?
questions.a: Checkpoints and every later node will carry it. Store an id instead.

building-nodes.explain:
## What it is

A **node** is just a function (sync or async) from state to a partial state update. Keep nodes small and single-purpose: one LLM call, one tool execution, one validation.

**Typical nodes**: `plan` (LLM), `call_tools` (executes tool calls from the last message), `validate` (pure code), `summarise` (LLM).

**Good practice**
- Return only the keys you change; do not mutate input state.
- Put side effects (API calls, writes) in nodes that are safe to re-run or idempotent, since resume and retries may re-execute them.
- Keep prompts and parsing inside the node so it is unit-testable by calling the function with a fake state.
- Use pure-code nodes for deterministic work; reserve LLM nodes for judgement.

Bad pattern: one giant node doing the whole agent loop internally, which hides steps from checkpoints, tracing and interrupts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Nodes are where work happens: model call, tool, deterministic transform, decision. Small nodes are testable. A node that does four things is a hidden loop.

Interviews: give an example of each kind.

## How it works + one small example

`call_model` writes `messages`. `run_tools` executes declared calls and writes results. `validate` is pure code. `route` writes a next-step label. Keep side effects in obvious nodes so interrupts can sit in front of them.

Unit-test `validate` without a model. That is the point.

## Failure modes

1. **Side effect at the start of a node that later interrupts — resume doubles the email.**

2. **Model call buried inside `validate`.**

3. **Untestable nodes that need the whole graph.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I build small nodes: model, tools, transform, decide. Side effects sit after interrupts. I unit-test the deterministic ones.

## A concrete walk-through

`send_email` used to sit in the same node as `draft`. Resume after approval resent the mail. You split draft | interrupt | send. The bug dies.

## Interview follow-up

They ask how big a node should be. Say: one reason to change.

## What I would measure

Node unit-test coverage, double-effect incidents, average node size.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Node unit-test coverage, double-effect incidents, average node size. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: One job per node. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I build small nodes: model, tools, transform, decide. Side effects sit after interrupts. I unit-test the deterministic ones. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask how big a node should be. Say: one reason to change. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Kinds: model, tool, transform, decide.
keyPoints: One job per node.
Kinds: model, tool, transform, decide.
Side effects after interrupts.
Deterministic nodes are unit-tested.
Do not bury a loop in a single node.
Name nodes after the artefact they produce.
Node = function(state) -> partial update
Small, testable, idempotent where side effects exist

questions.q: Why should nodes with side effects be idempotent?
questions.a: Retries, crash recovery and resuming from a checkpoint can re-run a node. Without idempotency a repeated step might double-charge, double-send or duplicate writes.

questions.q: Your team put the full agent loop in one node and cannot see where it fails. What do you change?
questions.a: Split it into separate nodes (plan, act, observe, validate) connected by edges, so each step is checkpointed, traced, individually testable and interruptible.

questions.q: A node sends email then interrupts; after approval the email goes twice. Fix?
questions.a: Move the side effect after the interrupt, or guard it with an idempotency flag. Resume restarts the node.

questions.q: Which nodes should you unit-test without a model?
questions.a: Validators, reducers, routers — anything deterministic.

questions.q: Name four kinds of nodes.
questions.a: Model call, tool execution, processing/transform, decision/route.

questions.q: Why split draft and send?
questions.a: So approval can sit between them and resume cannot resend.

conditional-edges.explain:
## What it is

A **conditional edge** picks the next node at runtime using a **routing function** that reads state and returns a node name (or a list for fan-out).

Example: after the `agent` node, route to `tools` if the last message contains tool calls, otherwise to `END`.

```
def route(s):
    return "tools" if s["messages"][-1].tool_calls else END
graph.add_conditional_edges("agent", route)
```
Routers can be plain code (cheap, deterministic) or an LLM classification. Prefer code when the signal is structured.

**Pitfalls**: returning a name that is not mapped, no route for an unexpected state (dead end), or an LLM router with free-text output; constrain it to an enum. Always include a default route and unit-test the router on edge-case states.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Conditional edges are how a graph branches without becoming an agent-in-a-node. A function of state returns the next node name from a closed set. That is a router you can test.

Open-ended “the model decides any node” is an agent again — name it and cap it.

## How it works + one small example

`def route(state): return "tools" if state.tool_calls else "end"`. Map every return value. Unknown labels fail closed.

For richer routing, a model emits a label from an enum; code maps the enum. Do not let the model return an arbitrary string that you `eval` into a jump.

## Failure modes

1. **A default edge that swallows bugs.**

2. **A router that can jump to a write node with no approval.**

3. **Unmapped labels that crash mid-run.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Conditional edges are tested functions from state to a closed set of next nodes. If the model picks freely among all nodes, I treat that as an agent and cap it.

## A concrete walk-through

A router returned `"pay"` on a typo path because of a fuzzy match. You fail closed on unknown labels. The graph stops at `needs_human` instead of paying.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about dynamic node creation. Say: I do not create nodes at runtime in production. I route among declared ones.

## What I would measure

Misroute rate, unknown-label rate, unit tests per router.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Misroute rate, unknown-label rate, unit tests per router. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Routers return a closed set of node names. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Conditional edges are tested functions from state to a closed set of next nodes. If the model picks freely among all nodes, I treat that as an agent and cap it. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about dynamic node creation. Say: I do not create nodes at runtime in production. I route among declared ones. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Unknown labels fail closed.

Unknown labels fail closed.
A model may choose an enum; code maps it.
Do not jump to writes without the approval edge.
Test routers as pure functions.
An unbounded jump table is an agent.
Router function maps state to next node(s)
Use deterministic code routes where possible; enum-constrain LLM routers

questions.q: How would you implement the standard 'continue if tool calls else finish' decision?
questions.a: A conditional edge after the agent node whose routing function inspects the last message: return the tools node when it has tool calls, otherwise END.

questions.q: An LLM-based router sometimes outputs a label no node matches and the run crashes. Fix?
questions.a: Constrain output to an enum via structured output, validate it, and add a default or fallback route and a retry, so unexpected values cannot leave the graph without a next node.

questions.q: What does a conditional edge do?
questions.a: It picks the next node from state using a function, preferably over a closed label set.

questions.q: The router emits a typo label. What should happen?
questions.a: Fail closed to a safe node (human or end), not a fuzzy match to pay.

questions.q: When is a conditional edge the wrong tool?
questions.a: When the next step is a free-form tool choice among many. That is a tool-calling agent node with a cap.

questions.q: Why unit-test the router?
questions.a: It is deterministic control flow. You can cover the branches without paying for a model.

loops-for-retries-iteration.explain:
## What it is

Graphs can have **cycles**, which is how you express "try, check, retry" and agent loops: `generate -> validate -> (fail) -> generate`.

**Safe loop design**
- Keep a **counter** in state (`attempts`) incremented per pass.
- The router exits when validation passes **or** the counter reaches a cap.
- Feed the failure reason back into the next attempt so retries differ.
- Have a distinct exit for "gave up": escalate or return best-effort with a flag.
- A framework recursion limit is a backstop, not the design.

Use loops for: fixing invalid JSON, code that fails tests, agent tool loops, iterative refinement. Pitfall: identical retries at temperature 0 produce identical failures; change the input (error message), model or strategy.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Graphs loop when you edge back: tool → model → tool, or validate → fix → validate. Loops need the same caps as an agent: attempt counter, error fed back, give-up route.

A graph without a give-up edge is a prettier infinite loop.

## How it works + one small example

Store `attempts` in state. The validate node increments. The conditional edge goes to `fix` while attempts < N and errors exist, else `give_up` or `end`.

Feed the error into state so the next model call sees it. Do not retry on the same input without that.

## Failure modes

1. **Unlimited retries at temperature 0 hoping luck changes.**

2. **Loop with no attempt key so the cap cannot work.**

3. **Retrying a permanent validation error (schema).**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Graph loops are edges plus a counter. I cap attempts, feed the error back, and have a give-up route.

## A concrete walk-through

JSON validate failed 40 times. You add `attempts` and a give-up that returns the last error to the user. Median retries become 1; p95 becomes 3.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about unbounded “until quality is good.” Say: quality is a score with a cap, not a feeling.

## What I would measure

Loop iterations p95, give-up rate, success after retry.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Loop iterations p95, give-up rate, success after retry. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Loops are edges, not magic. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Graph loops are edges plus a counter. I cap attempts, feed the error back, and have a give-up route. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about unbounded “until quality is good.” Say: quality is a score with a cap, not a feeling. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Store an attempt counter in state.
keyPoints: Loops are edges, not magic.
Store an attempt counter in state.
Feed errors into the next iteration.
Give-up is a real node.
Do not retry permanent errors.
Caps apply to graph loops the same as while-loops.
Cycles express retry and iteration
Counter + validation exit + cap in state

questions.q: What three elements make a retry loop safe?
questions.a: A validation check that can exit, an attempt counter with a hard cap, and a defined give-up path. Also pass the error back so attempts differ.

questions.q: A validate-retry loop reaches the recursion limit every time on one input. What is likely wrong?
questions.a: The retry is repeating the same input, so the same failure recurs, or the validator can never pass. Add error feedback, a cap with fallback, and examine the validator and the case.

questions.q: Which design makes a validate-and-retry loop safe?
questions.a: An attempt counter with a cap, the error fed back, and a give-up route.

questions.q: Why is temperature 0 not a retry strategy?
questions.a: The input did not change. You will fail the same way. Change the input or give up.

questions.q: Where does the attempt counter live?
questions.a: In state, incremented by a node, read by the conditional edge.

questions.q: When is a loop the wrong structure?
questions.a: When the next action is unknown among many tools — use a capped agent node instead of exploding the graph.

checkpointing-persistence.explain:
## What it is

A **checkpointer** saves the graph state after each step, keyed by a **thread id**. Backends range from in-memory (tests) to SQLite or Postgres (durable production use).

What you get:
- **Memory across turns**: invoking the same thread continues from saved state.
- **Fault tolerance**: after a crash, resume from the last checkpoint.
- **Time travel / debugging**: inspect or fork from earlier states.
- **Human-in-the-loop**: pausing requires saved state.

You pass the thread id via config: `{"configurable": {"thread_id": "user-42"}}`.

Design considerations: state must be serialisable, checkpoints store everything in state (mind sensitive data and size), and an in-memory saver loses everything on restart. Use a durable store in production and prune old threads. Distinct from long-term memory, which stores facts across threads.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A checkpoint is a snapshot of state after a step so a crash or deploy is not a restart. In-memory savers die with the process. Production needs a durable store.

This is why people adopt a graph runtime.

## How it works + one small example

After each node (or each “superstep”), write state plus a cursor. On resume, load the latest checkpoint and run the next edge. Version the state schema. Use thread ids so two users do not share a checkpoint.

Do not checkpoint secrets in the clear. Redact tool args that contain tokens.

## Failure modes

1. **In-memory checkpointer in prod.**

2. **Schema change that cannot load old checkpoints.**

3. **Checkpointing raw card numbers.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I persist a checkpoint after each node so a crash is not a restart. Durable store, thread id, versioned schema, redacted secrets.

## A concrete walk-through

A redeploy wiped in-memory graphs. Users lost 10-minute runs. You switch to a Postgres saver. The next deploy resumes mid-approval.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about checkpoint size. Say: store artefact ids, not PDFs, or the saver becomes the bottleneck.

## What I would measure

Resume success after kill, checkpoint bytes, schema-migration failures.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Resume success after kill, checkpoint bytes, schema-migration failures. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Checkpoint after each node (or superstep). If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I persist a checkpoint after each node so a crash is not a restart. Durable store, thread id, versioned schema, redacted secrets. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about checkpoint size. Say: store artefact ids, not PDFs, or the saver becomes the bottleneck. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Use a durable store in production.
keyPoints: Checkpoint after each node (or superstep).
Use a durable store in production.
Thread ids isolate runs.
Version state so old checkpoints load or migrate.
Redact secrets from checkpoints.
Store ids, not giant blobs.
Checkpointer persists state per step under a thread id
Enables memory, crash resume, time travel and interrupts

questions.q: Why does a graph need a thread id when checkpointing?
questions.a: It identifies which saved conversation or run to load and continue; different threads keep isolated state. Without it, runs cannot resume or be kept separate per user.

questions.q: An agent forgets everything after a deploy. Likely cause and fix?
questions.a: An in-memory checkpointer was used, so state vanished on restart. Switch to a durable checkpointer such as Postgres or SQLite and keep thread ids stable.

questions.q: After a redeploy, conversations lose history. Most probable cause?
questions.a: An in-memory checkpointer. Use a durable store.

questions.q: What is a checkpoint for?
questions.a: To persist state so execution can survive interruption and resume.

questions.q: What must you version?
questions.a: The state schema. Old runs will resume after you ship.

questions.q: Why redact checkpoints?
questions.a: They are a new database of user data and tokens. Treat them like logs.

resuming-long-runs.explain:
## What it is

Long runs (minutes to days: research jobs, approvals, batch work) must survive crashes, deploys and waiting.

**How resume works**: with a checkpointer, invoking with the same thread id (and no new input, or a resume command) continues from the last completed step. Nodes after the failed step run; completed ones are not repeated.

**Design points**
- Make steps **idempotent**; the interrupted step may re-run.
- Keep state small: store big artifacts externally and keep references.
- Record progress so a UI can show status.
- Run long work in a worker or background job, not in a request that times out; resume from a queue.
- Version your graph: changing nodes while old checkpoints exist can break resumption.

Interview probe: "what happens if the server dies mid tool call?" Answer: the step re-runs from the last checkpoint, so tool calls need idempotency keys.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Resume is the user-visible payoff of checkpoints: a 20-minute research job survives a deploy. Resume must be safe: side effects are idempotent, the user sees the same thread, and you do not replay a paid API blindly.

Interviews: “how do you resume without double-paying?”

## How it works + one small example

On start, if a thread id has a checkpoint and status is interrupted, load and continue. Nodes that pay or email check an idempotency key in state first.

Tell the user “resuming step 7: ranking sources.” Cancel still works. If the schema cannot migrate, fail into a human queue rather than a corrupt continue.

## Failure modes

1. **Always starting a new thread so “resume” is a lie.**

2. **Replaying a non-idempotent node.**

3. **Resuming into a different code version that misunderstands state.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I resume from the last checkpoint on the same thread, with idempotent side effects and a user-visible step title. I do not silently start over.

## A concrete walk-through

A worker dies at step 9 of 12. The next worker picks up the thread, skips the already-paid search API via keys, and finishes. The user sees one job, not two bills.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about changing the graph mid-flight. Say: I migrate or I park the run. I do not pretend old edges still exist.

## What I would measure

Resume success, duplicate side effects after resume, user-visible “started over” tickets.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Resume success, duplicate side effects after resume, user-visible “started over” tickets. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Resume loads the thread’s latest checkpoint. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I resume from the last checkpoint on the same thread, with idempotent side effects and a user-visible step title. I do not silently start over. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about changing the graph mid-flight. Say: I migrate or I park the run. I do not pretend old edges still exist. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Side-effect nodes are idempotent.

questions.q: What happens to a step that was in flight when the server crashed?
questions.a: It was not checkpointed as complete, so it re-runs on resume. Therefore side-effecting steps need idempotency keys or checks to avoid duplicates.

questions.q: You deploy a renamed node while jobs are mid-run. Risk and mitigation?
questions.a: Old checkpoints may reference the old node and fail to resume. Version graphs, keep backward-compatible node names or migrate/drain in-flight runs before the change.

questions.q: Production runs die on deploys. Best structural fix?
questions.a: Checkpoint each step with idempotent actions and resume in workers.

questions.q: What must be true of a pay node for resume to be safe?
questions.a: It checks an idempotency key / persisted status before executing.

questions.q: The graph changed and an old run resumes. What do you do?
questions.a: Migrate state or park for a human. Do not jump into missing nodes.

questions.q: How does the UI talk about resume?
questions.a: Same job id, current step title, elapsed time. Not a second spinner.

human-in-the-loop-interrupts.explain:
## What it is

An **interrupt** pauses the graph at a point so a human can review, approve, edit or supply input, then execution continues.

Two common styles: static breakpoints before/after named nodes, or a dynamic `interrupt(value)` call inside a node that surfaces a payload to the caller and waits. The caller later resumes with a value (e.g. approve, edited text) on the same thread.

**Needs a checkpointer**, since the run may wait hours and the process may exit.

Use for: approving a payment or email, confirming a destructive action, correcting a plan, handling low confidence.

Gotchas: a node that is interrupted may re-execute from its start on resume, so put code with side effects after the interrupt, and keep pre-interrupt code idempotent. Define timeouts and what happens if nobody responds.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

An interrupt is a first-class pause: the graph stops before a node, waits for a value (approval, edit, extra info), then resumes. It is not a comment in the prompt saying “ask the user.”

This is how consequential tools get a tick inside a graph.

## How it works + one small example

Place `interrupt` before `execute_refund`. The UI reads the pending payload (amount, recipient), collects a tick or an edit, and the runtime resumes with that value in state. Denial routes to `aborted`.

Timeouts: an interrupt that waits forever is a leaked job. Expire it.

Test denial: the side effect must not run.

## Failure modes

1. **Prompt-only “please confirm” while the next node still runs.**

2. **Side effect before the interrupt in the same node.**

3. **No expiry on pending approvals.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Approval is a node — an interrupt — not a comment in the prompt. I resume with the user’s value, and denial is a tested path.

## A concrete walk-through

You move `interrupt` before `send`. A denied run never hits send. An expired interrupt goes to `aborted` after 24h and the user gets mail.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if a chat “yes” can complete the interrupt. Say: only if the UI turns it into the approval value. The model does not self-approve.

## What I would measure

Denied runs with zero side effects, expiry rate, time-to-approve, double-send after resume.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. questions.a: The process may stop while waiting for the human, so state must be saved and later reloaded by thread id to resume exactly where it paused.

inspecting-state-to-debug.explain:
## What it is

Because state is explicit and checkpointed, graphs are easier to debug than opaque loops.

**Tools**
- `get_state(config)` returns the current state and next nodes for a thread.
- State **history** lists past checkpoints; you can **replay** or **fork** from one with modified state to test a fix.
- **Streaming** modes emit per-node updates, so you watch the run live.
- **Tracing** (e.g. LangSmith or any OpenTelemetry-based setup) records each node's inputs, outputs, latency and token use.

Workflow: reproduce with the thread id, find the first step whose state is wrong, check that node's input, fix prompt/code, fork from just before it and re-run. Unit-test nodes with crafted states, and log routing decisions as they are the usual bug.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A wrong final answer in a graph is a state problem. Find the first checkpoint where a key went bad, inspect that node, fork and replay from the previous checkpoint. That is faster than rewriting the prompt blindly.

This is the observability pitch for graphs.

## How it works + one small example

Every run has a thread id and a list of checkpoints. UI: step list, state diff, node name. On a bad answer, walk backward until `amount` was still right. Open that node’s inputs.

Fork: copy state from checkpoint k, change one field or the node code, rerun forward. Do this on fixtures, not only on prod threads.

## Failure modes

1. **Debugging only the last message.**

2. **No diffs, so you cannot see which key changed.**

3. **Re-running from scratch and hoping.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I debug a graph by walking checkpoints to the first bad state, inspecting that node, and forking a replay. I do not start with a prompt rewrite.

## A concrete walk-through

Final refund is $400. Checkpoint 4 still has $40. Node `apply_coupon` doubled then the model “helpfully” added a zero. You fix the node and replay from 3. The prompt never changed.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about logging every token. Say: I log state diffs and tool args (redacted). Full tokens are optional and expensive.

## What I would measure

Time-to-first-bad-checkpoint, replay-from-fork success, incidents fixed without prompt changes.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-first-bad-checkpoint, replay-from-fork success, incidents fixed without prompt changes. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Walk checkpoints to the first bad key. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I debug a graph by walking checkpoints to the first bad state, inspecting that node, and forking a replay. I do not start with a prompt rewrite. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about logging every token. Say: I log state diffs and tool args (redacted). Full tokens are optional and expensive. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Diff state between steps.
