surfacing-progress-without-leaking-chain.explain:
## What it is

**Show steps as user-safe titles.** That is the progress rule when legal or product forbids thought streaming. `search_orders` becomes “Looking up your recent orders.” The operator can still open a locked trace.

This is the specific wording the checklist wants on top of general UX.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Interview closer for agent UX. They want the mapping, not a philosophy. On the job this is also how you pass a privacy review.

## How it works + one small example

Maintain a map `{tool_or_node: title}`. Unknown tools get a generic “Working” plus an operator alert to add a title. Never interpolate raw args into the title (`Looking up ${email}` can leak).

If you must show an argument, show a user-owned one you already display elsewhere (their ticket id).

## Failure modes

1. **Titles that include emails from tool args.**

2. **Falling back to the model’s thought when the map misses.**

3. **Different titles every run so the user cannot learn the sequence.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Progress is a stable, safe title map — not thoughts and not raw args. Missing mappings get a generic title and an operator ticket, not a leak.

## A concrete walk-through

A title once showed another customer’s email from a tool arg. You ban args in titles and add a review. The map is now 100% for production tools.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about i18n. The map is translatable copy, which thoughts are not.

## What I would measure

Unmapped-title rate, arg-interpolation incidents (0), translation coverage.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Unmapped-title rate, arg-interpolation incidents (0), translation coverage. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Progress titles come from a map, not from thoughts. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Progress is a stable, safe title map — not thoughts and not raw args. Missing mappings get a generic title and an operator ticket, not a leak. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about i18n. The map is translatable copy, which thoughts are not. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Do not interpolate raw tool args.

## What would change my mind

Interview closer for agent UX. They want the mapping, not a philosophy. On the job this is also how you pass a privacy review. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Stable titles beat clever ones. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

idempotent-writes.explain:
## What it is

**A retried “create ticket” must not open two tickets.** That is the user-visible idempotency rule. The runtime supplies a key; the ticket API stores it; a replay returns ticket 1882 again.

If the vendor cannot do keys, your ledger does.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the reliability interview closer. They will say “we retry.” You say “and the write is keyed.” On the job this is the incident you only want once.

## How it works + one small example

`create_ticket(key=run_id+step, payload)`. First call creates. Second returns the same id. Tests: call twice, assert one row. Resume tests included.

Name the key in the trace so you can prove it in an incident review.

## Failure modes

1. **Key from the model (unstable).**

2. **Key from a timestamp (changes on retry).**

3. **No test that double-call is safe.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

A retried create must return the same artefact. I key the write in the runtime and I test double-call equals one row.

## A concrete walk-through

Support saw two tickets per flaky run. You add `Idempotency-Key`. A week later the duplicate graph is flat. The incident doc cites the test.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about deletes. Same idea: a keyed delete is a no-op the second time.

## What I would measure

Duplicate artefacts per keyed write (0), test coverage of double-call.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Duplicate artefacts per keyed write (0), test coverage of double-call. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Creates and other writes use a runtime key. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: A retried create must return the same artefact. I key the write in the runtime and I test double-call equals one row. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about deletes. Same idea: a keyed delete is a no-op the second time. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Double-call equals one artefact.

## What would change my mind

This is the reliability interview closer. They will say “we retry.” You say “and the write is keyed.” On the job this is the incident you only want once. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Keys are stable across retry and resume. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: Support saw two tickets per flaky run. You add `Idempotency-Key`. A week later the duplicate graph is flat. The incident doc cites the test. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: `create_ticket(key=run_id+step, payload)`. First call creates. Second returns the same id. Tests: call twice, assert one row. Resume tests included. Name the key in the trace so you can prove it in an incident review.
keyPoints: Creates and other writes use a runtime key.
Double-call equals one artefact.
Keys are stable across retry and resume.
The model does not invent the key.
Vendors without keys get a local ledger.
Test it; do not assume.

questions.q: A retried create_ticket opened two tickets. What was missing?
questions.a: An idempotency key stored with the first create so the second call returns the same id.

questions.q: Who creates the key?
questions.a: The runtime, from run and step ids — not the model, not the clock alone.

questions.q: How do you test it?
questions.a: Invoke the write twice in a test and assert one row / one id.

questions.q: The vendor has no header. Now what?
questions.a: A local ledger keyed by the step; skip the vendor call if the ledger says done.

questions.q: Does delete need the same treatment?
questions.a: Yes. A retried delete should be a no-op, not a surprising error that the agent misreads as “still there.”

one-agent-several-frameworks.explain:
## What it is

The capstone idea: build the **same agent** (say, a research-and-report agent with search, a calculator and an approval step) in several frameworks and compare. The agent's behaviour is the constant; the framework is the variable.

**Method**
1. Fix the spec: inputs, tools, success criteria, an eval set of 20-50 tasks.
2. Implement it in each framework (e.g. LangGraph, Google ADK, CrewAI, an Agno-style framework, the OpenAI Agents SDK).
3. Run the same evals; record accuracy, latency, tokens, lines of code, debugging effort, and deployment effort.
4. Write down what each framework made easy or hard.

**What you learn**: most frameworks wrap the same loop (model, tools, state); differences are in control flow, persistence, observability and ergonomics. Interview value: you can justify a choice from experience, not from marketing. Framework APIs change quickly, so check current docs.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

After the primitives, implement the same small agent in more than one framework. You learn what each abstracts (loop, state, tools, interrupts) and what you still own (evals, permissions, tool functions).

Interviews: “I built the same refund helper in X and Y; here is what moved and what did not.”

## How it works + one small example

Pick a 3-tool agent with one write and a cap. Port it to a graph runtime and a light SDK. Keep tools as plain functions or MCP. Keep the eval set outside.

Write down: who owns the loop, how you persist, how you approve, how you trace. That table is the capstone artefact.

## Failure modes

1. **Only clicking a quickstart and calling it a comparison.**

2. **Rewriting tools into each vendor’s wrapper so you cannot port.**

3. **No shared eval, so “better” is a vibe.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I implement the same small agent in more than one framework to see what each abstracts. Tools, prompts and evals stay mine.

## A concrete walk-through

You port a 80-line loop to LangGraph and the OpenAI Agents SDK. The eval is identical. You learn interrupts are cheaper in the graph and handoffs are cheaper in the SDK. The table goes in the write-up.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which you would pick. Point at the table and the product constraint, not a favourite logo.

## What I would measure

Shared eval scores, lines of framework-specific glue, time-to-add an approval.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Shared eval scores, lines of framework-specific glue, time-to-add an approval. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Same agent, several frameworks. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I implement the same small agent in more than one framework to see what each abstracts. Tools, prompts and evals stay mine. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask which you would pick. Point at the table and the product constraint, not a favourite logo. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Keep tools and evals outside the framework.
keyPoints: Same agent, several frameworks.
Keep tools and evals outside the framework.
Write a comparison table you can defend.
Quickstarts are not a comparison.
The loop primitive must still be explainable.
Pick from constraints, not logos.
Keep the agent spec and evals fixed; vary the framework
Compare accuracy, cost, latency, code size, debugging and deployment

questions.q: Why implement the same agent in several frameworks?
questions.a: To compare under identical specs and evals, exposing real trade-offs in control, persistence, observability, effort and cost, so a later choice is evidence-based.

questions.q: What must stay constant for the comparison to be fair?
questions.a: The task spec, tools, model, prompts as far as possible, and the eval set and metrics. Otherwise differences come from setup rather than the framework.

questions.q: What should stay outside the framework?
questions.a: Tool functions or MCP servers, prompts, and the eval set.

questions.q: A teammate rewrote every tool as a vendor class. What did they lose?
questions.a: Portability. The next framework now needs a rewrite.

questions.q: What goes in the comparison table?
questions.a: Loop ownership, persistence, approval, tracing, multi-agent, vendor lock-in.

graph-based-stateful-orchestration.explain:
## What it is

**Graph-based, stateful orchestration** (LangGraph is the best-known example) models the agent as nodes over shared state with explicit edges. State is a first-class object, checkpointed per step.

**Strengths**: precise control over branching and loops, durable resume, interrupts for approvals, time-travel debugging, clear multi-agent wiring, and each step visible in traces.

**Costs**: more upfront design, a graph vocabulary to learn, boilerplate for simple cases, and coupling to the framework's state and checkpoint formats.

**Mental test**: if you can draw your agent's flow as a state machine and you care about what happens on failure or waiting, the graph model fits. If it is "ask the model, run tools, repeat", it is more machinery than you need.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

LangGraph’s pitch in the capstone: low-level graph/state orchestration for long-running, stateful agents. Use it in the project when you actually need those properties.

Do not add it as a sticker.

## How it works + one small example

If your capstone has resume, approval, or a named graph of stages, implement those on a graph. If it is a weekend coder with three tools, a loop is the honest implementation — you can still discuss graphs in the write-up.

## Failure modes

1. **A graph of one node.**

2. **No checkpoint though the story was “stateful.”**

3. **Cannot explain a step without the library docs open.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use graph orchestration in the capstone when I need long-running state, not as decoration. I can still draw the primitive loop.

## A concrete walk-through

Your capstone is a claims helper with approval. You implement it as a graph with a saver. The write-up says why a loop would have lost deploys.

## Interview follow-up

They ask you to rewrite it as a loop on the whiteboard. You can.

## What I would measure

Whether resume and interrupt exist for real, and whether you can explain a step without docs.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether resume and interrupt exist for real, and whether you can explain a step without docs. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Graph/state orchestration is for long-running stateful work. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I use graph orchestration in the capstone when I need long-running state, not as decoration. I can still draw the primitive loop. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask you to rewrite it as a loop on the whiteboard. You can. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Use it when the capstone needs it.
keyPoints: Graph/state orchestration is for long-running stateful work.
Use it when the capstone needs it.
A one-node graph is theatre.
You must still explain the primitive loop.
Checkpoints must be real.
Write why you chose it.
Explicit nodes, edges and checkpointed state
Best for branching, durability, approvals and auditability

questions.q: What does a graph-based framework make first-class that simple loops do not?
questions.a: State and control flow: typed state, explicit edges and loops, per-step checkpoints, interrupts and inspection.

questions.q: Your flow is: classify, then one of three handlers, then review, then publish with approval. Fit?
questions.a: Strong fit for a graph: classification routes via a conditional edge, handlers are nodes, and approval needs an interrupt with persisted state.

questions.q: When does the capstone honestly need a graph?
questions.a: When you have durable resume, interrupts, or explicit stages you want in code.

questions.q: What is LangGraph positioned as?
questions.a: A low-level orchestration runtime for long-running, stateful agents.

questions.q: A one-node graph with an inner while-loop — verdict?
questions.a: An agent with extra ceremony. Either draw the stages or drop the graph.

questions.q: What must you still be able to do in the interview?
questions.a: Explain the underlying agent loop without the library.

where-explicit-control-flow-wins.explain:
## What it is

**Explicit control flow** means you, not the model, decide the sequence: code defines stages, branches and retry rules, and the LLM fills in content within each.

**It wins when**
- Compliance or safety requires certain steps always happen (verify identity before refund).
- The process is well understood (an SOP) so model-driven planning adds variance.
- You need predictable cost and latency.
- Failures must be handled deterministically.
- Testing needs reproducible paths.

**Autonomous agent loops win** for open-ended tasks where the steps are not known. Many production systems are **workflows with agentic pockets**: fixed skeleton, free tool use in a bounded step. A good rule: use the least autonomy that meets the task, and add autonomy where evals show it pays off.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Explicit control flow wins when compliance, persistence, loops you can test, or human-in-the-loop matter. That is the LangGraph-shaped corner of the capstone comparison.

If your only requirement is “try tools until done,” explicit edges are extra.

## How it works + one small example

List capstone requirements. Tick: must verify identity first? must persist? must approve? must retry validate at most 3? Those ticks are edges. Implement them as edges so you can show a test.

Leave open-ended research as a capped agent node inside the graph.

## Failure modes

1. **Putting compliance in the prompt because the graph felt heavy.**

2. **Explicit edges for a toy with no constraint.**

3. **Untested edges.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Explicit control flow wins for compliance, persistence, tested loops and approvals. I put those on edges. I leave true unknowns in a capped agent node.

## A concrete walk-through

Identity-then-refund is an edge. You write a test that execute is unreachable without verify. That test is the interview artefact.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if all agents should be graphs. No. Only those with these ticks.

## What I would measure

Requirements implemented as edges vs prompts, tests per edge.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Requirements implemented as edges vs prompts, tests per edge. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Wins: compliance order, persistence, tested loops, HITL. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Explicit control flow wins for compliance, persistence, tested loops and approvals. I put those on edges. I leave true unknowns in a capped agent node. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if all agents should be graphs. No. Only those with these ticks. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Those become edges you test.
keyPoints: Wins: compliance order, persistence, tested loops, HITL.
Those become edges you test.
Unknown research stays a capped node.
Prompt-only compliance is a fail.
Do not graph a toy.
The test is the artefact.
Code decides sequence; model fills in content
Wins for known processes, compliance, predictable cost

questions.q: When should you prefer explicit control flow over a free-running agent?
questions.a: When the process is known, steps must always happen for compliance or safety, cost and latency must be predictable, and deterministic failure handling and testing are needed.

questions.q: A refund agent sometimes skips the identity check. Fix?
questions.a: Make identity verification a mandatory node or gate in code before any refund tool is reachable, instead of relying on the prompt. Add tests asserting the refund tool cannot run without it.

questions.q: Which requirement most clearly favours a graph framework?
questions.a: Durable resumable runs with human approval steps, or a mandatory order you must test.

questions.q: Where should “verify identity first” live?
questions.a: As a mandatory edge/gate in code, not as a prompt sentence.

questions.q: When do explicit edges lose?
questions.a: When the path is unknown and short-lived and you have no resume need.

questions.q: How do you prove the gate?
questions.a: A test that the write node is unreachable without the verify state.

google-s-adk.explain:
## What it is

**Google's Agent Development Kit (ADK)** is an open-source, code-first framework for building agents and multi-agent systems (Python and other languages; check current docs). It is designed to work well with Gemini and Google Cloud but is model-agnostic in intent.

**Typical concepts**: agents (LLM agents), workflow agents for sequential, parallel and loop control flow, tools (functions, other agents, MCP tools), sessions and state, memory services, callbacks/guardrails, evaluation tooling, and a dev UI to run and trace agents.

**Where it fits**: teams on Google Cloud wanting a deploy path (e.g. to Vertex AI Agent Engine or Cloud Run) and built-in A2A support. Trade-offs: newer ecosystem than some peers, and tight convenience with Google services. Verify features against current documentation before relying on them in an interview.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Google’s Agent Development Kit is an open-source way to build agents with first-class agent, session/state, tools, multi-agent, deployment and A2A-related abstractions. In the capstone you touch it enough to say what it owns versus a raw loop.

You do not need to memorise every class.

## How it works + one small example

Build the same small agent: session state, a couple of tools, a child agent, a deploy path as documented. Note how sessions persist and how tools are declared. Compare to your loop: what did you stop writing?

Read current ADK docs; they move. Do not quote a blog from last year.

## Failure modes

1. **Listing ADK features you never ran.**

2. **Coupling the whole capstone to Google-only models if you did not mean to.**

3. **Skipping session state then claiming you “used ADK.”**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I used ADK enough to see its agent, session, tool and deploy abstractions. I can map them onto state/tools/policy/loop. I did not memorise the catalogue.

## A concrete walk-through

You port the 3-tool helper to ADK, deploy a local runner, and write four bullets: session, tool, child agent, deploy. That is enough for the comparison table.

## Interview follow-up

They ask A2A in ADK. Say what the current docs say and that A2A is agent-to-agent, not MCP.

## What I would measure

Whether you actually ran a session and a deploy, not just cloned the repo.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether you actually ran a session and a deploy, not just cloned the repo. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: ADK: agent, session/state, tools, multi-agent, deploy, A2A-related bits. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I used ADK enough to see its agent, session, tool and deploy abstractions. I can map them onto state/tools/policy/loop. I did not memorise the catalogue. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask A2A in ADK. Say what the current docs say and that A2A is agent-to-agent, not MCP. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Map them onto the four primitives.

building-debugging-deploying-agents.explain:
## What it is

The agent lifecycle in any framework has three phases.

**Build**: define instructions, tools (typed, well described), model, and state/memory; compose sub-agents or graph stages; write evals early.

**Debug**: use the framework's dev UI or tracing to see each model call, tool call, arguments and results; reproduce from saved sessions; replay with changes; check the first deviation. Unit-test tools and routers separately from the LLM.

**Deploy**: package as a service (container), expose an API (often streaming), persist sessions in a real database, set secrets via environment, add auth, rate limits and budgets, observability (traces, metrics, cost), and a rollout plan (versioned prompts, canary, rollback).

Common gaps: dev-only in-memory sessions, no timeouts, no tracing in production.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

ADK’s emphasis is the whole lifecycle: build, debug, evaluate, deploy — not a notebook `complete()`. The capstone should show at least one of each: a run, a trace you used to fix a bug, an eval number, a deploy path.

Interviews: “how did you debug a wrong step?”

## How it works + one small example

Keep traces on. Fix one real bug from a checkpoint or span. Run a 20-case eval before and after. Deploy via the documented path (local or cloud). Write the four screenshots/logs into the report.

If the kit’s eval story is thin, your external eval set still counts — say so.

## Failure modes

1. **Deploy without an eval.**

2. **Debug by rerunning hoping.**

3. **Build only in a notebook with no service.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I treat the kit as a lifecycle: I can point to a trace I used, an eval I ran, and a deploy I did. A notebook call is not the capstone.

## A concrete walk-through

A wrong tool showed up in the trace. You tighten the description, eval +8 points, deploy the same runner. The write-up has the three artefacts.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about production deploy. Name the path you actually used and the gap that remains.

## What I would measure

Bugs found via traces, eval delta, whether a second machine can hit the deployed agent.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Bugs found via traces, eval delta, whether a second machine can hit the deployed agent. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Lifecycle: build, debug, evaluate, deploy. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

## What it is

**CrewAI** offers two layers. **Crews** are teams of role-based agents (each with a role, goal, backstory and tools) working on **tasks** with a process (sequential or hierarchical with a manager). **Flows** are the event-driven, more deterministic layer: Python methods connected by decorators to control state, branching and the order in which crews or plain code run.

**Why both**: crews give quick collaborative agents; flows add structure, state and control, which production needs.

**Use**: crews for self-contained collaborative subtasks; wrap them in a flow for predictable orchestration, retries and persistence. Trade-offs: role prompts can encourage verbose, costly agent chatter; check current docs as APIs evolve.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

CrewAI splits collaborative Crews (role-based agents) from Flows (more controlled workflow-style orchestration). The capstone lesson is when you want roles versus when you want a flow.

Do not use a crew for a known three-step file job.

## How it works + one small example

Build a tiny crew (researcher + writer) and a tiny flow (extract → validate → store). Run the same eval. Note variance and latency. Put the numbers in the table.

Read current CrewAI docs for the exact names; do not invent APIs.

## Failure modes

1. **A crew on a deterministic pipeline.**

2. **A flow that still lets every node call every tool unbounded.**

3. **No numbers.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Crews are role-based collaboration. Flows are controlled orchestration. I use a crew only when roles help; I use a flow when the path is known.

## A concrete walk-through

Invoice filing as a crew wanders. As a flow it is boring and faster. You keep the crew for a research memo. The table has both.

## Interview follow-up

They ask which is “more agentic.” Say: the crew. That is not a compliment on a known path.

## What I would measure

Variance and latency crew vs flow on the same task.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Variance and latency crew vs flow on the same task. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Crews: role-based collaboration. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Crews are role-based collaboration. Flows are controlled orchestration. I use a crew only when roles help; I use a flow when the path is known. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask which is “more agentic.” Say: the crew. That is not a compliment on a known path. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Flows: workflow-style control.

role-based-vs-graph-orchestration.explain:
## What it is

Two mental models for multi-agent design:

**Role-based** (CrewAI style): you describe agents as team members (researcher, writer, reviewer) with roles and goals, and assign tasks. Quick to express, readable by non-engineers, but control flow is partly implicit and can be harder to make deterministic.

**Graph-based** (LangGraph style): you describe states, nodes and transitions. More verbose, but control, persistence and failure paths are explicit.

**Choose** role-based for prototypes and collaborative content tasks; graph-based when you need guarantees, resumability, approvals or fine debugging. They are not exclusive: role-like prompts can live inside graph nodes. Interview answer: describe the control-versus-speed trade-off and what you measured.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Role-based systems are fast to write (“you are the researcher”). Graphs are explicit about edges. The capstone comparison is taste plus constraints: audit and resume push graph; a low-risk draft can be roles.

Say the failure mode of each.

## How it works + one small example

Role risk: hidden control flow, harder tests, leftover roles. Graph risk: ceremony, slower first demo. For the write-up, implement a slice both ways or be honest that you implemented one and reasoned the other.

## Failure modes

1. **Declaring a winner without a eval.**

2. **Roles with no output contract.**

3. **A graph nobody on the team can draw.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Roles are fast and fuzzy. Graphs are explicit and heavier. I pick from audit/resume needs versus speed, and I name the failure mode I am accepting.

## A concrete walk-through

A policy team needs an audit path: you graph it. A blog outline: you crew it. You refuse to use one style for both just for consistency theatre.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if roles can be tested. Yes, if you add contracts; at that point you have a graph in disguise.

## What I would measure

Time-to-first-demo vs test coverage of the path.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-first-demo vs test coverage of the path. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Roles: speed, hidden edges. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Roles are fast and fuzzy. Graphs are explicit and heavier. I pick from audit/resume needs versus speed, and I name the failure mode I am accepting. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if roles can be tested. Yes, if you add contracts; at that point you have a graph in disguise. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Graphs: explicit edges, more ceremony.

agents-teams-workflows.explain:
## What it is

Some frameworks (the Agno family is one example) organise building blocks as three levels:

- **Agent**: a model with instructions, tools, knowledge and memory.
- **Team**: several agents coordinated by a leader that delegates, routes or collaborates.
- **Workflow**: a defined, deterministic sequence of steps (agents, teams or code) with state, branching and loops.

This maps to the autonomy ladder: use a single **agent** for open-ended tasks, a **team** when specialisation helps, and a **workflow** when the process is known and must be repeatable. Start at the lowest level that works.

Check current docs for exact names and features, as these frameworks evolve fast.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Agno (and similar kits) split Agents, Teams and Workflows: autonomy, coordination, and deterministic paths. The capstone is to use the right noun. Calling everything an agent is how reviews go nowhere.

## How it works + one small example

Implement one of each if the kit allows: a single agent, a two-member team, a three-step workflow. Same eval. Write the distinction in your words, not the landing page’s.

Autonomy still needs a cap. A “team” still needs a contract.

## Failure modes

1. **A team of one.**

2. **A workflow that is secretly an unbounded team.**

3. **Copy-pasted marketing definitions.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Agent is autonomy, team is coordination, workflow is a known path. I use the noun that matches the control-flow owner, and I cap autonomy.

## A concrete walk-through

You file invoices with a workflow, research with an agent, and a rare multi-source brief with a team. The write-up uses those three examples.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if Agno is required. Say: the nouns are the lesson; the kit is one implementation.

## What I would measure

Whether each noun in the project matches the actual control flow.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether each noun in the project matches the actual control flow. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Agent = autonomy (capped). If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Agent is autonomy, team is coordination, workflow is a known path. I use the noun that matches the control-flow owner, and I cap autonomy. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if Agno is required. Say: the nouns are the lesson; the kit is one implementation. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Team = coordination.

## What would change my mind

Agno (and similar kits) split Agents, Teams and Workflows: autonomy, coordination, and deterministic paths. The capstone is to use the right noun. Calling everything an agent is how reviews go nowhere. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Workflow = known path. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

the-production-runtime-layer.explain:
## What it is

Frameworks often separate **defining agents** from **running them in production**. The production runtime layer provides what an agent library alone does not:

- An **API server** with streaming endpoints and session handling.
- **Persistent** sessions, memory and run history.
- **Auth, rate limiting, multi-tenant isolation.**
- **Background execution**, queues, scheduling, retries.
- **Tracing, metrics and monitoring**; a UI to inspect runs.
- **Deployment** packaging (containers) in your own cloud.

Whether the runtime comes from the framework (AgentOS-style offerings), a cloud platform, or your own FastAPI plus a queue, the checklist is the same. Prefer runtimes that keep data in your environment if privacy matters. Verify what is open source versus hosted before committing.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

A runtime layer is how an agent becomes a service: HTTP or queue in, auth, session, concurrency, timeouts, traces out. The capstone should expose the agent as something another process can call, not only a CLI.

This is what “production” means at this level.

## How it works + one small example

Wrap `run(thread_id, message)` behind a small server. Add auth, a timeout, a concurrency cap, and a trace id. Persist sessions. Document how to call it.

If the kit has a runtime, use it and note what it gave you. If not, a thin FastAPI/worker is enough to talk about.

## Failure modes

1. **CLI-only capstone claiming production.**

2. **No timeout on the service.**

3. **One global session for all users.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Production runtime means the agent is a service: auth, session, timeout, concurrency, traces. A CLI is a demo.

## A concrete walk-through

You add a `/runs` endpoint with a thread id and a 60s timeout. A second terminal can talk to it. The write-up shows the curl and the trace id.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about Kubernetes. Say: I have a process with those properties; the rest is packaging I can name but did not need for the lesson.

## What I would measure

Whether a second process can call it, timeout behaviour, session isolation.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Whether a second process can call it, timeout behaviour, session isolation. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Runtime: service interface, auth, session, timeout, concurrency, traces. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Production runtime means the agent is a service: auth, session, timeout, concurrency, traces. A CLI is a demo. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about Kubernetes. Say: I have a process with those properties; the rest is packaging I can name but did not need for the lesson. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: CLI-only is not production.

## What it is

The **OpenAI Agents SDK** style is code-first and lightweight: you define **agents** (instructions, tools, model), and an agent can **hand off** to another agent, which then takes over the conversation. A runner executes the loop, with **guardrails** for input and output checks and built-in **tracing**.

**Handoff vs tool**: a tool call returns control to the caller with a result; a handoff transfers control so the new agent responds directly. Use handoffs for routing to specialists (triage -> billing / tech), tools/agent-as-tool for delegated sub-work where the caller stays in charge.

Benefits: few concepts, easy to read. Limits: less built-in graph/persistence machinery, so durability, complex branching and approval flows are yours to build or pair with other tools. Check current docs for API details.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

The OpenAI Agents SDK style is code-first: tools, handoffs, sessions, guardrails, tracing, specialist agents as Python. The capstone uses it to feel a light loop with first-class handoffs.

Compare that lightness to a graph when you need interrupts.

## How it works + one small example

Implement two specialists and a handoff, a guardrail on a write, and look at the trace UI. Keep the same eval. Note what you did not get (durable graph interrupts) and what you did (fast handoff).

## Failure modes

1. **Handoff without a contract.**

2. **Ignoring guardrails then claiming the SDK lesson.**

3. **No look at traces.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I built a code-first agent with tools, a handoff, a guardrail and a trace. I know when I would still want a graph (durable approval).

## A concrete walk-through

Triage agent hands off to billing with a typed brief. A guardrail blocks a refund over a cap. The trace shows the hop. That is the SDK page of the table.

## Interview follow-up

They ask SDK vs LangGraph. Light loop + handoffs vs durable graph. You have both rows.

## What I would measure

Handoff contract-valid rate, guardrail blocks, time-to-first-trace.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Handoff contract-valid rate, guardrail blocks, time-to-first-trace. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: SDK style: code-first tools, handoffs, sessions, guardrails, traces. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I built a code-first agent with tools, a handoff, a guardrail and a trace. I know when I would still want a graph (durable approval). If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask SDK vs LangGraph. Light loop + handoffs vs durable graph. You have both rows. ## What it is

**Lightweight SDKs** (agents, tools, handoffs, a runner) have a small surface and quick start. **Graph frameworks** have more concepts (state, reducers, checkpointers, edges) but give control and durability.

| Need | Lean towards |
|---|---|
| Prototype, routing among a few specialists | Lightweight SDK |
| Long runs, approvals, resumability | Graph framework |
| Complex branching and parallelism | Graph framework |
| Minimal dependencies and readability | Lightweight SDK |

Both can use the same models and tools (often via MCP). Migration cost is real: prompts and tools port easily; state and flow logic do not. Pick based on the requirement list, and keep tools and prompts framework-independent to preserve options.

This is the comparison row: a lightweight SDK-style loop versus a graph-oriented or multi-agent-first framework. Constraints decide. Do not pick from Twitter.

I compare a light SDK loop to a graph by constraint: resume and approval versus speed and handoffs. I do not pick a side for identity.

## A concrete walk-through

Your table: SDK wins time-to-demo; graph wins kill-test resume. You pick graph for the graded capstone because approval was required.

## Interview follow-up

## What I would measure

Time-to-demo, resume test, approval test — all in the table.

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-demo, resume test, approval test — all in the table. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Compare by constraint, not identity. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They try to bait a favourite. Repeat the constraint. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. abstraction-level.explain:
## What it is

Frameworks sit on a spectrum of **abstraction**.

- **Low**: raw model API + your loop. Max control, most code.
- **Mid**: SDK with agents, tools, handoffs; small abstractions you can read.
- **High**: role/crew/team metaphors, auto-planning, many built-ins. Fast start, but behaviour hides in prompts and internals.

**Trade-offs**: higher abstraction speeds the demo and hurts when you must debug, customise prompts or control costs, because behaviour is opaque. Lower abstraction costs time up front and pays back in transparency.

Heuristic: choose the lowest abstraction whose conveniences you would otherwise write yourself, and be able to see the actual prompts and API calls the framework sends (use tracing). If you cannot, that is a warning sign.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Abstraction level is how much loop/state/tool wiring you still write. High abstraction (crews) is fast and opaque. Low (hand-rolled loop or LangGraph) is verbose and inspectable. The capstone table needs this row.

Neither is morally better.

## How it works + one small example

For each kit, write: what you no longer see (call ids? checkpoints? prompts?). If you cannot debug without reading the source, the abstraction is high. If you wrote 200 lines to send an email, it is low.

Pick the lowest abstraction that still ships the constraint.

## Failure modes

1. **Highest abstraction as a default.**

2. **Lowest as a flex on a toy.**

3. **Not knowing what is hidden.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I choose the lowest abstraction that still meets the constraint. I can name what each kit hides. Hidden call ids are a cost.

## A concrete walk-through

Crew hid a retry you did not want. You dropped to a graph for that path. The table’s “abstraction” row says so.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for a number. Say: I count the layers between my tool function and the model call.

## What I would measure

Layers between tool and model, time-to-find a call id in a trace.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Layers between tool and model, time-to-find a call id in a trace. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Abstraction = how much of the loop is hidden. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I choose the lowest abstraction that still meets the constraint. I can name what each kit hides. Hidden call ids are a cost. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask for a number. Say: I count the layers between my tool function and the model call. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: High: fast, opaque.

questions.a: Behaviour is hidden in framework prompts and internals, making debugging, cost control and customisation hard when something goes wrong.

control-over-execution.explain:
## What it is

How much control you have over **how the run proceeds** differs by framework.

Dimensions to compare:
- Can you **force** a step order or gate a tool behind a check?
- Can you **limit** steps, time, tokens and tool calls?
- Can you **pause** for approval and **resume** later?
- Can you **intercept** model/tool calls (callbacks, middleware) for guardrails, logging and redaction?
- Can you run steps **in parallel** and control concurrency?
- Is the **loop** itself overridable?

Graph frameworks tend to offer the most explicit control; role/agentic frameworks offer convenience but less determinism; lightweight SDKs sit between, with hooks and guardrails. Match control to risk: the more costly a wrong action, the more explicit control you need.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Control is whether you can force an order, a cap, an interrupt. Frameworks differ. The capstone row is “can I make verify-then-pay a guarantee?” If the answer is “I asked the model,” control is low.

## How it works + one small example

For each kit, try to implement a mandatory gate. If you can write a test that execute is unreachable, control is high. If you can only prompt, control is low.

Write the result in the table. This row often decides the graded project.

## Failure modes

1. **Claiming control you did not test.**

2. **Prompt-only gates in a “high control” kit because you did not read the interrupt docs.**

3. **Ignoring caps as control.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Control means I can force order, caps and interrupts in code and test them. I do not call prompt advice control.

## A concrete walk-through

SDK: you implement a guardrail. Graph: you implement an interrupt. Crew: you cannot prove order. The table is honest.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if control always wins. No — if you do not need it, paying for it is ceremony.

## What I would measure

Gates you can test, prompt-only gates remaining.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Gates you can test, prompt-only gates remaining. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Control = forced order, caps, interrupts in code. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Control means I can force order, caps and interrupts in code and test them. I do not call prompt advice control. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if control always wins. No — if you do not need it, paying for it is ceremony. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Prompt advice is not control.

questions.q: What execution controls would you check when evaluating a framework?
questions.a: Ability to enforce step order and gates, set budgets, pause/resume with approval, intercept model and tool calls, control parallelism, and override the loop.

questions.q: You need every tool call logged and PII redacted before reaching the model. What capability matters?
questions.a: Interception hooks or middleware around model and tool calls, so redaction and logging apply uniformly regardless of what the agent decides.

questions.q: How do you know a framework gives control over execution?
questions.a: You can implement a gate in code and test that a write is unreachable without it.

questions.a: No. The model can skip it. Control is a runtime edge.

questions.a: Control — especially approval and mandatory order.

questions.q: You used a high-control kit but only prompted. Verdict?
questions.a: You left the control on the table. Implement the interrupt or do not claim the row.

state-persistence.explain:
## What it is

**State** is what the agent knows during a run (messages, plan, results); **persistence** keeps it beyond the process.

Frameworks differ:
- **Graph frameworks**: checkpointers save state per step under a thread id.
- **SDKs**: session objects store message history (in memory, SQLite, or a database).
- **Role/team frameworks**: memory modules, storage for sessions and run history.

Questions to ask: where is it stored; can I use my own database; is state serialisable and versioned; can I resume mid-run, or only continue a conversation; how do I delete data (privacy); and can I separate **short-term** (thread) from **long-term** (cross-session) memory?

Resume mid-run is the hard capability: continuing a chat is easy, restarting a half-finished tool-using run safely is not.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

State/persistence is whether a run survives a process death and whether structured flags exist. Compare savers, thread ids, and what is actually stored. A “memory” feature that is only the last messages is not persistence.

## How it works + one small example

Kill-test each kit you used. Note in-memory defaults. Note whether flags besides messages persist. That is the row.

If a kit cannot persist, say so and keep the loop short or add your own store.

## Failure modes

1. **Calling chat history persistence.**

2. **Skipping the kill-test.**

3. **Secrets in the saver.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I compare persistence by kill-test and by whether structured flags survive, not by a memory marketing word.

## A concrete walk-through

Graph: kill-test passes with Postgres. SDK session: messages survive, flags you added in a dict may not unless you stored them. You write that gap down.

## Interview follow-up

They ask if you can bolt on Redis. Yes — then it is your persistence, not the kit’s. Say so.

## What I would measure

Kill-test per kit, flags survived, secret scans on the store.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Kill-test per kit, flags survived, secret scans on the store. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Persistence = survive process death. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I compare persistence by kill-test and by whether structured flags survive, not by a memory marketing word. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask if you can bolt on Redis. Yes — then it is your persistence, not the kit’s. Say so. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Kill-test every kit.

Kill-test every kit.
Messages-only is not enough.
Flags and keys must survive.
In-memory defaults fail prod.
Bolted-on stores are yours, not the kit’s.
Compare storage backend, serialisation, versioning, resume granularity
Distinguish thread state from long-term memory

questions.q: Distinguish conversation persistence from run resumption.
questions.a: Conversation persistence reloads message history for the next turn; run resumption continues a half-finished multi-step run from the last completed step, needing step-level checkpoints and idempotent actions.

questions.q: Compliance needs deletion of a user's data on request. What state design supports it?
questions.a: Key all persisted state and memory by user id or thread id in a store you control, with a delete path covering checkpoints, memories and traces, plus retention limits.

questions.q: How do you compare state/persistence across frameworks?
questions.a: Kill-test them and check whether structured flags and keys survive, not just messages.

questions.q: Chat history survived a restart. Is that enough?
questions.a: Not if flags like already_paid died. You will double-write.

questions.q: In-memory saver in a demo — what do you write in the table?
questions.a: “Not production persistence.”

questions.q: You added Redis yourself. Whose persistence is it?
questions.a: Yours. The kit did not provide the row.

multi-agent-support.explain:
## What it is

Frameworks support multi-agent designs in different ways:

- **Graph frameworks**: agents as nodes or subgraphs; supervisors, swarms and hand-offs via edges.
- **Handoff SDKs**: agents transfer control; agents can also be tools.
- **Role/team frameworks**: crews/teams with a leader or process type.
- **Workflow agents** (ADK style): sequential, parallel, loop compositions plus LLM-driven delegation.

Evaluate: how is state shared between agents; can workers run in parallel; how are failures isolated; can I trace across agents with one run id; are there built-in patterns (supervisor, router); and does it speak A2A for remote agents.

Whatever the framework, the design rules from earlier modules still apply: clear briefs, typed outputs, caps, and justify each added agent with evals.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Kits differ: first-class teams, handoffs, or “roll your own.” The capstone row is what you actually used and whether it gave you contracts or just extra prompts.

Do not invent a crew to fill the row.

## How it works + one small example

If you needed two specialists, use the kit’s primitive (handoff, team, graph nodes) and note the contract. If you did not need them, write “not used; one agent sufficed” — that is a valid, strong row.

## Failure modes

1. **A ceremonial second agent.**

2. **No contract on a kit “team.”**

3. **Leaving the row blank.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I use a kit’s multi-agent primitive only when a bake-off needs it, and I note whether it gave me a contract. “Not used” is a valid row.

## A concrete walk-through

You needed no crew. The table says “not used; one agent + tools.” A second student added four roles and lost the eval. You both learned.

## Interview follow-up

They pressure you to add agents. Point at the bake-off.

## What I would measure

Agents used, contract-valid hops, eval vs one-agent.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Agents used, contract-valid hops, eval vs one-agent. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Use the primitive only if needed. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I use a kit’s multi-agent primitive only when a bake-off needs it, and I note whether it gave me a contract. “Not used” is a valid row. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They pressure you to add agents. Point at the bake-off. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Note contracts vs extra prompts.

## What would change my mind

Kits differ: first-class teams, handoffs, or “roll your own.” The capstone row is what you actually used and whether it gave you contracts or just extra prompts. Do not invent a crew to fill the row. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: “Not used” is a valid comparison row. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

questions.a: Whether state is shared or passed explicitly, how concurrent writes merge, how large artifacts pass by reference, and whether a single trace spans all agents.

questions.q: Remote partner agents must collaborate with yours. What framework feature helps?
questions.a: Support for an agent-to-agent protocol such as A2A (and MCP for tools), so remote agents are discoverable and callable without custom glue.

questions.a: “Not used; one agent + tools.” That is a legitimate comparison.

questions.a: It adds hops and can lose the eval you already won.

tool-integrations.explain:
## What it is

Tools are how agents act. Compare how frameworks define and connect them.

- **Plain functions** with type hints/docstrings converted to schemas (most frameworks).
- **Prebuilt toolkits** (search, code execution, databases).
- **MCP servers** consumed as tools, which makes tools reusable across frameworks.
- **Agents as tools**.
- **Framework-specific wrappers** (watch for lock-in).

Things that matter: schema quality (clear names, descriptions, typed arguments), error handling returned to the model in a useful form, timeouts, auth and secret handling, parallel tool calls, and permission gating for risky tools.

Advice: write tools once as framework-neutral functions or MCP servers and adapt them thinly, so swapping frameworks is cheap.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

How you attach tools: plain functions, OpenAPI, MCP, vendor wrappers. The capstone prefers portable functions/MCP so the comparison is about orchestration, not about rewriting tools four times.

## How it works + one small example

One tool module imported by every port. If a kit demands a wrapper, write a 5-line adapter. Note MCP support as a bonus, not a requirement for the graded path.

## Failure modes

1. **Four copies of `lookup_customer`.**

2. **A wrapper that hides the schema.**

3. **Tools that only work inside one kit’s decorator.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep tools portable — functions or MCP — and write thin adapters. I do not rewrite the catalogue per framework.

## A concrete walk-through

`tools.py` is imported by the loop, the graph, and the SDK. The table’s tool row is “adapter, 5–10 lines.” A classmate rewrote tools thrice and could not finish.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about hosted tool stores. Fine, if the schema still exits to your eval.

## What I would measure

Copies of each tool, adapter line count, schema visible in traces.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Copies of each tool, adapter line count, schema visible in traces. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Prefer portable functions or MCP. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I keep tools portable — functions or MCP — and write thin adapters. I do not rewrite the catalogue per framework. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about hosted tool stores. Fine, if the schema still exits to your eval. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Thin adapters per kit.

## What would change my mind

How you attach tools: plain functions, OpenAPI, MCP, vendor wrappers. The capstone prefers portable functions/MCP so the comparison is about orchestration, not about rewriting tools four times. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Do not fork the catalogue. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

Thin adapters per kit.

questions.q: Why are MCP-based tools attractive across frameworks?
questions.a: They are defined once as a server and consumed by any MCP-capable framework, avoiding rewriting integrations and reducing lock-in.

questions.q: A tool returns a stack trace on failure and the agent loops. Fix?
questions.a: Return a concise structured error with a hint about what to change, distinguish retryable from permanent errors, and cap retries so the model does not repeat the same call.

questions.q: How should tools be shared across framework ports?
questions.a: One module of plain functions or MCP servers plus thin adapters.

questions.q: A decorator hides the JSON schema. Risk?
questions.a: You cannot reuse or eval argument validity outside the kit.

questions.q: Is MCP required for the capstone?
questions.a: No. It is a plus if you already have a server. Portability is the requirement.

questions.q: What is a bad tool row in the table?
questions.a: “Rewrote all tools for each framework.”

mcp-a2a-support.explain:
## What it is

**MCP** connects agents to tools and data; **A2A** connects agents to other agents. Many frameworks now support one or both, but depth varies.

**MCP support to check**: act as an MCP client (consume servers), transports supported, auth handling, tool filtering and approvals, and ability to expose your own agent's tools as an MCP server.

**A2A support to check**: publish an agent card, receive and send tasks, streaming and long-running task status, auth between agents.

Practical stance: use MCP when an existing server saves you integration work; use A2A when delegating to autonomous remote agents. Treat remote tool and agent output as untrusted, apply permissions, and verify current specs and framework versions since both protocols are evolving.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

MCP and A2A support is a comparison axis: can the kit attach MCP servers, and can it talk A2A to foreign agents? Check current docs. Do not claim support you did not run.

Capstone: one MCP server you already built is enough to fill the MCP cell.

## How it works + one small example

Connect the capstone agent to your helpdesk MCP server if the kit can. If not, write “adapter not first-class.” For A2A, only fill the cell if you actually delegated to another agent. “Docs mention A2A” is a footnote, not a tick.

## Failure modes

1. **Ticking both from a landing page.**

2. **Confusing MCP with A2A in the table.**

3. **Connecting an untrusted community server for a tick.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I tick MCP/A2A only if I ran them. MCP is tools; A2A is foreign agents. A landing page is not a cell in my table.

## A concrete walk-through

LangGraph-side: you attach MCP. SDK-side: you wrap the same tools as functions. A2A: not run; cell says “not exercised.” That honesty scores.

## Interview follow-up

They ask why A2A is empty. Because you had no foreign agent. Correct.

## What I would measure

Cells backed by a run vs cells backed by a blog.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Cells backed by a run vs cells backed by a blog. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Tick only what you ran. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I tick MCP/A2A only if I ran them. MCP is tools; A2A is foreign agents. A landing page is not a cell in my table. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask why A2A is empty. Because you had no foreign agent. Correct. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: MCP ≠ A2A.

## What would change my mind

MCP and A2A support is a comparison axis: can the kit attach MCP servers, and can it talk A2A to foreign agents? Check current docs. Do not claim support you did not run. Capstone: one MCP server you already built is enough to fill the MCP cell. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: One first-party MCP server is enough. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

questions.q: What would you verify when a framework claims MCP support?
questions.a: That it works as an MCP client over the transports you need, handles auth, allows filtering and approval of tools, and optionally can expose your tools as a server.

questions.q: A third-party MCP server's tool descriptions contain instructions. Risk and response?
questions.a: Tool metadata and outputs can carry prompt injection. Review servers before use, restrict exposed tools, require approval for risky actions, and treat returned content as data.

questions.q: How should the MCP/A2A row be filled?
questions.a: Only for what you actually ran. MCP is tool servers; A2A is foreign agents.

debugging-observability.explain:
## What it is

Agents fail in ways unit tests miss, so observability is a selection criterion.

**Look for**
- **Traces** showing every model call, prompt, tool call, arguments, results, latency and tokens, grouped by run.
- **OpenTelemetry** export or integrations with tracing platforms (LangSmith, Langfuse, Arize, others).
- **Replay / fork** from a step with modified state.
- A **dev UI** to chat and inspect.
- **Eval hooks** to score runs and datasets from production traces.
- **Cost attribution** per step, user and feature.

Without these you debug by print statements. In production, sample traces, redact PII, alert on step-count and cost anomalies, and link user feedback to traces so failures become eval cases.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Can you see steps, state, tool args, and replay? That is the observability row. A pretty UI that hides call ids loses to a JSON trace you can grep.

The capstone needs one story: “I found the bug in the trace.”

## How it works + one small example

For each kit: dump a trace, find a call id, find a state key. Note spans vs checkpoints. If you cannot get args out, the row is weak.

Keep traces redacted in the write-up.

## Failure modes

1. **Screenshots of a UI with no call id.**

2. **Traces full of secrets in the repo.**

3. **No bug-found-via-trace story.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Observability is whether I can grep a call id and a state key and fix a bug from that. I do not commit secrets in traces.

## A concrete walk-through

You catch a wrong id in a span, fix the brief, and paste a redacted snippet in the report. That paragraph is the row.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about OpenTelemetry. Fine if it actually has the fields you need.

## What I would measure

Time-to-find a call id, bugs fixed from traces, secret scans on committed logs.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Time-to-find a call id, bugs fixed from traces, secret scans on committed logs. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Need steps, args, state keys, replay if possible. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Observability is whether I can grep a call id and a state key and fix a bug from that. I do not commit secrets in traces. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about OpenTelemetry. Fine if it actually has the fields you need. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: A UI without ids is weak.

## What would change my mind

Can you see steps, state, tool args, and replay? That is the observability row. A pretty UI that hides call ids loses to a JSON trace you can grep. The capstone needs one story: “I found the bug in the trace.” I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: One trace-driven fix in the write-up. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

questions.q: Which observability features matter most for agents?
questions.a: Per-run traces of every model and tool call with inputs, outputs, latency and tokens, replay/fork, cost attribution, and the ability to turn traces into eval datasets.

questions.q: How do you catch a regression where agents suddenly take 3x more steps?
questions.a: Monitor step count and cost per run in traces, alert on shifts, compare traces before and after the prompt or model change, and run evals before rollout.

deployment.explain:
## What it is

Deployment options differ in effort and control.

- **Self-hosted container** (FastAPI/Node + Docker) on Cloud Run, ECS, Kubernetes or a VM: most control.
- **Serverless functions**: fine for short runs, but timeouts and cold starts hurt long agents; use queues for long jobs.
- **Managed agent platforms** (cloud vendor runtimes, framework-hosted services): less ops, more lock-in.
- **Workers + queue** for background runs, with a streaming gateway.

Checklist: durable state store, secrets management, auth, rate limits and budgets, health checks, graceful shutdown (finish or checkpoint in-flight runs), versioned prompts and graph, canary/rollback, and tracing. Streaming responses need infrastructure that supports SSE/WebSockets and long timeouts.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Deployment is how a stranger (or you next week) runs the agent: container, documented env, health, timeout. Compare kits on what they package versus what you had to invent.

A README-only deploy is still a deploy if it works twice.

## How it works + one small example

Run the agent on a second machine or a container. Note: env vars, ports, persistence dependency, how to pass a thread id. That is the row.

If a kit deploys to a cloud in one command, try it once and write the catch (lock-in, region, cost).

## Failure modes

1. **Works on my laptop only.**

2. **Secrets in the image.**

3. **No health or timeout.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Deployment in the table is “I ran it somewhere else with documented env, a timeout and no secrets in the image.” Cloud one-clicks get a catch noted.

## A concrete walk-through

Docker run on a spare laptop hits `/health` and `/runs`. The graph needs Postgres — you document it. The SDK version is stateless — you document that too.

## Interview follow-up

They ask Kubernetes. You name it as packaging, not as the lesson.

## What I would measure

Second-environment success, secrets in images (0), documented deps.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Second-environment success, secrets in images (0), documented deps. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Second environment is the test. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Deployment in the table is “I ran it somewhere else with documented env, a timeout and no secrets in the image.” Cloud one-clicks get a catch noted. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask Kubernetes. You name it as packaging, not as the lesson. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Document env, deps, thread id.

No secrets in images.
Timeout and health belong.

Container, serverless, managed platform or workers + queue
