questions.q: Why do long agent runs fit badly in plain serverless request handlers?
questions.a: Execution time limits and cold starts can cut a run mid-way; use background workers/queues with checkpointing and stream progress separately.

questions.q: During a deploy, in-flight runs are killed. How do you handle it?
questions.a: Checkpoint state each step and make steps idempotent so workers resume the run after restart; drain gracefully on shutdown and keep graph and prompt versions compatible with live runs.

questions.q: What counts as a real deploy in the capstone?
questions.a: A second environment or container with documented env, a timeout, and no baked secrets.

questions.q: The kit one-clicks to a vendor cloud. What do you write?
questions.a: The steps, the region/cost/lock-in catch, and that you actually ran it.

questions.q: Laptop-only — what is the row?
questions.a: Not deployed. Say so.

questions.q: Why document the persistence dependency?
questions.a: A graph that needs Postgres will fail in an empty container. That is a deploy bug.

vendor-model-flexibility.explain:
## What it is

Can you switch models or providers without rewriting the agent? Reasons to care: cost, outages, quality changes, data-residency rules and negotiating leverage.

**Check**
- Native support for multiple providers, or via an adapter layer or gateway (e.g. LiteLLM-style routing).
- Handling of provider differences: tool-call formats, structured output, streaming, context sizes, reasoning options.
- Ability to set different models per agent or step (cheap router, strong planner).
- Fallback on errors or rate limits.

**Caveat**: swapping a model is not free. Prompts tuned for one model may regress on another, so keep an **eval set** and rerun on every switch. Vendor-owned frameworks may favour their own models and hosted tools; check which features work only with the vendor's models.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

Can you swap the model or the provider without rewriting the agent? Flexibility is a wrapper around `complete()` plus evals. Kits that bake one vendor into every tool hurt this row.

The capstone should run at least two model ids on the same eval.

## How it works + one small example

Put the model id in config. Run the eval on a cheap and a strong model. If a kit cannot point at another provider, write the gap. Do not confuse “supports OpenAI-compatible” with “we tried it.”

## Failure modes

1. **Hard-coded model strings in five files.**

2. **Claiming flexibility you did not run.**

3. **Switching models with no eval.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

I keep the model id in config and I run the same eval on two ids. Flexibility I did not exercise is a footnote, not a tick.

## A concrete walk-through

You switch the capstone from a strong model to a cheap one; quality drops 6 points on tool use. That number is the row, and it is why you did not silently switch in prod.

## Interview follow-up

They ask about local models. Same rule: config + eval, or you did not do it.

## What I would measure

Model ids exercised, files that hard-code a vendor, eval deltas.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Model ids exercised, files that hard-code a vendor, eval deltas. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Model id in config. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: I keep the model id in config and I run the same eval on two ids. Flexibility I did not exercise is a footnote, not a tick. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask about local models. Same rule: config + eval, or you did not do it. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: Same eval on at least two ids.

Same eval on at least two ids.
Do not hard-code vendors in tools.
“Compatible” ≠ “we ran it.”
A silent model swap is a product incident.

Look for provider adapters, per-step models and fallbacks

questions.q: Why keep an eval set when you make an agent model-agnostic?
questions.a: Prompts and tool use behave differently across models, so each switch needs regression measurement to confirm quality, cost and reliability.

questions.q: A vendor framework offers a hosted tool that only works with its own models. What do you weigh?
questions.a: The convenience against lock-in and portability: whether you can replace it with a model-neutral tool, the cost of migration, and how critical the feature is.

questions.q: An agent is switched to a cheaper model and quality drops silently. What would have caught it?
questions.a: A regression eval set run on every model change.

questions.q: How do you score vendor/model flexibility?
questions.a: By actually running two ids and by how few files hard-code a vendor.

questions.q: The kit says OpenAI-compatible. Do you tick the row?
questions.a: Not until you pointed it at a second endpoint and ran the eval.

questions.q: Where does the model id live?
questions.a: In config, not in five tool files.

budgets-in-the-capstone.explain:
## What it is

**Step, time and cost limits are part of the demo, not extras.** A capstone without numbers is a toy. Show the config, a forced-stop, and a partial artefact. Interviewers will ask what happens at the cap; you should be able to trigger it live.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is how you prove you heard Level 5. Many students ship a crew with no cap. The ones who pass have a config file and a screenshot of a budget stop.

## How it works + one small example

`max_steps`, `max_seconds`, `max_usd` in the repo. A script that forces a loop and shows the stop. The README says how to change the numbers. The write-up includes p95 from your eval versus the cap.

## Failure modes

1. **Caps only in a slide.**

2. **A cap you never triggered.**

3. **No partial artefact on stop.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

The demo includes budgets. I can trigger a stop and show a partial. Caps are in config, not in a slide.

## A concrete walk-through

You run `make blow-the-cap` in the review. The agent stops at 12 steps with a memo. The reviewer ticks the box.

## Interview follow-up

They ask to raise the cap live. You change config and rerun. That is the point.

## What I would measure

Forced-stop demo works, config exists, p95 < cap on the happy path.

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Forced-stop demo works, config exists, p95 < cap on the happy path. That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Caps are in the repo config. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: The demo includes budgets. I can trigger a stop and show a partial. Caps are in config, not in a slide. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask to raise the cap live. You change config and rerun. That is the point. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: You can trigger a stop in the demo.

## What would change my mind

This is how you prove you heard Level 5. Many students ship a crew with no cap. The ones who pass have a config file and a screenshot of a budget stop. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Partial artefact on stop. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.

## How this shows up in a log

In a real trace I want to see the decision, the evidence, and the stop. A reviewer should be able to replay this walk-through from the log: You run `make blow-the-cap` in the review. The agent stops at 12 steps with a memo. The reviewer ticks the box. If the log cannot support that story, the feature is not observable yet. I also want the cheap how-it-works sketch nearby so a new teammate can implement the same check: `max_steps`, `max_seconds`, `max_usd` in the repo. A script that forces a loop and shows the stop. The README says how to change the numbers. The write-up includes p95 from your eval versus the cap.
keyPoints: Caps are in the repo config.
You can trigger a stop in the demo.
Partial artefact on stop.
p95 from eval versus cap is in the write-up.
Slides are not enforcement.
Changing the number is a config edit.

questions.q: What budgets belong in the capstone demo?
questions.a: Step, time and cost/token limits in config, with a forced-stop you can show.

questions.q: The reviewer asks what happens at the cap. What do you show?
questions.a: A live or recorded stop with a partial artefact and a reason.

questions.q: Caps in the README only — verdict?
questions.a: Not part of the demo. Put them in the worker config.

questions.q: Why show p95 versus the cap?
questions.a: To prove the happy path fits and the cap is for tails, not for everyday kills.

questions.q: Who can change the number in the review?
questions.a: You, by editing config — that is the interface.

a-replayable-trace.explain:
## What it is

**You should be able to explain every tool call from the log.** A replayable trace has thread id, steps, tool names, redacted args, results sizes, decisions, and timestamps. You can sit in a review and narrate the run without opening the model’s mind.

If you cannot replay, you cannot debug or defend.

## Why it matters on the job and in an interview

This is the capstone closer. Interviewers will pick a run and ask “why this call?” The log answers. On the job this is also how you write the incident doc.

## How it works + one small example

Store a JSONL or use the kit’s trace export. Fields: `thread, step, node, tool, arg_hash, result_tokens, error, decision`. Practise narrating one good and one bad run.

Redact before you put traces in the repo. A replay script that re-executes writes is dangerous; replay means “read the log,” not “pay twice.”

## Failure modes

1. **Traces that omit tool names.**

2. **Replaying writes in a script.**

3. **Unredacted traces in git.**

## What you would say in 30 seconds

Every tool call is in a redacted log I can narrate. Replay means read, not re-pay. If I cannot explain a call, the trace is incomplete.

## A concrete walk-through

In the review you open run `a3f2` and walk six calls. The extra search is an identical-call miss you then fix. The trace was the product.

## Interview follow-up

They ask for a video of thoughts. You refuse and offer the log.

## What I would measure

Percent of runs with complete traces, review time to explain a call, secrets in git (0).

## How I would implement this tomorrow

I would not start by rewriting a prompt. I would start by making one check real. The first numbers I would collect are: Percent of runs with complete traces, review time to explain a call, secrets in git (0). That means a small fixture, a checker that can fail on purpose, and a stored score so tomorrow's change has a baseline. The first key point I would encode as a test is: Trace fields: thread, step, tool, arg hash, result size, error, decision. If I cannot fail a run on purpose, I do not yet have an implementation — I have a story.

## Common interview traps

The cheap answer is a vendor name or a slogan. The answer I want is a mechanism plus a fail. My thirty-second line is: Every tool call is in a redacted log I can narrate. Replay means read, not re-pay. If I cannot explain a call, the trace is incomplete. If they ask the obvious follow-up I continue with: They ask for a video of thoughts. You refuse and offer the log. I will not invent a metric I cannot compute on a napkin fixture. A second point I will say out loud: You can narrate any run.

## What would change my mind

This is the capstone closer. Interviewers will pick a run and ask “why this call?” The log answers. On the job this is also how you write the incident doc. I change the design when a held-out slice moves, not when a demo is prettier. A third point that would force a redesign is: Replay = read the log, not re-execute writes. One counter-example that lives in the golden set beats a week of vibe testing.
keyPoints: Trace fields: thread, step, tool, arg hash, result size, error, decision.
You can narrate any run.
Replay = read the log, not re-execute writes.
Redact before commit.
Missing tool names = incomplete.
The trace is a capstone artefact.

questions.q: What makes a trace replayable for a review?
questions.a: A complete, redacted log of steps and tool calls you can narrate without re-executing writes.

questions.q: Why not re-run the write tools to “replay”?
questions.a: You will double-pay or double-ticket. Replay is reading the log.

questions.q: Which fields are mandatory?
questions.a: Thread, step, tool name, arg hash, result size or error, decision/next.

questions.q: A run you cannot explain — what is missing?
questions.a: The trace. Fix the logger before you add features.

questions.q: May traces live in git?
questions.a: Only redacted fixtures. Not live user runs.
